articles.title: The Importance of Great Follow Up

articles.content:
Not all Vision Meetings are created equal. Some produce a steady stream of committed Core Group members. Others leave you wondering why attendance keeps dropping and commitments stay flat.

The difference comes down to eight critical success factors. Master these, and your Vision Meetings become a powerful engine for growth. Neglect them, and you'll spin your wheels wondering what went wrong.

---

## 1. Great Attendance

The first critical factor is simple: people need to show up. A Vision Meeting with the right people in attendance has completely different energy than one with empty chairs.

**Who owns this responsibility?**

Both the Core Group and the Senior Pastor own the responsibility of inviting and delivering a steady stream of new people. This cannot be delegated to one person or left to chance.

<Callout type="important">
  Building the Core Group is job number one for every Core Group member. If your existing members aren't consistently bringing new people, your growth will plateau.
</Callout>

**What "great attendance" looks like:**

- Core Group members each bring at least one new person or couple
- Members leverage their networks, not just the Senior Pastor's
- A mix of brand new faces and people who've attended before
- People who are genuinely seeking, not just doing a favor

The people you attract must have the potential to become **COMMITTED, COMPELLED, CONTAGIOUS, and COURAGEOUS**. Quality matters as much as quantity.

---

## 2. An Acceptable Location

Where you hold your Vision Meeting shapes how people perceive the church you're planting. A poor location creates unnecessary barriers.

**What makes a location acceptable:**

- **Easy to find** — Clear directions, good signage, not confusing to navigate
- **Welcoming atmosphere** — Clean, comfortable, appropriately sized for your group
- **Conducive for both mingling and hearing** — Space for fellowship before/after and good acoustics for the presentation
- **Free from distractions** — No competing noise, interruptions, or awkward arrangements

<Callout type="tip">
  Scout your location in advance. Sit where attendees will sit. Can you hear clearly? Is the seating comfortable? Is the space too big (feels empty) or too small (feels cramped)?
</Callout>

**Common location options:**

- Living rooms (intimate, personal)
- Church fellowship halls (neutral, professional)
- Community center meeting rooms (accessible, affordable)
- Restaurant private rooms (convenient, casual)

Match your location to the size and formality of the meeting you're planning.

---

## 3. Great Logistics

Details matter. When logistics are handled poorly, people notice. When they're handled well, people don't notice—but they feel comfortable and cared for.

**Logistics checklist:**

- [ ] Room ready before the first guest arrives
- [ ] AV equipment set up and tested (no fumbling with technology during the meeting)
- [ ] Seating arranged appropriately
- [ ] Signage and banners properly placed
- [ ] Sign-in station visible and accessible
- [ ] Nametags prepared
- [ ] Handouts organized and ready
- [ ] Food and drinks prepared (if applicable)
- [ ] Greeters trained and positioned

**The 30-minute rule:** Arrive at least 30 minutes before the scheduled start time. Everything should be ready so you can focus on greeting people, not scrambling with setup.

---

## 4. A Clear Agenda

Winging it communicates that you haven't thought carefully about the meeting. A clear agenda communicates professionalism and respect for people's time.

**Your agenda should be:**

- Planned out in detail and written down
- Designed to start on time and end on time
- Balanced with sufficient time for introduction, presentation, Q&A, and close

| Element | Time Allocation |
|---------|-----------------|
| Meet and Greet, Sign-in | 15 minutes |
| Ice Breaker, Introduction | 15 minutes |
| Presentation | 30 minutes |
| Q&A | 30 minutes |
| Strong Close | 15 minutes |
| Fellowship/Food | 30 minutes |

<Callout type="tip">
  Practice your presentation with a timer. Know exactly how long each section takes so you can adjust in real-time without rushing or dragging.
</Callout>

---

## 5. A Great Vibe

The atmosphere of your Vision Meeting tells people what your church will feel like. If the meeting feels cold and formal, they'll expect a cold and formal church. If it feels warm and welcoming, they'll expect the same on Sunday mornings.

**Creating the right vibe:**

- **Warm and inviting** — Smile. Make eye contact. Use people's names.
- **Sense of community** — Core Group members should mingle with guests, not cluster together
- **Spirit of genuine friendliness** — Not salesy enthusiasm, but authentic warmth
- **Contagious enthusiasm** — Your excitement about the vision should be evident without being forced

**The temperature check:** After your next Vision Meeting, ask yourself: Would I want to come back based on how I was treated tonight?

---

## 6. A Compelling Message

This is the heart of the Vision Meeting. You're not just sharing information—you're casting a vision that could change people's lives.

**Elements of a compelling message:**

- **Vision presented clearly** — People should understand what you're trying to accomplish
- **Vision presented compellingly** — People should feel drawn to be part of it
- **Clear picture** — Use visual aids (PowerPoint, videos) effectively
- **Strong communication skills** — Practice until your delivery is confident and engaging
- **Concise** — Don't ramble. Every word should serve a purpose.

<Callout type="insight">
  The goal isn't to tell people everything about the church. The goal is to tell them enough that they want to learn more and consider joining.
</Callout>

**What to include:**

- Your personal story and calling
- The distinctives and values of the church
- The vision for what God will accomplish
- Why this church, in this place, at this time

---

## 7. A Strong Close

How you end the meeting matters as much as how you begin it. A weak close wastes the momentum you've built. A strong close moves people toward commitment.

**Components of a strong close:**

- **Motivate** — Remind people why this matters and what's at stake
- **Call the right people** — Be clear about who you're looking for
- **Genuine and non-manipulative** — Don't pressure; invite
- **Clear call to action** — What specifically do you want them to do next?

**The ask:** Don't be afraid to ask people to commit. Many people are waiting to be asked. A direct, genuine invitation often makes the difference between "interested" and "committed."

<Callout type="warning">
  A strong close is not manipulative or high-pressure. It's clear, direct, and honest. People should feel invited, not trapped.
</Callout>

---

## 8. Clear Next Steps

People who leave your Vision Meeting unsure of what to do next will often do nothing. Remove that barrier by making the next steps crystal clear.

**Before the meeting ends:**

- Dates for next meetings, trainings, and get-togethers are determined
- Calendar is in writing and ready to distribute
- Specific actions are assigned (e.g., "Fill out the response card," "Attend the follow-up coffee")
- Contact information has been collected from everyone

**The calendar test:** Can everyone who attended tell a friend exactly what happens next and when? If not, your next steps weren't clear enough.

---

## Putting It All Together

These eight factors work together. Great attendance means nothing if the message isn't compelling. A compelling message is wasted if there's no clear next step. Strong logistics set the stage for everything else.

**Self-assessment after each Vision Meeting:**

| Factor | Rating (1-5) | Notes for Improvement |
|--------|--------------|----------------------|
| Great Attendance | | |
| Acceptable Location | | |
| Great Logistics | | |
| Clear Agenda | | |
| Great Vibe | | |
| Compelling Message | | |
| Strong Close | | |
| Clear Next Steps | | |

Review this after every Vision Meeting. Identify your weakest area and focus on improving it for the next meeting.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Whatever you do, do your work heartily, as for the Lord rather than for men,"* — Colossians 3:23 (LSB)
</Callout>

Excellence in Vision Meetings isn't about impressing people—it's about stewarding well the opportunity God has given you to share His vision.
articles.excerpt: The eight factors that determine whether your Vision Meetings will effectively build your Core Group.
articles.title: 8 Critical Success Factors for Vision Meetings

articles.content:
The most prepared Vision Meeting accomplishes nothing with empty chairs. Your ability to consistently fill those chairs with the right people will determine how quickly your Core Group grows.

This guide covers proven strategies for inviting people effectively.

---

## The Cardinal Principle

Before diving into tactics, understand the foundational principle that makes everything else work:

**The Core Group needs to own the responsibility with the Senior Pastor in building the Core Group numerically. Building the Core Group is job number one for every Core Group member.**

This isn't optional. If only the Senior Pastor is inviting people, growth will plateau. When every Core Group member actively invites, growth compounds.

<Callout type="important">
  Every member of the Core Group must feel the weight of this responsibility. They're not just attending—they're building. If they're not inviting, they're not fully engaged.
</Callout>

---

## The Ask, Seek, Knock Approach

This biblical framework provides the foundation for your invitation strategy.

### Ask the Lord of Harvest

Before you ask anyone to attend, ask God to raise up workers for the harvest.

- Pray specifically for names and faces to come to mind
- Ask God to prepare hearts before you approach them
- Seek wisdom about timing and approach
- Trust that God is already at work drawing people

### Seek Them Out

Actively look for potential Core Group members in your sphere of influence:

- **Friends** — People you already have relationship with
- **Acquaintances** — People you know but haven't gone deep with
- **Connections of connections** — Friends of friends who might be interested
- **New relationships** — Intentionally build relationships with potential members

### Knock and Invite

Once you've identified potential members, extend a clear invitation:

- Be direct about what you're inviting them to
- Explain why you think they'd be a good fit
- Make it easy for them to say yes (or no)
- Follow up if they express interest

---

## Invitation Methods Ranked by Effectiveness

Not all invitations are created equal. Here's how different methods stack up:

| Method | Effectiveness | Best For |
|--------|---------------|----------|
| **Personal conversation** | Highest | People you know well |
| **Phone call** | High | Personal contacts, follow-up |
| **Personal text/message** | Medium-High | Initial outreach, reminders |
| **Personalized email** | Medium | Detailed information, scheduling |
| **Social media post** | Low-Medium | Broad awareness, new networks |
| **Mass email blast** | Low | Announcements, not recruitment |

<Callout type="insight">
  The more personal the invitation, the more likely someone is to attend. A face-to-face conversation is worth more than 100 social media posts.
</Callout>

---

## Having the Conversation

When you identify someone to invite, here's how to approach the conversation:

### The Framework

1. **Share your excitement** — Let your enthusiasm show
2. **Explain the opportunity** — What the church plant is and why it matters
3. **Make the connection** — Why you thought of them specifically
4. **Extend the invitation** — Clearly ask them to attend
5. **Handle objections** — Address concerns graciously
6. **Confirm next steps** — Get a commitment or clear follow-up

### Sample Scripts

**For someone you know well:**

*"Hey, I wanted to tell you about something I'm really excited about. I'm part of planting a new church, and we're looking for people who want to be part of building something from the ground up. Honestly, you were one of the first people I thought of. Would you come to our next Vision Meeting on [date] to hear more about it?"*

**For an acquaintance:**

*"I've been meaning to reach out to you. I'm involved in starting a new church in [area], and we're gathering people who are passionate about making a difference. I don't know if this is on your radar at all, but would you be open to coming to hear more about what we're doing?"*

**For someone referred to you:**

*"[Mutual friend] mentioned that you might be interested in what we're building. We're planting a new church and looking for people who want to be part of the Core Group. Could I tell you more about it over coffee, or would you want to come to our next gathering?"*

---

## Setting Invitation Goals

Vague commitments produce vague results. Set specific goals for your Core Group:

### Individual Goals

Each Core Group member should commit to:

- Invite at least **5 people** to every Vision Meeting
- Bring at least **one person or couple** to every meeting
- Have at least **3 invitation conversations** per week

### Group Goals

Track and celebrate as a group:

- Total number of invitations extended
- Total number of first-time attendees
- Conversion rate from invitation to attendance

<Callout type="tip">
  What gets measured gets managed. Track invitation activity and celebrate wins. When someone brings a guest who joins the Core Group, make it a big deal.
</Callout>

---

## Leveraging Your Network

### Direct Network

People you already know personally:

- Friends from work, neighborhood, gym, etc.
- Family members (even distant relatives)
- Former church members or ministry connections
- College friends, old roommates, colleagues

### Indirect Network

People your network knows:

- Ask Core Group members: "Who do you know who might be interested?"
- Ask friends: "Who in your circle is looking for a church?"
- Ask family: "Do you know anyone in [area] who loves Jesus?"

### Expanding Your Network

Intentionally build new relationships:

- Join community groups, clubs, or activities
- Attend local events and get involved
- Volunteer in community organizations
- Build relationships with neighbors you don't know yet

---

## Using Invitation Cards

Physical invitation cards are a powerful tool for several reasons:

- **Tangible reminder** — Harder to forget than a verbal invitation
- **Easy to share** — The invitee can pass it to someone else
- **Professional appearance** — Communicates this is legitimate
- **All the details** — Date, time, location, contact info in one place

### What to Include

- Church name and logo
- "You're Invited to a Vision Meeting"
- Date, time, location
- Brief description (1-2 sentences)
- Your website or QR code
- Contact information

### Distribution Strategy

- Give 5-10 cards to every Core Group member
- Encourage them to always have cards available
- Train them to hand cards out during conversations
- Replenish regularly

---

## Social Media Strategy

Social media can extend your reach beyond your immediate network.

### Effective Approaches

**Personal posts:**
Share your excitement about what you're building. Be authentic, not salesy.

*"I'm so excited about this new church we're planting. If you're in [area] and curious about being part of something new, message me."*

**Event invitations:**
Create Facebook events for Vision Meetings. Invite friends and ask Core Group members to do the same.

**Share stories:**
Post photos and updates from Vision Meetings (with permission). Let people see the energy and community.

### What to Avoid

- Don't spam people with repeated invitations
- Don't make promises you can't keep
- Don't criticize other churches
- Don't be pushy or manipulative

<Callout type="warning">
  Social media reaches many people but converts few. Use it to create awareness and open doors, but don't rely on it for your primary invitation strategy.
</Callout>

---

## Training Your Core Group

Don't assume Core Group members know how to invite effectively. Train them:

### Regular Training Topics

- How to share your personal story and excitement
- How to handle common objections
- How to identify potential Core Group members
- How to follow up after an invitation

### Role Playing

Practice invitation conversations:
- One person plays the inviter, another plays the potential guest
- Work through different scenarios and objections
- Give feedback and coaching
- Build confidence through repetition

### Accountability

Create a rhythm of accountability:
- Weekly check-in: "How many invitation conversations did you have?"
- Monthly review: "Who did you bring this month?"
- Quarterly celebration: "Look how God has grown our group!"

---

## Handling "No" Gracefully

Not everyone will say yes. Handle rejection well:

### In the Moment

- Thank them for considering it
- Don't argue or pressure
- Leave the door open: "If anything changes, let me know"
- Maintain the relationship

### After a "No"

- Don't take it personally
- Don't give up on the relationship
- Circle back in a few months if appropriate
- Ask if they know anyone else who might be interested

<Callout type="insight">
  A "no" today might be a "yes" later. Life circumstances change. Keep the relationship warm, and you may find the door opens in the future.
</Callout>

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Then He said to His disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into His harvest.”"* — Matthew 9:37-38 (LSB)
</Callout>

God is preparing hearts. Your job is to find them, invite them, and welcome them into the work He's doing.

articles.title: Invitation Strategies

articles.content:
Effective Vision Meetings don't happen by accident. They require thoughtful planning, careful preparation, and attention to detail. The good news is that with a solid planning process, you can consistently deliver meetings that move people from interested to committed.

This guide walks you through planning a Vision Meeting from start to finish.

---

## Start with the End in Mind

Before diving into logistics, clarify what you want to accomplish with this specific meeting.

**Questions to answer:**

- What type of meeting is this? (Formal presentation, informal gathering, one-on-one)
- Who is the target audience? (First-timers, people who've attended before, specific network)
- What action do you want people to take afterward?
- How does this meeting fit into your overall rhythm of Vision Meetings?

<Callout type="insight">
  Not every Vision Meeting needs to be a large, formal event. A series of smaller, informal gatherings can be just as effective—sometimes more so—for building genuine relationships and commitment.
</Callout>

---

## Timeline for Planning

### 4 Weeks Out

**Lock down the fundamentals:**

- [ ] Date, time, and duration confirmed
- [ ] Location secured and deposit paid (if required)
- [ ] Basic format decided (formal/informal, size expectations)
- [ ] Core Group members notified and asked to begin inviting

### 2 Weeks Out

**Finalize details:**

- [ ] Agenda written and timed
- [ ] Presentation prepared and practiced
- [ ] AV needs identified and equipment confirmed
- [ ] Food/refreshments planned
- [ ] Printed materials ordered or prepared
- [ ] Greeters and helpers assigned roles

### 1 Week Out

**Confirm everything:**

- [ ] Final attendance estimate from Core Group members
- [ ] Room setup plan finalized
- [ ] All materials printed and organized
- [ ] AV equipment tested at location (if possible)
- [ ] Reminder sent to all confirmed attendees
- [ ] Core Group reminded of their invitation goals

### Day Before

**Final preparations:**

- [ ] All supplies packed and ready
- [ ] Transportation arranged for equipment
- [ ] Final run-through of presentation
- [ ] Weather/traffic considerations addressed
- [ ] Emergency contact list prepared

### Day Of

**Execute with excellence:**

- [ ] Arrive early (30+ minutes before guests)
- [ ] Set up room completely before first arrival
- [ ] Test all AV equipment
- [ ] Brief helpers on their roles
- [ ] Pray together as a team before guests arrive

---

## Choosing Your Format

Different situations call for different formats. Here's guidance on when to use each:

### Large Formal Meeting (25+ people)

**Best for:**
- Reaching new networks beyond your immediate sphere
- Creating momentum and energy
- Launching a new season of Vision Meetings

**Considerations:**
- Requires more planning and resources
- Less personal interaction with each guest
- Higher stakes if things go wrong

### Small Group Setting (8-15 people)

**Best for:**
- Deeper conversations and Q&A
- Building relationships with potential Core Group members
- Following up with people who've attended a larger meeting

**Considerations:**
- More intimate atmosphere
- Easier to manage logistics
- Allows everyone to participate in discussion

### Informal Gathering (2-5 people)

**Best for:**
- Personal invitation from Core Group members
- Answering specific questions
- Gauging interest before inviting to larger meeting

**Considerations:**
- Feels more like a conversation than a presentation
- Can be done at coffee shops, homes, or restaurants
- Lower commitment for potential attendees

<Callout type="tip">
  Mix your formats. Use large meetings to cast broad vision and reach new people. Use small gatherings to deepen relationships and answer questions. Use informal conversations to personally challenge people to commit.
</Callout>

---

## Location Selection

The right location removes barriers and sets the tone. The wrong location creates unnecessary obstacles.

### Evaluation Criteria

| Factor | Questions to Ask |
|--------|------------------|
| **Accessibility** | Is it easy to find? Adequate parking? ADA accessible? |
| **Atmosphere** | Does it feel welcoming? Clean? Appropriate for your brand? |
| **Size** | Right capacity for expected attendance? Not too big or small? |
| **Acoustics** | Can people hear clearly? Background noise manageable? |
| **Cost** | Within budget? What's included vs. extra? |
| **Availability** | Can you get it consistently? Backup options? |

### Common Location Types

**Homes**
- Pros: Intimate, personal, low cost
- Cons: Limited capacity, dependent on host availability

**Church facilities**
- Pros: Appropriate atmosphere, often affordable, good equipment
- Cons: May feel formal, requires relationship with host church

**Community centers**
- Pros: Neutral location, good capacity, professional setting
- Cons: Can feel sterile, may have restrictions

**Restaurants (private rooms)**
- Pros: Convenient, food handled for you
- Cons: Can be noisy, limited control, cost per person

---

## Building Your Agenda

A well-structured agenda keeps your meeting on track and ensures you accomplish your objectives.

### Standard Agenda Template

| Time | Activity | Purpose |
|------|----------|---------|
| 6:00 - 6:30 | Setup | Room ready, AV tested, team briefed |
| 6:45 - 7:00 | Meet and Greet | Sign in, nametags, gather contact info |
| 7:00 - 7:15 | Ice Breaker / Introduction | Connect people, set the tone |
| 7:15 - 7:45 | Presentation | Cast vision, share distinctives |
| 7:45 - 8:15 | Q&A | Address questions, clarify concerns |
| 8:15 - 8:30 | Strong Close | Call to action, next steps |
| 8:30 - 9:00 | Fellowship | Dessert, conversation, relationship building |

<Callout type="warning">
  Respect people's time. Start on time, end on time. If you say the meeting ends at 9:00, end at 9:00. People who stay longer choose to stay; don't hold anyone hostage.
</Callout>

### Adjusting for Format

**For smaller gatherings:**
- Shorten formal presentation
- Increase time for discussion and Q&A
- Make it more conversational

**For larger meetings:**
- Build in more time for logistics (sign-in, seating)
- Consider breakout discussions after presentation
- Plan for coffee/refreshment flow

---

## Preparing Your Message

Your presentation is the centerpiece of the Vision Meeting. It deserves careful preparation.

### Content to Include

1. **Your story** — How God called you to plant this church
2. **The church's distinctives** — What makes this church unique
3. **The vision** — What God wants to accomplish through this church
4. **The invitation** — How people can be part of it

### Presentation Tips

- **Practice out loud** — Reading it and saying it are different skills
- **Time yourself** — Know exactly how long each section takes
- **Use visuals wisely** — PowerPoint supports your message, doesn't replace it
- **Tell stories** — People remember stories more than bullet points
- **Be yourself** — Authenticity matters more than polish

---

## The Invitation Strategy

Great meetings with empty chairs accomplish nothing. You need a strategy for getting people there.

### Core Group Responsibility

Every Core Group member should understand that bringing people to Vision Meetings is a primary responsibility—not an optional extra.

**Set clear expectations:**
- Each member commits to inviting at least 5 people per meeting
- Goal: Each member brings at least one person or couple to every meeting
- Track and celebrate successes

### Invitation Methods

- Personal invitation (most effective)
- Phone calls to personal contacts
- Text messages with meeting details
- Social media posts and shares
- Email to personal networks
- Printed invitation cards to hand out

<Callout type="important">
  Personal invitation is always the most effective method. A text blast might reach more people, but a personal conversation is far more likely to result in attendance.
</Callout>

---

## After the Meeting

Planning doesn't end when the meeting does. Post-meeting activities are crucial for converting attendance into commitment.

### Immediate (within 48 hours)

- [ ] Send thank-you email to all attendees
- [ ] Enter all contact information into database
- [ ] Assign follow-up responsibilities
- [ ] Debrief with Core Group (what worked, what didn't)

### Within One Week

- [ ] Personal follow-up calls with all first-time attendees
- [ ] Schedule one-on-one conversations with interested individuals
- [ ] Update attendance tracking
- [ ] Begin planning next Vision Meeting

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"For which one of you, when he wants to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost to see if he has enough to complete it?"* — Luke 14:28 (LSB)
</Callout>

Good planning honors God by stewarding well the opportunities He gives you. Plan thoroughly, execute excellently, and trust Him for the results.

articles.title: Planning Your Vision Meeting

articles.content:
You've planned the meeting, invited the guests, and prepared your materials. Now it's time to execute. This guide walks you through running an effective Vision Meeting, from the moment you arrive to the last guest leaving.

---

## Arrival and Setup

### Getting There Early

Arrive at least 30 minutes before the scheduled start time. This gives you time to:

- Set up the room without rushing
- Test all technology
- Brief your team
- Collect yourself mentally and spiritually
- Pray over the space and the people coming

<Callout type="important">
  If you're rushing when the first guest arrives, you've already lost. Early arrival is non-negotiable.
</Callout>

### Room Setup Checklist

Work systematically through setup:

- [ ] Seating arranged (appropriate for expected attendance)
- [ ] Banners and signage positioned
- [ ] Sign-in table ready near entrance
- [ ] Name tags and pens laid out
- [ ] Handouts organized and accessible
- [ ] Projector/screen tested and focused
- [ ] Audio tested from multiple seats
- [ ] Presentation loaded and cued
- [ ] Food/refreshments ready (if applicable)
- [ ] Temperature comfortable

### Team Briefing

Gather your Core Group team for a quick briefing:

1. **Review assignments** — Who's greeting? Who's handling sign-in? Who's working the room?
2. **Set expectations** — "Let's make sure every guest feels welcomed and engaged"
3. **Address any concerns** — Last-minute questions or issues
4. **Pray together** — Ask God to work through this gathering

---

## As Guests Arrive

The first few minutes shape the entire experience. Make them count.

### The Greeting Station

Position your warmest, most welcoming people at the door:

- Greet everyone by name if you know them
- Introduce yourself if you don't
- Direct them to sign-in
- Offer a name tag
- Hand them any materials
- Introduce them to someone in the room

### Sign-In Process

Make sign-in quick and painless:

- Friendly person manning the table (not buried in paperwork)
- Clear instructions: "Just your name, email, and phone number"
- Pen that works
- Brief explanation: "We'll use this to follow up with more information"

### Working the Room

Core Group members should be mingling, not clustering:

- Each Core Group member engages with at least one guest
- Make introductions: "Have you met Sarah? Sarah, this is John—he's in real estate too."
- Keep conversations light: "How do you know [inviter]?" "What brought you out tonight?"
- Watch for wallflowers and engage them

<Callout type="tip">
  Assign specific Core Group members to be "floaters" whose only job is to engage anyone who looks disconnected. No guest should feel invisible.
</Callout>

---

## Opening the Meeting

Transition from mingling to the formal meeting with intentionality.

### The Call to Attention

- Give a 2-minute warning: "We'll get started in a couple minutes, grab your seat"
- Dim the lights slightly or adjust the room
- Move to the front and wait for attention
- Begin with warmth: "Good evening, everyone. Thank you for being here."

### The Welcome

Keep it brief but warm:

- Thank people for coming
- Acknowledge how busy everyone is
- Express genuine excitement about the gathering
- Preview what's coming: "Tonight you'll hear about what we're building and how you might be part of it"

### The Ice Breaker

Execute your planned ice breaker with energy:

- Give clear instructions
- Model participation if needed
- Keep it moving (don't let it drag)
- Laugh and be human

Example: "Let's go around the room. Share your name and one thing you're passionate about outside of work. I'll start—I'm John, and I'm passionate about hiking in the mountains."

---

## Delivering Your Presentation

This is the heart of the meeting. Everything has built to this moment.

### Managing Your Nerves

Everyone gets nervous. Channel it productively:

- Take a deep breath before you begin
- Remember: these people want you to succeed
- Focus on serving them, not impressing them
- Trust your preparation

### Presentation Mechanics

**Eye contact:**
- Look at individuals, not the room in general
- Sweep the room, connecting with different sections
- Don't stare at your slides or notes

**Voice:**
- Speak louder than feels natural
- Vary your tone and pace
- Pause for emphasis
- Don't rush

**Movement:**
- Use the space (don't stand frozen)
- Move toward people when making key points
- Gesture naturally
- Don't pace nervously

**Slides:**
- Advance slides smoothly (practice with clicker)
- Don't read slides verbatim
- Use slides to support, not replace, your message
- Look at the audience, not the screen

<Callout type="insight">
  The most compelling presentations feel like conversations, not lectures. You're sharing something you care deeply about with people you want to join you. Let that genuine enthusiasm come through.
</Callout>

### Handling Disruptions

Things happen. Handle them gracefully:

**Technology failure:**
- Stay calm: "Technology keeping us humble!"
- Pivot to your backup plan
- Keep going without missing a beat

**Late arrivals:**
- Acknowledge briefly with a smile
- Have someone quietly hand them materials
- Don't restart or over-explain

**Crying baby/noise:**
- Pause briefly if needed
- Continue without commentary
- Let parents handle it

**Difficult questions mid-presentation:**
- "Great question—let's hold that for Q&A so I can give it proper attention"

---

## Question and Answer

Q&A is where you address concerns and move people toward commitment.

### Setting Up Q&A

Transition smoothly from presentation:

- "I've shared a lot tonight. Now I want to hear from you."
- "What questions do you have? Nothing is off limits."

If silence follows:

- Wait patiently (count to 10 in your head)
- Have a Core Group member ready with a seed question
- Ask the room: "What resonated with you? What made you curious?"

### Answering Questions Well

**Listen fully:**
- Let them finish before responding
- Repeat or paraphrase to confirm understanding
- "So what you're asking is..."

**Answer directly:**
- Don't be evasive or overly lengthy
- If you don't know, say so: "I don't know, but I'll find out and follow up with you"
- Be honest about challenges and unknowns

**Stay balanced:**
- Avoid letting one person dominate
- "Let me get to a few other questions, and we can continue this conversation afterward"

<Callout type="warning">
  Never argue with a questioner. If someone seems hostile or determined to derail, stay calm, give a brief answer, and move on: "I appreciate your perspective. Let's talk more after the meeting."
</Callout>

### Timing Q&A

Watch the clock:
- Know when you need to move to the close
- "We have time for one or two more questions"
- "I want to respect everyone's time, so let me make a few closing remarks"

---

## The Close

This is where you call people to action. Don't be timid.

### Transition to the Close

Signal you're wrapping up:
- "As we close tonight, I want to leave you with something important."
- "Let me tell you why I believe this matters."

### The Emotional Connection

This is where a powerful video or story can make an impact:
- Baptism testimonial video
- Brief story of life change
- Vision of what this church could become

Don't manipulate, but do connect with people's hearts.

### The Ask

Be clear and direct:

*"We're looking for people who are ready to commit—people who are COMMITTED to the vision, COMPELLED by what God is doing, CONTAGIOUS in their enthusiasm, and COURAGEOUS enough to step out in faith. If that's you, I'm inviting you to join us."*

Tell them exactly what to do:
- "Fill out the response card and indicate your interest level"
- "Check the box that says you want to learn more about joining the Core Group"
- "I'll be following up with each of you personally this week"

### Next Steps

Make next steps crystal clear:
- "Our next Vision Meeting is [date]"
- "Core Group meets every other Sunday at [time]"
- "I'll be calling each of you within the next 48 hours"

---

## After the Formal Close

The meeting isn't over when you stop talking.

### Transition to Fellowship

- "Thank you for being here. Please stick around for dessert and conversation."
- Move toward the food/refreshment area
- Begin engaging guests personally

### Working the Room

For the next 30 minutes, you and your Core Group should be:
- Having one-on-one conversations
- Answering lingering questions
- Getting to know people personally
- Gathering response cards

### Watch for Signals

- Who's lingering? They may have more questions or higher interest.
- Who's heading for the door? Get to them before they leave.
- Who's talking to Core Group members? Those conversations may be significant.

<Callout type="tip">
  The person who stays latest often has the most questions—and the most interest. Don't rush them out. This may be your best opportunity for a meaningful conversation.
</Callout>

---

## Wrapping Up

### As Guests Leave

- Thank each person for coming
- Remind them of next steps
- Confirm you'll be following up
- Walk them out if possible

### After the Last Guest

- Collect all sign-in sheets and response cards
- Quick debrief with Core Group: What went well? What could improve?
- Pack up and leave the space better than you found it
- Pray together thanking God and committing the follow-up to Him

### Immediate Follow-Up Tasks

Before you go to bed:
- Review response cards
- Note anyone who seemed particularly interested (or concerned)
- Begin planning follow-up calls for tomorrow

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love."* — 1 Corinthians 16:13-14 (LSB)
</Callout>

Excellence in execution honors God and serves people. Give your best, trust Him for the results, and follow up faithfully.

articles.title: Running the Meeting

articles.content:
Running effective Vision Meetings requires the right tools and materials. A well-prepared Vision Meeting Kit ensures you're never caught scrambling for supplies or apologizing for missing materials.

This guide covers everything you need to assemble a complete kit that you can grab and go.

---

## Why a Prepared Kit Matters

Having a dedicated Vision Meeting Kit accomplishes several things:

- **Eliminates last-minute scrambling** — Everything is ready before you need it
- **Ensures consistency** — Every meeting has the same professional materials
- **Reduces stress** — You can focus on people instead of logistics
- **Projects professionalism** — Preparedness communicates you take this seriously

<Callout type="tip">
  Designate a Core Group member as the "Kit Keeper" who ensures the kit is complete, organized, and transported to every Vision Meeting. This frees you to focus on preparation and people.
</Callout>

---

## The Complete Vision Meeting Kit

### Guest Experience Materials

These items shape how guests experience your meeting from the moment they arrive.

| Item | Purpose | Quantity |
|------|---------|----------|
| **Guest Sign-in Sheet** | Capture contact information | 3-5 sheets |
| **Name Tags** | Help people connect | 50+ blank tags |
| **Welcome Brochure** | Overview of church vision and values | 50+ copies |
| **Constitution Brochure** | Doctrinal distinctives and governance | 25+ copies |
| **Response Card** | Capture interest level and next steps | 50+ copies |
| **Business Cards** | Your contact information for follow-up | 100+ cards |

### Visual Branding Materials

Professional visual elements communicate that this is a serious, well-organized effort.

| Item | Purpose | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| **4 Pillars Banner w/Stand** | Visual representation of church foundation | Retractable banner stand |
| **Worship/Walk/Work Banner w/Stand** | Ministry model visualization | Retractable banner stand |
| **Mission Statement Banner w/Stand** | Core mission prominently displayed | Retractable banner stand |
| **Yard Signs** | Direct people to the location | 2-4 signs with stakes |

<Callout type="insight">
  Quality banners and signage are worth the investment. They'll be used at dozens of Vision Meetings and eventually at your church services. Cheap materials communicate a cheap operation.
</Callout>

### Presentation Technology

Everything needed to deliver your message effectively.

| Item | Purpose | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| **2 GB+ Flash Drive** | Backup of all digital content | Preloaded with PowerPoint, videos |
| **Laptop Speakers** | Audio for video playback | Portable, battery-powered ideal |
| **Extension Cord** | Power for equipment | 25+ feet |
| **HDMI/Adapter Cables** | Connect laptop to projector | Multiple adapter types |

**Flash Drive Contents:**
- Main presentation (PowerPoint/Keynote)
- Promotional video
- Baptism highlight video (for emotional close)
- Backup copies of all printed materials (PDF)

### Administrative Supplies

The small items that keep everything running smoothly.

| Item | Purpose | Quantity |
|------|---------|----------|
| **Pens** | Sign-in, response cards | 20+ pens |
| **Clipboards** | Writing surface for guests | 5-10 clipboards |
| **Black Markers** | Nametags, signs | 5+ markers |
| **Content Boxes & Labels** | Organize materials | 2-3 boxes |
| **Tape** | Signs, fixes | Masking and clear tape |
| **Scissors** | Cutting, opening | 1 pair |

### Organization and Transport

Keep everything together and portable.

| Item | Purpose | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| **Suitcase/Rolling Case** | Transport all materials | Large enough for everything |
| **Content Boxes with Labels** | Organize by category | Pre-meeting, During, Post-meeting |
| **Checklist** | Verify kit is complete | Laminated for reuse |

---

## Printed Materials Deep Dive

### Guest Sign-in Sheet

Your sign-in sheet should capture essential information without feeling like an interrogation.

**Include:**
- Name
- Email address
- Phone number
- How they heard about tonight's meeting

**Format tips:**
- Large enough to write comfortably
- Clear headings
- Space for 15-20 names per sheet
- Your church logo at the top

### Response Card

The response card is how you gauge interest and know how to follow up.

**Include:**
- Name (pre-filled if possible)
- Interest level checkboxes:
  - "I'd like more information"
  - "I'm interested in joining the Core Group"
  - "I'm ready to commit"
  - "This isn't for me right now"
- Questions or concerns (open field)
- Best way to contact them

<Callout type="important">
  Make it easy for people to indicate they're not interested. Paradoxically, this makes people more willing to fill out the card honestly. You want accurate information, not polite pretenses.
</Callout>

### Welcome Brochure

A take-home piece that summarizes what you shared.

**Include:**
- Church name and mission statement
- Brief version of your story
- Core values and distinctives
- Contact information and website
- Upcoming meeting dates

**Design tips:**
- Professional quality paper and printing
- Consistent branding with banners and signage
- Compelling photos or graphics
- QR code linking to more information

---

## Technology Preparation

### Before Every Meeting

1. **Test your presentation** on the actual equipment you'll use
2. **Verify videos play** with sound working properly
3. **Charge all batteries** (speakers, clicker, laptop)
4. **Load backup onto flash drive** in case of laptop failure

### Have a Backup Plan

Technology fails at the worst times. Know what you'll do if:

- The projector doesn't work → Printed handouts of key slides
- Audio fails → Speak louder, skip videos, or use phone speaker
- Laptop dies → Flash drive with presentation ready for another computer
- Internet is needed but unavailable → All content stored locally

<Callout type="warning">
  Never assume technology will work. Test everything at the venue before guests arrive. Have a plan B for every piece of equipment.
</Callout>

---

## Kit Maintenance

### After Every Meeting

- [ ] Return all materials to kit
- [ ] Count remaining supplies
- [ ] Note what needs to be replenished
- [ ] Charge all electronic devices
- [ ] File sign-in sheets and response cards (don't leave in kit)

### Weekly/Monthly

- [ ] Restock printed materials
- [ ] Update flash drive with latest versions
- [ ] Replace worn items (markers, tape)
- [ ] Clean and organize boxes
- [ ] Review kit against master checklist

### Quarterly

- [ ] Update printed materials if information changed
- [ ] Replace items showing wear
- [ ] Evaluate what's being used vs. what's dead weight
- [ ] Add new items based on experience

---

## Kit Checklist

Use this checklist to verify your kit is complete before every Vision Meeting.

### Guest Materials
- [ ] Sign-in sheets (3-5)
- [ ] Name tags (50+)
- [ ] Welcome brochures (50+)
- [ ] Constitution brochures (25+)
- [ ] Response cards (50+)
- [ ] Business cards (100+)

### Visual Branding
- [ ] 4 Pillars banner w/stand
- [ ] Worship/Walk/Work banner w/stand
- [ ] Mission Statement banner w/stand
- [ ] Yard signs with stakes

### Technology
- [ ] Flash drive (loaded)
- [ ] Laptop speakers
- [ ] Extension cord (25+ ft)
- [ ] HDMI/adapter cables
- [ ] Presentation clicker (with batteries)

### Supplies
- [ ] Pens (20+)
- [ ] Clipboards (5-10)
- [ ] Black markers (5+)
- [ ] Tape (masking and clear)
- [ ] Scissors

### Organization
- [ ] Everything in suitcase/case
- [ ] Content boxes labeled
- [ ] This checklist (laminated)

---

## Building Your Kit Over Time

You don't need everything on day one. Build your kit strategically:

### Phase 1: Essentials

Start with what you absolutely must have:
- Sign-in sheets
- Name tags
- Pens
- Response cards
- Your laptop with presentation

### Phase 2: Professional

Add items that increase professionalism:
- Printed brochures
- Business cards
- Banner stands
- Portable speakers

### Phase 3: Complete

Round out with convenience items:
- Rolling case for transport
- Organized boxes with labels
- Backup technology
- Extra supplies

<Callout type="tip">
  Ask Core Group members to contribute specific items. One person provides clipboards, another prints brochures, another donates pens. It builds ownership and spreads the cost.
</Callout>

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might;"* — Ecclesiastes 9:10 (LSB)
</Callout>

Preparation is stewardship. A well-prepared kit frees you to focus on what matters most—connecting with people and casting vision.

articles.content:
A Vision Meeting agenda looks simple on paper, but executing each element effectively requires understanding what you're trying to accomplish and how to do it well. This deep dive breaks down each component so you can lead with confidence.

---

## Before the Meeting Begins

### Setup (6:00 - 6:30)

What seems like "just setup" actually sets the stage for everything that follows. Arrive early enough that you're never rushed.

**Room arrangement:**
- Seating arranged to facilitate both presentation and conversation
- Clear sightlines to presentation screen
- Space for mingling before and after
- Sign-in table positioned near entrance

**AV check:**
- Projector/screen tested and focused
- Audio tested (can people hear clearly from all seats?)
- Presentation loaded and working
- Backup plan if technology fails

**Materials ready:**
- Sign-in sheets and pens
- Nametags (pre-printed or blank with markers)
- Handouts organized and accessible
- Response cards ready for distribution

<Callout type="tip">
  Always have a backup plan for technology failures. Know how you'd deliver your message if the projector died. A printout of key slides or the ability to speak without visuals keeps a tech failure from becoming a disaster.
</Callout>

---

## Meet and Greet (6:45 - 7:00)

This window isn't dead time before the "real" meeting starts. It's prime time for making first impressions and beginning relationships.

### What You're Accomplishing

- Welcoming people warmly as they arrive
- Capturing contact information before anyone slips away
- Beginning to build relationships through casual conversation
- Creating a warm, inviting atmosphere

### How to Execute

**At the door:**
- Greeter welcomes each person by name (if known) or introduces themselves
- Direct to sign-in table
- Offer nametag

**At the sign-in table:**
- Friendly face (not buried in paperwork)
- Quick, efficient process
- Capture name, email, phone at minimum
- Hand them any materials they need

**In the room:**
- Core Group members mingle with guests (not clustered together)
- Introduce guests to each other
- Casual conversation—don't start selling yet
- Offer refreshments if available

<Callout type="warning">
  Core Group members must resist the temptation to cluster together. Every Core Group member should be engaging with guests, not catching up with each other.
</Callout>

### Common Mistakes

- Making sign-in feel like an interrogation
- Allowing guests to sit alone without being engaged
- Starting late because you weren't ready
- Letting the room feel cold or unwelcoming

---

## Ice Breaker and Introduction (7:00 - 7:15)

The transition from casual mingling to the formal meeting requires intentionality. A good ice breaker breaks the tension and helps everyone feel included.

### Purpose of the Ice Breaker

- Transition attention from conversations to the group
- Help people feel comfortable speaking in the group
- Create shared experience and laughter
- Set a warm, non-intimidating tone

### Effective Ice Breaker Qualities

- **Quick** — 5-7 minutes maximum
- **Easy** — Everyone can participate without feeling put on the spot
- **Relevant** — Connects somehow to the purpose of the meeting
- **Fun** — Creates positive energy

### Sample Ice Breakers

**Two Truths and a Lie:**
Each person shares three statements about themselves—two true, one false. The group guesses which is the lie.

**Finish the Sentence:**
"I'm excited about the possibility of a new church because..." or "One thing I'm looking for in a church is..."

**Quick Connections:**
"Turn to someone you don't know and share one thing you love about this community/area."

<Callout type="insight">
  The best ice breakers feel natural, not forced. If you're uncomfortable with structured activities, try simply asking everyone to briefly introduce themselves with their name and one interesting fact.
</Callout>

### The Transition to Introduction

After the ice breaker, smoothly transition into introducing yourself and the purpose of the meeting:

- Thank everyone for coming
- Briefly introduce yourself (save the full story for the presentation)
- Preview what the next hour will look like
- Set expectations (Q&A time coming, response cards, etc.)

---

## The Presentation (7:15 - 7:45)

This is the heart of your Vision Meeting—where you cast the vision that will transform interested individuals into committed Core Group members.

### Structure Your Presentation

**1. Your Story (5-7 minutes)**

How God called you to plant this church. Include:
- Your spiritual journey and calling to ministry
- The specific moment or process when church planting became clear
- Why this location, this time, this community
- What you're leaving behind to pursue this calling

People follow people, not programs. Your story builds trust and demonstrates authenticity.

**2. The Church's Identity (10-12 minutes)**

What makes this church unique. Cover:
- Core values and convictions
- The 4 Pillars that guide your approach
- The Worship/Walk/Work model
- What visitors can expect on Sunday mornings
- What membership looks like

Use visuals effectively here—slides with key points, brief video clips, images that communicate culture.

**3. The Vision (8-10 minutes)**

What God wants to accomplish through this church. Paint a picture of:
- Lives transformed by the gospel
- Community impact you're believing God for
- The kind of church you're building
- Specific goals (launch date, launch team size, etc.)

This is where you cast compelling vision. Be specific enough to be believable, bold enough to require God to show up.

### Presentation Tips

| Do | Don't |
|-----|-------|
| Speak with passion and conviction | Read from notes or slides |
| Make eye contact | Stay glued to one spot |
| Tell stories that illustrate points | Bury people in information |
| Keep it concise | Ramble or repeat yourself |
| Use slides to support, not replace | Read slides word-for-word |
| Practice until confident | Wing it |

<Callout type="important">
  Your presentation should be well-rehearsed but not memorized. You want to communicate naturally, not robotically. Practice enough that you know the content cold, then let your personality come through in delivery.
</Callout>

---

## Question and Answer (7:45 - 8:15)

Q&A is not just a formality—it's a crucial opportunity to address concerns that could prevent people from committing.

### Setting Up Q&A

- Invite questions warmly: "What questions do you have?"
- If no one speaks first, have a Core Group member ready with a question
- Make it safe to ask anything: "There are no bad questions"

### Handling Different Types of Questions

**Legitimate information questions:**
Answer directly and thoroughly. These are easy.

**Skeptical questions:**
Don't get defensive. Acknowledge the concern, answer honestly, and move on. "That's a fair question. Here's how we think about that..."

**Tangent questions:**
Redirect graciously. "That's a great topic. Let's connect after and I can share more about that specifically."

**Challenging questions:**
Stay calm and humble. "I appreciate you asking that directly. Here's my honest answer..." If you don't know, say so.

### What If Nobody Has Questions?

- Be patient—sometimes people need a moment
- Have your planted question ready
- Ask a question of them: "What about what you heard tonight resonates with you?"
- Don't panic—it's not always a bad sign

<Callout type="tip">
  Keep track of questions you receive repeatedly. These are telling you what people care about most and may indicate areas where your presentation needs more clarity.
</Callout>

---

## The Strong Close (8:15 - 8:30)

This is where many Vision Meetings fail. You've built momentum—now you need to direct it toward action.

### Components of a Strong Close

**1. Summarize the Opportunity**

Briefly recap what you've shared and why it matters:
- What God is doing
- What you're building
- Why it matters
- Why now is the time

**2. Describe Who You're Looking For**

Be specific about the kind of people you need. Reference the 4 C's:

*"We're looking for people who are COMMITTED—willing to prioritize this above other good things. COMPELLED—driven by conviction, not convenience. CONTAGIOUS—whose enthusiasm will spread to others. And COURAGEOUS—willing to step out in faith."*

**3. Make the Ask**

Don't be vague. Tell people specifically what you want them to do:

- "We're asking you to prayerfully consider joining the Core Group."
- "Fill out the response card to indicate your level of interest."
- "Meet with me this week for a follow-up conversation."

**4. Outline Next Steps**

What happens after tonight?

- "Our next Vision Meeting is [date]. Mark it down."
- "I'll be following up personally with everyone this week."
- "Core Group meets every other Sunday at 4 PM."
- "Here's the calendar for the next two months."

### The Call Without Manipulation

<Callout type="warning">
  A strong close is direct, not manipulative. You're inviting, not pressuring. People should feel challenged, not trapped. If they're not ready, that's okay—but they need to be asked.
</Callout>

**Do:**
- Be clear about what you're asking
- Express genuine desire for them to join
- Create urgency without false pressure
- Make it easy to say yes

**Don't:**
- Use emotional manipulation
- Imply they're less spiritual if they don't join
- Rush people into premature commitment
- Ignore legitimate concerns or questions

---

## Fellowship and Dessert (8:30 - 9:00)

The meeting isn't over when the formal presentation ends. Some of your best relationship-building happens in this window.

### What You're Accomplishing

- Deepening connections begun earlier
- Having one-on-one conversations with interested individuals
- Answering questions people didn't want to ask publicly
- Allowing your Core Group to engage guests personally

### How to Maximize This Time

- Don't pack up immediately—stay present and engaged
- Move around the room, not staying in one conversation too long
- Core Group members should each target one guest for deeper conversation
- Watch for people leaving alone or seeming disconnected—engage them

<Callout type="insight">
  The guest who lingers after everyone else has left often has the most questions—and the most interest. Don't rush them out. This may be your best opportunity for a meaningful conversation.
</Callout>

---

## After the Last Person Leaves

Your work isn't done when guests leave.

### Immediate Tasks

- Collect all sign-in sheets and response cards
- Brief debrief with Core Group: What went well? What could improve?
- Note any specific follow-up needed (questions to answer, concerns raised)
- Pack up and leave the location better than you found it

### Within 48 Hours

- Enter all contact information into your database
- Assign follow-up calls to team members
- Send thank-you email to all attendees
- Begin personal follow-up with interested individuals

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>

A well-executed agenda isn't about rigid formality—it's about stewarding people's time and attention so that the message has maximum impact.

articles.content:
The Vision Meeting is the main engine driving your entire launch process. It sits at the top of the funnel that transforms interested individuals into committed Core Group members who will help you plant a thriving church.

Understanding what a Vision Meeting is—and what it isn't—will shape how you approach this critical activity.

---

## The Heart of the Launch Process

A Vision Meeting is any gathering, large or small, formal or informal, where you and your key leaders cast a clear, compelling, and challenging vision to individuals considering joining the Core Group.

This definition is intentionally broad. Vision Meetings can take many forms:

- **Informal gatherings** — Coffee with 2-3 people interested in learning more
- **Small group settings** — Living room conversations with 8-10 potential members
- **Formal presentations** — Larger events targeting 30-50 attendees

The format matters less than the purpose: casting vision in such a way that transforms interested individuals into **COMMITTED, COMPELLED, CONTAGIOUS, and COURAGEOUS** Core Group members.

<Callout type="insight">
  Vision Meetings aren't about selling people on your church. They're about clearly articulating where God is leading and inviting the right people to join the journey.
</Callout>

---

## Seven Essential Elements

Every effective Vision Meeting includes these seven elements, regardless of size or format:

### 1. CONNECT

Connect authentically with the people attending. Create an atmosphere where genuine relationship can begin. People don't join visions—they join people with visions.

### 2. INFORM

Share the history, distinctives, values, and DNA of the church you're planting. Give people a clear picture of who you are and what you believe.

### 3. CAST VISION

Present the vision clearly, compellingly, and challengingly. Help people see what God is doing and what He wants to accomplish through this church plant.

### 4. ANSWER

Provide time for questions. People need their concerns addressed before they can commit. An unanswered question often becomes a reason not to join.

### 5. CALL FOR ACTION

Issue a genuine, non-manipulative call to commitment. Don't shy away from the ask—people need to be challenged to step forward.

### 6. CAPTURE

Gather contact information from everyone who attends. You cannot follow up with people you can't reach.

### 7. FOLLOW UP

Communicate clear next steps. What happens after tonight? When is the next meeting? What should they do if they want to learn more?

---

## What a Vision Meeting Is NOT

Understanding what to avoid is just as important as knowing what to include:

**Not a church service** — You're not trying to replicate Sunday morning. This is a recruitment and vision-casting event.

**Not a sales pitch** — You're not selling a product. You're inviting people into a calling.

**Not about you** — While your story matters, the focus should be on what God is doing and inviting them to be part of it.

**Not for everyone** — You're looking for specific kinds of people. Not everyone who attends will be the right fit, and that's okay.

---

## Frequency Matters

Schedule Vision Meetings at minimum every other week. Continue until the Lord brings a critical mass of **COMMITTED, COMPELLED, CONTAGIOUS, and COURAGEOUS** individuals. This methodology's benchmark for that critical mass is 50-100 adults.

<Callout type="important">
  Consistency is key. One great Vision Meeting won't build your Core Group. A steady rhythm of meetings over months will.
</Callout>

The frequency also allows different formats to serve different purposes:

- **Larger, formal meetings** — Cast the broad vision and reach new networks
- **Smaller, informal meetings** — Deepen relationships and answer detailed questions
- **One-on-one conversations** — Address specific concerns and personally challenge individuals to commit

---

## The Funnel in Action

Vision Meetings sit at the top of a funnel that moves people through a clear process:

| Stage | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| **Network** | Friends, acquaintances, social connections—your sphere of influence |
| **Vision Meeting** | Cast vision, share distinctives, call for commitment |
| **Follow Up** | Answer questions, interview for fit, personally challenge |
| **Core Group** | Committed members who pray, give, and grow the group |

Every person who eventually joins your Core Group—and eventually your Launch Team—enters through this funnel. The Vision Meeting is your primary tool for moving people from "interested" to "committed."

---

## Why This Matters

Your Core Group will only be as strong as your Vision Meetings are effective. Weak Vision Meetings produce weak Core Groups. Strong Vision Meetings attract and develop the kind of people who can help you plant a thriving church.

This is why we dedicate so much attention to Vision Meetings in this playbook. Master this, and you'll have the foundation for everything that follows.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Commit your works to Yahweh And your plans will be established."* — Proverbs 16:3 (LSB)
</Callout>

Vision Meetings are where you share God's vision and invite others to join you in seeing it become reality.
articles.excerpt: Understanding the Vision Meeting as the primary engine for casting vision and growing your Core Group.
articles.title: What is a Vision Meeting?

articles.content:
Your first Vision Meeting is a milestone. It marks the transition from dreaming about planting a church to actively recruiting your Core Group. The pressure can feel intense, but with proper preparation, your first meeting can set a strong foundation for everything that follows.

This guide walks you through the entire process from initial planning to follow-up.

---

## Setting Expectations

Before diving into logistics, set realistic expectations for your first meeting.

### What Success Looks Like

For a first Vision Meeting, success is:
- 10-15 attendees (not counting you and any existing team)
- Clear presentation of vision and distinctives
- Contact information captured from everyone
- 3-5 people expressing genuine interest in learning more
- A positive experience that generates word-of-mouth

### What Success Is NOT

Don't expect:
- Massive attendance (that comes later)
- Everyone committing on the spot
- Perfection in your presentation
- Zero hiccups with logistics

<Callout type="insight">
  Your first Vision Meeting is a first draft. You'll get better with practice. Focus on execution, learn from mistakes, and improve for the next one.
</Callout>

---

## Phase 1: Foundation (4-6 Weeks Out)

### Choose Your Date

Pick a date that:
- Gives you adequate preparation time (minimum 4 weeks)
- Avoids major holidays and competing events
- Works for the people you most want to attend
- Allows for evening timing (7:00 PM start is typical)

### Secure Your Location

For a first meeting, keep it simple:
- A living room works great for 10-20 people
- A church fellowship hall if you need more space
- A community center or library meeting room as backup

**Questions to answer:**
- Can it comfortably hold your target attendance?
- Is it easy to find with good parking?
- Can you control the environment (temperature, noise)?
- What's the cost?

### Identify Your First Invitees

Make a list of everyone you'll personally invite:
- Close friends who might be interested
- Family members in the area
- Former church connections
- Colleagues who share your faith
- Acquaintances you've been wanting to engage

Aim for a list of 30+ names—you'll need this many to get 10-15 attendees.

---

## Phase 2: Preparation (2-4 Weeks Out)

### Build Your Presentation

Your presentation should cover:

1. **Your story** (5-7 minutes)
   - How God called you to ministry
   - Why church planting specifically
   - Why this community, this time

2. **The church identity** (10 minutes)
   - Core values and beliefs
   - The 4 Pillars
   - The Worship/Walk/Work model
   - What Sundays will look like

3. **The vision** (8 minutes)
   - What God wants to accomplish
   - Lives changed, community impacted
   - Specific goals (launch date, launch team size)
   - Why this matters

4. **The invitation** (5 minutes)
   - Who you're looking for
   - What commitment looks like
   - Next steps

**Total: 28-30 minutes**

<Callout type="tip">
  Practice your presentation at least 5 times before the meeting. Record yourself if possible. Time each section so you know exactly where you are during delivery.
</Callout>

### Prepare Your Materials

For your first meeting, you need at minimum:
- Sign-in sheets
- Name tags and markers
- Printed handout with church overview
- Response cards
- Pens

Nice to have:
- Welcome brochure
- Banner or visual display
- Business cards

### Create Your Agenda

| Time | Activity | Notes |
|------|----------|-------|
| 6:30 | You arrive, setup | Everything ready before guests |
| 6:45 | Doors open | Greeting, sign-in begins |
| 7:00 | Welcome, ice breaker | 15 minutes |
| 7:15 | Presentation | 30 minutes |
| 7:45 | Q&A | 20 minutes |
| 8:05 | Close and next steps | 10 minutes |
| 8:15 | Fellowship/dessert | 30+ minutes |

### Begin Inviting

Start your invitation push:
- Personal conversations with your top prospects
- Phone calls to people you know
- Text messages with key details
- Social media announcement
- Email to your broader network

Remember: **Personal invitation is most effective.** Don't rely on mass communication alone.

---

## Phase 3: Final Week

### Confirm Attendance

Reach out to everyone who's shown interest:
- "Looking forward to seeing you Thursday!"
- "Can I count on you being there?"
- "Do you need directions or have any questions?"

### Finalize Logistics

- [ ] Location confirmed and accessible
- [ ] Room setup plan clear
- [ ] AV equipment tested
- [ ] Materials printed and organized
- [ ] Refreshments planned
- [ ] Transportation arranged for equipment

### Recruit Help

Even for your first meeting, you need some help:
- Someone to greet and handle sign-in
- Someone to manage refreshments
- Someone to help with setup/teardown

These might be your spouse, a close friend, or an early committed person. Don't try to do everything yourself.

### Prepare Spiritually

This is a spiritual work. Prepare accordingly:
- Dedicated prayer for the meeting and attendees
- Fasting if you're led to
- Asking others to pray for you
- Resting adequately the night before

---

## Phase 4: Meeting Day

### Before Guests Arrive

**2 hours before:**
- Arrive at location
- Begin room setup
- Test all technology

**1 hour before:**
- Materials laid out
- Refreshments ready
- Quick walk-through of the room
- Final tech test

**30 minutes before:**
- Brief your helpers
- Pray together
- Final mental preparation
- Ready to greet

<Callout type="important">
  You should be completely ready and relaxed when the first guest walks in. If you're still setting up, you've started behind.
</Callout>

### During the Meeting

**Greeting phase:**
- Be at the door to welcome people
- Make introductions
- Ensure everyone signs in

**Presentation phase:**
- Stick to your agenda
- Watch the clock
- Be yourself—authentic beats polished

**Q&A phase:**
- Encourage questions
- Answer honestly
- Don't rush this section

**Close:**
- Be clear about what you're asking
- Make next steps explicit
- Express genuine hope they'll join

**Fellowship:**
- Work the room
- Have meaningful conversations
- Don't retreat to familiar people

### After the Last Guest Leaves

Before you leave:
- Collect all sign-in sheets and response cards
- Quick debrief: What went well? What was challenging?
- Clean up and return room to original condition
- Thank your helpers

---

## Phase 5: Follow-Up (24-72 Hours)

### Day 1: Immediate Follow-Up

**Send thank-you email to everyone:**

> Subject: Great meeting you last night!
>
> Thank you for coming to our Vision Meeting last night. It was great to share our vision with you, and I enjoyed getting to know you.
>
> If you have any questions, please don't hesitate to reach out. I'll be calling you in the next day or two to follow up.
>
> Our next gathering is [date]. Hope to see you there!

**Enter all contacts into your database**

**Review response cards and categorize:**
- High interest (want to join or learn more)
- Moderate interest (curious, need more info)
- Low interest (not for them right now)
- Unclear (need conversation to clarify)

### Days 2-3: Personal Follow-Up Calls

Call everyone who attended. For your first meeting, you should make these calls yourself.

**Call structure:**
1. Thank them for coming
2. Ask what they thought
3. Answer any questions
4. Gauge their interest level
5. Invite to next gathering or schedule one-on-one

**For high-interest people:**
Schedule a one-on-one coffee or meeting to go deeper and personally invite them to commit.

**For moderate-interest people:**
Answer questions, invite to the next Vision Meeting, note any concerns to address.

**For low-interest people:**
Thank them graciously, leave the door open, ask if they know anyone else who might be interested.

<Callout type="tip">
  Keep detailed notes from every follow-up call. What were their questions? What concerns did they express? What's their story? This information is gold for future conversations.
</Callout>

---

## After Your First Meeting: Evaluate

### What Worked?

Note what went well so you can repeat it:
- Which parts of your presentation landed?
- What questions came up?
- How did people respond to the close?
- What did your helpers observe?

### What Could Improve?

Be honest about areas for growth:
- Was anything confusing?
- Did anything run too long or too short?
- Were there logistics issues?
- What feedback did you receive?

### Adjust for Meeting #2

Based on your evaluation:
- Refine your presentation
- Adjust your timing
- Improve your materials
- Set a date for the next meeting (within 2 weeks)

---

## First Meeting FAQ

### How many people should I expect?

For a first meeting, 10-15 attendees is a healthy target. If you're personally inviting 30+ people, expect about 30-40% to actually show up.

### What if hardly anyone comes?

Don't be discouraged. Evaluate what happened:
- Were invitations personal enough?
- Was the timing bad?
- Did something else compete for attention?

Adjust and try again. Many successful churches had rocky first meetings.

### What if I freeze during the presentation?

It happens. Take a breath, glance at your notes, and keep going. No one expects perfection. Authenticity matters more than polish.

### How do I handle awkward silence during Q&A?

Wait longer than feels comfortable. Have a Core Group member ready with a seed question. You can also prompt: "What resonated with you? What made you curious?"

### What if someone is clearly not a good fit?

Be gracious. Thank them for coming. Some people will self-select out, and that's okay. You're not trying to recruit everyone.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"For who has despised the day of small things? But these seven will be glad when they see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel—these are the eyes of Yahweh which roam to and fro throughout the earth."* — Zechariah 4:10 (LSB)
</Callout>

Your first Vision Meeting is a beginning, not a destination. Trust God with the outcome, learn from the experience, and keep building. Every great church started with a small group of people who caught a vision and said yes.
articles.excerpt: A step-by-step guide for planning and executing your very first Vision Meeting.
articles.title: Your First Vision Meeting

articles.content:
Beyond your foundational pillars, every church develops a set of values, distinctives, and DNA that shape its culture. These aren't abstract concepts—they're the lived reality of who you are and how you operate.

Defining these clearly before you launch sets the trajectory for everything that follows.

---

## Pillars vs. Values vs. Distinctives

These terms are related but distinct:

| Term | Definition | Example |
|------|------------|---------|
| **Pillars** | Fundamental, non-negotiable biblical commitments | "We are committed to the authority of Scripture" |
| **Values** | How you prioritize and operate | "We value excellence in everything we do" |
| **Distinctives** | What makes you unique compared to other churches | "We emphasize expository preaching through books of the Bible" |
| **DNA** | The embedded culture that shapes behavior | "We're a church that celebrates publicly and cares privately" |

Your pillars are load-bearing walls. Values, distinctives, and DNA are the interior design—how the space feels and functions.

<Callout type="insight">
  Pillars answer "What do we believe?" Values answer "How do we operate?" Distinctives answer "What makes us unique?"
</Callout>

---

## Why Values Matter

Values guide behavior when no one is watching and when policies don't apply. They shape:

- **How decisions get made** — What factors carry the most weight?
- **How people are treated** — What does respect and care look like here?
- **How conflict is handled** — What's acceptable and unacceptable?
- **How excellence is defined** — What standard are we aiming for?
- **How newcomers are welcomed** — What's the first impression?

Unclear values lead to inconsistent behavior. People don't know what's expected, and leaders make contradictory decisions.

---

## Common Church Values

Here are values that healthy churches often embrace. Use these as a starting point for identifying your own:

### Ministry Values

| Value | What It Means |
|-------|---------------|
| **Biblical fidelity** | Scripture shapes everything we do |
| **Excellence** | We give our best in all things |
| **Authenticity** | We're real about struggles and growth |
| **Accessibility** | We remove barriers for newcomers |
| **Multiplication** | We exist to reproduce, not just grow |

### Relational Values

| Value | What It Means |
|-------|---------------|
| **Community** | Relationships matter more than programs |
| **Hospitality** | Guests feel genuinely welcomed |
| **Transparency** | Leaders are open and honest |
| **Unity** | We pursue harmony and resolve conflict |
| **Care** | We shepherd people, not just manage them |

### Operational Values

| Value | What It Means |
|-------|---------------|
| **Stewardship** | We manage resources responsibly |
| **Simplicity** | We avoid unnecessary complexity |
| **Flexibility** | We adapt methods while holding convictions |
| **Accountability** | We hold each other to commitments |
| **Planning** | We prepare thoroughly, not haphazardly |

---

## Process for Defining Your Values

### Step 1: Reflect on What Matters Most

Start with these questions:

- What do you want people to experience when they encounter your church?
- What behaviors do you want to characterize your community?
- What would make you say "That's not who we are"?
- What patterns from healthy churches do you want to replicate?
- What mistakes from unhealthy churches do you want to avoid?

Write freely. Don't edit yet.

### Step 2: Identify Patterns

Review what you've written and look for themes. Group similar ideas together. You're looking for the core commitments that keep appearing.

### Step 3: Prioritize Ruthlessly

You can't emphasize everything equally. Choose 5-7 values that are most important. These should be:

- **Genuine** — You actually believe and practice them
- **Specific** — Clear enough to guide behavior
- **Memorable** — Easy to recall and communicate
- **Distinctive** — Not generic statements everyone would claim

<Callout type="warning">
  Avoid values so generic they're meaningless. Every church claims to "love people" and "follow Jesus." What specifically characterizes how you do this?
</Callout>

### Step 4: Define Each Value Clearly

For each value, write:

1. **A concise statement** — One sentence capturing the value
2. **What it means** — Explanation in plain language
3. **What it looks like** — Concrete examples of the value in action
4. **What it doesn't mean** — Clarifying boundaries and misconceptions

### Step 5: Test Against Reality

Ask honest questions:

- Do I actually live this value, or just aspire to it?
- Would people who know me recognize this in my leadership?
- Is this realistic for our context and resources?
- Will this still be true in 10 years?

If a value is aspirational rather than actual, either commit to changing or acknowledge it's a goal, not a current reality.

---

## Defining Your Distinctives

Distinctives are what make your church different from the church down the street. They answer: "If someone visited both churches, what would they notice that's unique about us?"

### Categories of Distinctives

**Theological distinctives:**
- Denominational affiliation or independence
- Specific doctrinal emphases
- Approach to controversial issues

**Methodological distinctives:**
- Preaching style (expository, topical, narrative)
- Worship style (traditional, contemporary, blended)
- Service format and length

**Cultural distinctives:**
- Formality level
- Demographic focus
- Neighborhood engagement approach

**Programmatic distinctives:**
- Small group model
- Discipleship pathway
- Missional commitments

<Callout type="tip">
  Your distinctives should be honest, not aspirational. Describe what you actually are and do, not what you wish you were.
</Callout>

---

## Embedding Values in DNA

Values on paper aren't the same as values in practice. To embed values into your church's DNA:

### Model Them Consistently

People watch leaders more than they listen to them. If you value excellence but are consistently unprepared, your stated value is meaningless.

### Talk About Them Regularly

Reference values in:
- Teaching and preaching
- Leadership meetings
- Decision explanations
- Celebration and correction

### Hire and Recruit for Them

When adding staff or key volunteers, evaluate candidates against your values. Skills can be developed; values alignment is harder to change.

### Correct Violations Promptly

When behavior contradicts stated values, address it. Silence communicates that the values aren't really important.

### Celebrate Examples

When someone embodies a value well, point it out publicly. Stories of values in action teach better than statements.

---

## Teaching Values to Your Core Group

Your Core Group must understand and embrace your values deeply. They'll carry these into every interaction and ministry.

**In Vision Meetings:**
- Introduce values as part of the presentation
- Explain why each one matters
- Give examples of what they look like

**In Core Group Meetings:**
- Reinforce values through teaching and devotions
- Point out when values are being lived out
- Address when values are being violated

**In One-on-One Conversations:**
- Discuss how values apply to specific situations
- Coach people in living out the values
- Address concerns or misunderstandings

<Callout type="important">
  The goal isn't that people can recite your values. It's that they instinctively live them without thinking about it.
</Callout>

---

## Values Document Template
