Consider creating a simple document that captures your values:

```
OUR VALUES

1. [VALUE NAME]
   We believe... [concise statement]
   This means... [explanation]
   This looks like... [examples]

2. [VALUE NAME]
   We believe... [concise statement]
   This means... [explanation]
   This looks like... [examples]

[Continue for each value]
```

Keep it simple. One page is ideal. Make it something people can actually read and remember.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is dignified, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence and if anything worthy of praise, consider these things."* — Philippians 4:8 (LSB)
</Callout>

Your values shape your culture. Your culture shapes your impact. Take time to define clearly what you stand for and how you operate. The clarity you establish now will guide your church for years to come.
articles.excerpt: A practical guide to articulating the values, distinctives, and DNA that will shape your church's culture and decision-making.
articles.title: Defining Your Church Values

articles.content:
The Launch Playbook consistently references working with a "coach"—someone who guides you through the planting process, provides accountability, and shares wisdom from experience. Finding the right mentor is one of the most important things you can do before launching.

You don't have to figure this out alone. In fact, you shouldn't.

---

## Why Mentors Matter

Church planting is too complex and too important to navigate solo. A good mentor provides:

| Benefit | How It Helps |
|---------|--------------|
| **Wisdom** | Learn from their successes and mistakes |
| **Accountability** | Someone who asks hard questions |
| **Perspective** | Outside view when you're too close to see clearly |
| **Encouragement** | Support during inevitable discouragements |
| **Connections** | Access to their network and relationships |
| **Credibility** | Their endorsement opens doors |

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Without consultation, plans are frustrated, But with many counselors they succeed."* — Proverbs 15:22 (LSB)
</Callout>

The Launch Playbook assumes you have a coach for good reason. Critical decisions—budgeting, facility selection, timeline setting—benefit enormously from experienced input.

---

## Types of Mentors You Need

Most church planters benefit from multiple mentors serving different roles:

### Primary Coach

Your main accountability relationship throughout the planting process. This person:
- Meets with you regularly (weekly or bi-weekly)
- Knows the details of your plant
- Provides ongoing guidance and accountability
- Helps with major decisions
- Often comes through your network or sending church

### Experienced Planter

Someone who has successfully planted a church and can speak from direct experience:
- Understands the emotional journey
- Can share practical lessons learned
- Validates your struggles as normal
- Provides hope that it's possible

### Life Mentor

Someone who invests in you as a person, not just as a planter:
- Focuses on character and spiritual health
- Helps with marriage and family priorities
- Provides perspective beyond ministry
- May not have church planting experience

### Specialized Advisors

People with expertise in specific areas:
- Financial management
- Legal and organizational setup
- Marketing and communications
- Leadership development

<Callout type="tip">
  Don't expect one person to fill all these roles. Build a team of mentors who collectively provide what you need.
</Callout>

---

## How to Find a Mentor

Mentors rarely appear automatically. You'll need to be intentional.

### Observe People Around You

Start by looking at who's already in your life:
- Church leaders you respect
- Successful planters in your network
- Business leaders in your congregation or community
- Older believers whose character you admire

Good mentors are often closer than you think. The godly businessperson at your gym, the experienced pastor at a partner church, the leader in your network who has planted before—they're all potential mentors.

<Callout type="insight">
  Not every mentor needs to be a pastor. Some of the best leadership and life principles come from godly people in business, nonprofit leadership, or other fields. Look for high character and proven wisdom, not just ministry credentials.
</Callout>

### Look for Specific Qualities

When evaluating potential mentors, consider:

| Quality | Why It Matters |
|---------|----------------|
| **Character** | High integrity and godly behavior |
| **Experience** | Relevant knowledge to share |
| **Availability** | Actually able to meet with you |
| **Chemistry** | Natural connection and comfort |
| **Honesty** | Willing to tell you hard truths |
| **Humility** | Not trying to create a clone of themselves |

### Ask People You Respect

Talk to:
- Your sending church leadership
- Your denomination or network leaders
- Other church planters
- Seminary professors or ministry trainers

Ask: "Who do you know that might be able to mentor me through this process?"

### Leverage Your Network

If you're planting through a network or denomination:
- Ask about formal coaching programs
- Request mentor recommendations
- Attend network events to meet potential mentors
- Ask other planters who mentored them

---

## Making the Ask

Many people hesitate to ask someone to mentor them. Don't. Most experienced leaders are honored to be asked and willing to invest if approached well.

### Be Specific About What You're Asking

Don't ask vaguely for "mentoring." Be clear:
- How often you'd like to meet
- What you're hoping to learn
- What time commitment you're requesting
- How long you envision the relationship lasting

### Make It Easy to Say Yes

- Suggest meeting at their convenience
- Come prepared with questions
- Take responsibility for scheduling
- Respect their time constraints

### Be Honest About Why You Chose Them

Tell them specifically what you've observed that made you ask them:
- "I've watched how you lead with both strength and humility"
- "Your church plant has thrived, and I want to learn from your experience"
- "I've seen how you balance ministry and family well"

People respond to genuine, specific appreciation.

### Give Them an Out

Make it easy to decline without awkwardness:
- "I understand if your schedule doesn't allow for this"
- "Even if ongoing mentoring doesn't work, could we meet once for your input?"
- "If this isn't the right fit, could you recommend someone else?"

---

## Getting the Most from Mentoring

Once you have a mentor, maximize the relationship:

### Come Prepared

Do the work to make meetings productive:
- Have specific questions written down
- Share updates concisely
- Bring real challenges you're facing
- Take notes on their input

### Take Initiative

Don't wait for your mentor to lead:
- Schedule the meetings
- Set the agenda
- Follow up on action items
- Report back on how you applied their advice

### Apply What You Learn

Mentoring is wasted if you don't act on it:
- Implement their suggestions
- Try their recommended approaches
- Report back on results
- Ask follow-up questions

### Be Honest

Don't hide struggles to look good:
- Share real challenges
- Admit mistakes and failures
- Ask for help with hard situations
- Be vulnerable about fears and doubts

<Callout type="warning">
  If you only share successes, you'll only get congratulations. Mentors can only help with problems they know about.
</Callout>

### Express Gratitude

Mentors invest without compensation. Show appreciation:
- Thank them regularly
- Tell them how their input helped
- Update them on wins
- Acknowledge their investment publicly when appropriate

---

## The 5 A's of Effective Mentoring

Research on effective mentoring relationships identifies five key elements:

### 1. Affinity

There must be natural connection between mentor and mentee. You should genuinely like each other and be drawn to spend time together. Without affinity, meetings become obligations rather than opportunities.

### 2. Availability

Both parties must have time to invest. A brilliant mentor who never has time to meet isn't actually a mentor. Be realistic about schedules on both sides.

### 3. Adaptability

Good mentoring adapts to what the mentee needs in each season. Sometimes you need tough accountability. Other times you need encouragement. A good mentor reads the situation and adjusts.

### 4. Attentiveness

Mentoring requires active listening. The mentor shouldn't do all the talking. Good mentors ask questions, listen carefully, and help you process your own experiences.

### 5. Activation

The goal of mentoring is action, not just conversation. A good mentor activates your gifts, sends you out to lead, and lets go of control. You're not trying to become a clone of your mentor.

---

## When to Move On

Mentoring relationships don't have to last forever:

- **Seasonal mentoring** — A mentor for a specific challenge or season
- **Transitional mentoring** — As you grow, you may need different input
- **Completion** — Some relationships naturally conclude

Moving on from a mentor isn't failure—it's often a sign of growth. Maintain the relationship even if formal mentoring ends.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Iron sharpens iron, So one man sharpens another."* — Proverbs 27:17 (LSB)
</Callout>

Don't plant alone. Find mentors who will walk with you, challenge you, and help you become the leader your church needs. The investment in these relationships will pay dividends throughout your ministry.
articles.excerpt: How to identify, approach, and cultivate mentoring relationships that will support you throughout your church planting journey.
articles.title: Finding a Coach/Mentor

articles.content:
Before diving into the mechanics of church planting, you must answer a fundamental question: Is this what God has called you to do?

Planting a church is a high calling. It requires **much faith**, **much work**, and **much perseverance**. It is a supernatural work of Jesus building His church (Matt. 16:18), and we have the tremendous privilege of partnering with Him in this work. But not everyone is called to this particular form of ministry.

---

## The Weight of the Calling

Church planting isn't a career move or a way to escape a difficult ministry situation. It's a divine assignment that will cost you more than you can imagine—and reward you more than you could hope.

<Callout type="important">
  Church planting is not for those looking for an easier path. It's often harder, lonelier, and more demanding than established church ministry.
</Callout>

### What Church Planting Requires

The Launch Playbook makes clear that successful church planting demands:

- **Much faith** — You'll face situations where only God can make a way
- **Much work** — The hours are long and the tasks are endless
- **Much perseverance** — Setbacks, disappointments, and discouragement are guaranteed

If any of these requirements gives you pause, that's not necessarily disqualifying—but it should prompt serious reflection.

---

## Questions to Discern Your Calling

### Spiritual Questions

**Is there an internal compulsion?**

A calling is more than interest or excitement. It's a deep, persistent sense that you *must* do this—that you won't be fully obedient to God if you don't. This compulsion survives discouragement, criticism, and doubt.

**Have others affirmed this calling?**

God rarely calls in isolation. Has your spouse affirmed this direction? Your pastor? Mature believers who know you well? If those closest to you consistently express concern, pay attention.

**Are you running toward something or away from something?**

Church planting should be a response to a positive calling, not an escape from a difficult situation. If you're frustrated with your current church or leadership, that's not a sufficient reason to plant.

### Character Questions

**Can you handle ambiguity and uncertainty?**

Church planting involves constant unknowns—where you'll meet, who will come, how you'll fund it, what challenges will arise. If you need predictability to thrive, this will be difficult.

**How do you respond to criticism and rejection?**

You will be criticized. People will leave. Some will actively oppose you. Your response to these realities reveals whether you have the resilience church planting requires.

**Are you teachable?**

Church planters who think they have all the answers rarely succeed. The best planters are hungry learners who seek wisdom from mentors, coaches, and predecessors.

<Callout type="tip">
  Ask three people who know you well to honestly assess your readiness. Give them permission to be candid—even if it's uncomfortable to hear.
</Callout>

### Practical Questions

**Is your family prepared for this?**

Church planting affects your entire household. Your spouse must be fully supportive—not just tolerant. If you have children, consider the impact on their stability, friendships, and church experience.

**Are you financially prepared for sacrifice?**

Most church planters experience significant financial pressure, especially in the early years. Some go without salary. Others take substantial pay cuts. Is your family prepared for this reality?

**Do you have the necessary skills—or access to them?**

Effective church planters need a combination of gifts: teaching, leadership, evangelism, administration, and pastoral care. You don't need all of these personally, but you need access to them through your team.

---

## Signs That Point Toward Calling

While every situation is unique, these indicators often accompany a genuine calling to church planting:

| Indicator | What It Looks Like |
|-----------|-------------------|
| **Persistent burden** | The desire doesn't fade with time or difficulty |
| **External affirmation** | Others consistently recognize leadership gifts |
| **Evangelistic fruit** | Track record of leading people to faith |
| **Leadership emergence** | People naturally follow and respond to your leadership |
| **Resilience under pressure** | You bounce back from setbacks rather than being crushed |
| **Alignment of circumstances** | Doors open, resources appear, people emerge |

---

## Signs That Suggest Waiting

Not every season is right for church planting, even if the calling is genuine:

- **Unresolved character issues** — Deal with these before planting
- **Marriage or family instability** — Shore up your foundation first
- **Lack of ministry experience** — Gain experience under another leader
- **No external affirmation** — Seek input from trusted voices
- **Running from problems** — Address current challenges first
- **Financial crisis** — Stabilize before adding the pressure of planting

<Callout type="warning">
  Planting a church will amplify existing weaknesses, not fix them. Address character issues and relational problems before you plant.
</Callout>

---

## The Role of Your Sending Church

If you're part of a church network or have a sending church, their affirmation matters significantly. They know you, have observed your ministry, and can speak to your readiness.

Churches that plant churches well typically have:

- A formal assessment process for potential planters
- Coaching and mentoring relationships
- Financial and relational support structures
- Accountability throughout the planting process

If your church or network doesn't affirm your readiness, take that seriously. They may see blind spots you can't.

---

## What If You're Unsure?

Uncertainty isn't disqualifying. Most church planters experience seasons of doubt. Consider these steps:

1. **Pray persistently** — Ask God to clarify your calling
2. **Seek counsel** — Talk with experienced church planters and mentors
3. **Get assessed** — Many networks offer formal assessment processes
4. **Serve faithfully** — Continue serving where you are while discerning
5. **Wait actively** — Preparation during uncertainty is never wasted

The goal isn't certainty—it's faithfulness. Move forward as God makes the path clear.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And I also say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build My church; and the gates of Hades will not overpower it."* — Matthew 16:18 (LSB)
</Callout>

Jesus builds His church. If He's calling you to partner with Him in planting, He will provide what you need. Your job is to discern, prepare, and obey.
articles.excerpt: A guide to discerning whether God is calling you to plant a church, with honest questions to consider before taking the leap.
articles.title: Is Church Planting Your Calling?

articles.content:
Before you launch, you need a clear picture of what you're aiming for. Vague aspirations like "plant a healthy church" don't provide enough direction. Specific, measurable goals give your team something concrete to work toward.

---

## Primary Launch Objectives

The Launch Playbook establishes two overarching objectives for church planting:

### Objective 1: Launch with a Mature Core

**Launch the church with a cohesive, mature group of 50-100 adult believers fully aligned with the vision, mission, and distinctives.**

This isn't just about numbers—it's about quality. You need people who are:
- **Cohesive** — Unified and working together
- **Mature** — Spiritually developed and stable
- **Aligned** — Embracing your vision, mission, and distinctives

<Callout type="important">
  Within this methodology, 50 is the lower end of the benchmark range and 100 is the target. Below 50 adults this model treats a plant as underpowered for launch: every person is critical, and normal attrition can create crisis. These are the benchmarks of this planting methodology, not a universal definition of a healthy church. Different contexts and models reasonably launch at very different sizes.
</Callout>

### Objective 2: Execute the Ministry Model

**Launch the church in such a way that it can bear fruit quickly by fully executing the ministry model for discipleship (ministry funnel).**

You're not just starting services—you're launching a disciple-making system. The [Worship/Walk/Work/Witness model](/wiki/discovery/the-worship-walk-work-witness-model) should be operational from day one, not something you'll "get to eventually."

---

## The 8 Key Objectives

The Launch Playbook identifies 8 specific objectives to accomplish before launch:

| # | Objective | Description |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | **Launch Team Size** | Grow to 50-100 adult believers prior to launch |
| 2 | **Facilities Secured** | Worship services, office space, and storage confirmed |
| 3 | **High Impact Service** | Service and ministry funnel ready to execute |
| 4 | **Finances in Place** | Budget funded; financial processes established |
| 5 | **Equipment Purchased** | All necessary equipment acquired and tested |
| 6 | **Training Completed** | Key responsibilities trained and ready |
| 7 | **Promotion Executed** | Community awareness campaign completed |
| 8 | **Ministry Teams Established** | Teams formed, trained, and ready to serve |

### Breaking Down Each Objective

**1. Launch Team Size (50-100 adults)**

This is your critical mass goal. Track your progress throughout the Core Group development phase:

| Core Group Size | Status |
|----------------|--------|
| Under 30 | High risk—keep growing |
| 30-50 | Minimum viable—proceed with caution |
| 50-75 | Solid foundation—good position |
| 75-100 | Strong—positioned for growth |
| 100+ | Excellent—ready to launch strong |

**2. Facilities Secured**

You need three types of space:
- **Worship facility** — Where you'll hold Sunday services
- **Office space** — Where ministry administration happens
- **Storage** — Where equipment is kept between services

Start the search early. Finding the right facility takes longer than expected.

**3. High Impact Service**

Your first service sets expectations. Plan for:
- Excellent worship experience
- Clear, compelling message
- Smooth children's ministry
- Effective guest assimilation
- Professional-level execution

**4. Finances in Place**

Before launch, establish:
- Operating budget for first year
- Financial reserves (3-6 months recommended)
- Giving processes and systems
- Financial accountability structures

**5. Equipment Purchased**

Major categories include:
- Sound system
- Video/projection
- Lighting
- Staging and signage
- Children's ministry supplies
- Hospitality equipment

**6. Training Completed**

Key areas requiring training:
- Ministry philosophy and values
- Role-specific responsibilities
- Technical skills (sound, video, etc.)
- Guest assimilation processes
- Safety and security protocols

**7. Promotion Executed**

Get the word out through:
- Personal invitations (most effective)
- Social media presence
- Community advertising
- Direct mail (if appropriate)
- Partner church announcements

**8. Ministry Teams Established**

Form teams for each major area:
- Worship and production
- Children's ministry
- Guest services and assimilation
- Small groups
- Facilities and setup
- Administration and finance
- Promotion and communications
- Technology
- Prayer

---

## Ministry Teams to Establish

The Launch Playbook specifically identifies these teams to have operational by launch:

| Team | Primary Responsibility |
|------|----------------------|
| **Worship Leader and Team** | Leading corporate worship |
| **Children's Ministry** | Safe, engaging children's experiences |
| **Assimilation** | Guest follow-up and integration |
| **Small Groups** | Community and discipleship structure |
| **Administration/Finance** | Financial management and operations |
| **Facilities** | Setup, teardown, and facility care |
| **Promotion** | Marketing and community awareness |
| **Technology** | Website, systems, and technical support |

<Callout type="tip">
  You don't need large teams—you need competent leaders. In many cases, a leader with 2-3 volunteers is sufficient for launch. Teams grow after launch as the church grows.
</Callout>

---

## Setting Your Personal Goals

Beyond organizational objectives, establish personal goals for yourself as the planter:

### Spiritual Goals

- Daily prayer and Scripture engagement
- Weekly Sabbath rest
- Regular time with a mentor or coach
- Specific areas of character growth

### Relational Goals

- Protected family time
- Investment in Core Group relationships
- Building relationships outside the church plant
- Maintaining existing friendships

### Leadership Goals

- Skills to develop
- Books to read
- Training to complete
- Habits to establish

<Callout type="warning">
  Church planters often sacrifice personal health for ministry progress. Don't do this. A burned-out planter hurts the church more than a delayed launch.
</Callout>

---

## Making Goals SMART

Effective goals are SMART:

| Element | Question | Example |
|---------|----------|---------|
| **Specific** | What exactly will you accomplish? | "Recruit 60 adults for Core Group" |
| **Measurable** | How will you know you've achieved it? | "Track weekly attendance" |
| **Achievable** | Is this realistic? | "Based on network size and timeline" |
| **Relevant** | Does this matter for the mission? | "Critical mass enables launch" |
| **Time-bound** | When will this be complete? | "By March 1st" |

Convert vague goals into SMART goals:

| Vague Goal | SMART Goal |
|------------|------------|
| "Build a Core Group" | "Recruit and develop 75 committed adults by June 1st" |
| "Raise money" | "Secure $50,000 in committed monthly giving by launch date" |
| "Find a facility" | "Sign facility agreement by April 15th" |
| "Train the team" | "Complete Peak Performance training for all ministry leaders by August 1st" |

---

## Tracking Progress

Goals mean nothing without accountability. Establish systems to track progress:

### Weekly Review

Each week, assess:
- Core Group attendance and growth
- Giving totals and trends
- Key milestones approaching
- Obstacles or concerns

### Monthly Reporting

Monthly, report to your coach, elders, or accountability partners:
- Progress against each objective
- Wins and celebrations
- Challenges and needs
- Adjustments to plans

### Milestone Celebrations

When you hit key milestones, celebrate! This:
- Encourages the team
- Builds momentum
- Reinforces progress
- Creates memories

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"The thoughts of the diligent lead surely to profit, But everyone who is hasty comes surely to poverty."* — Proverbs 21:5 (LSB)
</Callout>

Clear goals provide direction. Measured progress provides motivation. Set your targets, track your progress, and adjust as you learn. God honors faithful planning even as He sovereignly directs your steps.
articles.excerpt: Establish clear, measurable goals for your church plant launch, including primary objectives and key milestones to aim for.
articles.title: Setting Your Initial Goals

articles.content:
At the heart of effective church ministry is a clear model for discipleship—a pathway that moves people from wherever they are toward spiritual maturity. The **Worship/Walk/Work/Witness** model (the 4 W's) provides this framework, guiding both individual growth and church structure.

---

## What is the Worship/Walk/Work/Witness Model?

The 4 W's model describes four dimensions of authentic discipleship. A mature follower of Jesus doesn't just embrace one dimension—they integrate all four:

| Dimension | Focus | Key Question |
|-----------|-------|--------------|
| **Worship** | Relationship with God | "Am I loving God with all my heart?" |
| **Walk** | Relationship with believers | "Am I growing in community with other Christians?" |
| **Work** | Service to the body | "Am I using my gifts to serve the church?" |
| **Witness** | Sharing the Gospel | "Am I sharing Jesus with those who don't know Him?" |

This isn't a sequential process where you complete one before starting another. All four dimensions develop simultaneously, though emphasis may shift in different seasons.

<Callout type="insight">
  Healthy disciples don't just worship, or just walk, or just work, or just witness. They integrate all four in a rhythm of life that reflects the fullness of following Jesus.
</Callout>

---

## The Four Dimensions Explained

### WORSHIP — Loving God

Worship encompasses everything we do to cultivate our relationship with God:

- **Corporate worship** — Gathering with believers to praise, pray, and hear God's Word
- **Personal devotion** — Daily time in Scripture, prayer, and reflection
- **Lifestyle worship** — Living all of life as an offering to God

**Signs of growth in worship:**
- Hunger for God's Word
- Consistent prayer life
- Awareness of God's presence throughout the day
- Hearts moved by God's character and works
- Priority of gathering with God's people

**Dangers of worship in isolation:**
- Private faith disconnected from community
- Spiritual consumption without contribution
- Self-focused spirituality

---

### WALK — Growing in Community

Walk encompasses our relationships with other believers and our growth in community:

- **Small groups** — Intentional, consistent gatherings for study, prayer, and care
- **Discipleship relationships** — One-on-one mentoring and accountability
- **Church family** — Belonging to a community of believers

**Signs of growth in walk:**
- Deep, authentic relationships with other believers
- Willingness to be known and to know others
- Active participation in a small group
- Giving and receiving care in times of need
- Pursuing reconciliation when conflict arises

**Dangers of walk in isolation:**
- Holy huddle mentality
- Inward-focused community
- Shallow relationships without spiritual depth

---

### WORK — Serving the Body

Work encompasses how we use our gifts to serve the church and build up the body:

- **Ministry service** — Using gifts to serve within the church
- **Team participation** — Contributing to ministry teams
- **Leadership development** — Growing in responsibility and influence

**Signs of growth in work:**
- Active service in the church
- Faithful stewardship of gifts and abilities
- Willingness to take on responsibility
- Generosity with time, talent, and treasure
- Investment in developing others

**Dangers of work in isolation:**
- Burnout from serving without being filled
- Activity without intimacy with God
- Ministry becoming identity rather than overflow

---

### WITNESS — Sharing the Gospel

Witness is the outward dimension of discipleship—sharing the Good News about Jesus Christ with those who don't yet know Him. This is a vital aspect in the life of a growing disciple.

- **Personal evangelism** — Sharing your faith in everyday conversations
- **Intentional relationships** — Building authentic connections with non-believers
- **Gospel proclamation** — Clearly communicating the message of salvation

**Signs of growth in witness:**
- Natural conversations about faith with non-believers
- Relationships with people outside the church
- Confidence in articulating the Gospel
- Heart broken for the lost
- Inviting others to church and spiritual conversations
- Praying regularly for specific non-believers

**Dangers of witness in isolation:**
- Evangelism without discipleship (converts without community)
- Treating people as projects rather than people
- Neglecting personal spiritual health while focused on others

<Callout type="important">
  Sharing the Good News about Jesus Christ is a vital aspect in the life of a growing disciple. Encourage believers to share the Gospel with those around them in loving and intentional ways.
</Callout>

---

## The Ministry Funnel

The 4 W's model also shapes how churches structure their ministries. Think of it as a funnel that moves people toward deeper engagement, with witness as the outward overflow:

```
      WORSHIP
  (Corporate Gatherings)
          ↓
        WALK
    (Small Groups)
          ↓
        WORK
   (Ministry Teams)
          ↓
      WITNESS
  (Reaching the Lost)
          ↓
    [New people enter at Worship]
```

### How the Funnel Works

**Entry Point: Corporate Worship**

Most people first encounter the church through Sunday services. This is the widest part of the funnel—the most accessible entry point. Here people:
- Experience worship and teaching
- Begin to understand the church's values and vision
- See the community in action
- Feel welcomed and valued

**Deeper Engagement: Small Groups (Walk)**

From corporate worship, people are invited into small groups where they:
- Build authentic relationships
- Study Scripture together
- Share life's joys and struggles
- Receive care and provide care to others
- Experience accountability and encouragement

**Active Investment: Ministry Teams (Work)**

As people grow, they move into active service through ministry teams:
- Using their gifts to serve others
- Taking ownership of the church's mission
- Multiplying their impact through leadership
- Supporting the church's ministries

**Outward Overflow: Evangelism (Witness)**

Mature disciples naturally overflow into witness:
- Sharing their faith with friends, family, and neighbors
- Inviting others into the community
- Living as ambassadors for Christ in daily life
- Bringing new people into the funnel at Worship

<Callout type="tip">
  The funnel isn't about hierarchy or status. It's about depth of engagement and spiritual maturity. Someone active in witness should still be worshiping, walking in community, and working in service.
</Callout>

---

## Why This Model Matters for Church Planting

Understanding the 4 W's shapes your church plant in several ways:

### It Defines Discipleship Goals

You're not just trying to get people to attend services. You're developing **authentic disciples who Worship God, Walk with believers, Work in service, and Witness for Christ**. This holistic vision prevents the common mistake of measuring success by attendance alone.

### It Structures Your Ministries

As you plan what ministries to launch, the model guides your priorities:

| Phase | Ministry Focus |
|-------|----------------|
| **Pre-Launch** | Small group foundation (Walk) |
| **Launch** | Corporate worship established (Worship) |
| **Post-Launch** | Ministry teams developed (Work) |
| **Ongoing** | Evangelism culture cultivated (Witness) |

### It Guides Your Measurements

Instead of just counting attendance, you evaluate health across all four dimensions:
- Are people engaging in corporate worship?
- Are people connected in small groups?
- Are people serving in ministry?
- Are people sharing their faith and bringing others?

### It Shapes Your Training

Your Core Group and Launch Team need training in all four areas:
- Leading and participating in worship
- Facilitating and participating in small groups
- Serving effectively in ministry roles
- Sharing faith naturally and confidently

---

## Implementing the 4 W's

### In Vision Meetings

Teach the model early. Use visual banners for each of the 4 W's mentioned in the Vision Meeting Kit. Help prospective Core Group members understand:
- This is how we define spiritual maturity
- This is how our church will be structured
- This is what we're inviting you into

### In Core Group Development

Model all four dimensions in your Core Group gatherings:
- **Worship** — Begin with worship and devotion
- **Walk** — Foster authentic community and care
- **Work** — Assign responsibilities and serve together
- **Witness** — Encourage and train for personal evangelism

### In Launch Team Training

Train your team specifically in each dimension:
- **Worship** — Peak Performance training on worship philosophy
- **Walk** — Small Group 101 training
- **Work** — Ministry-specific training for service roles
- **Witness** — Evangelism training and accountability

<Callout type="important">
  Don't wait until launch to implement the model. Your Core Group experience should embody all 4 W's from the beginning.
</Callout>

---

## Balanced Growth

The healthiest churches—and the healthiest disciples—maintain balance across all four dimensions. Watch for imbalance:

| Imbalance | Symptoms | Correction |
|-----------|----------|------------|
| **All Worship** | Consumers not contributors; no outward focus | Emphasize community, service, and witness |
| **All Walk** | Inward-focused; holy huddle mentality | Emphasize service and evangelism |
| **All Work** | Burnout; activity without intimacy | Emphasize rest, worship, and community |
| **All Witness** | Shallow converts; no discipleship depth | Emphasize worship, community, and service |

Regular evaluation helps identify and correct drift before it becomes entrenched.

---

## The Witness Imperative

While all four dimensions matter equally, witness deserves special emphasis because it's often neglected. Many Christians are comfortable worshiping, walking in community, and even serving—but sharing their faith feels intimidating.

**Why witness matters:**
- It's commanded by Christ (Matthew 28:19-20)
- It's the natural overflow of a transformed life
- It's how the church grows and multiplies
- It keeps the church from becoming inward-focused

**How to cultivate a witness culture:**
- Model it — Leaders share their own evangelism stories
- Train for it — Equip people with simple tools and approaches
- Celebrate it — Publicly honor those who share their faith
- Expect it — Make witness a normal part of discipleship conversations
- Pray for it — Regularly pray for the lost and for boldness

<Callout type="tip">
  Witness doesn't require a special gift or personality. Every believer can learn to share their story and the Gospel in natural, loving ways. Start by training your Core Group to share their testimony in 2-3 minutes.
</Callout>

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be My witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the end of the earth."* — Acts 1:8 (LSB)
</Callout>

The Worship/Walk/Work/Witness model provides a simple, biblical framework for developing disciples and structuring ministry. Embrace it, teach it, and build your church around it. A church strong in all 4 W's will be healthy, growing, and multiplying.
articles.excerpt: Understanding the 4 W's discipleship model—Worship, Walk, Work, and Witness—that guides spiritual formation and church structure.
articles.title: The Worship/Walk/Work/Witness Model

articles.content:
Every healthy church is built on foundational pillars—non-negotiable, biblically-rooted values that define the congregation's identity, culture, and direction. Before you launch, you need to know what your pillars are and why they matter.

---

## What Are Church Pillars?

**Church pillars are the fundamental, non-negotiable, and biblically-based core values that define a congregation's identity, culture, and strategic direction.**

Think of them as the load-bearing walls of your church. Everything else can be adjusted, renovated, or changed over time—but the pillars remain constant. They answer the question: *What will this church always be about, regardless of circumstances?*

<Callout type="insight">
  Pillars aren't programs or preferences. They're the unchanging commitments that shape every decision, ministry, and priority in your church.
</Callout>

### Why Pillars Matter

Pillars serve several critical functions:

| Function | How It Works |
|----------|--------------|
| **Identity** | They define who you are as a church |
| **Decision-making** | They provide criteria for evaluating opportunities |
| **Unity** | They create alignment among leaders and members |
| **Accountability** | They establish standards for evaluating faithfulness |
| **Communication** | They give language for explaining your church to others |

Without clear pillars, churches drift. Decisions become arbitrary. Unity becomes difficult. New members don't understand what makes this church distinctive.

---

## Biblical Foundation for Pillars

The concept of church pillars is rooted in Scripture. The early church in Acts 2 provides a foundational model:

> *"And they were continually devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers."* — Acts 2:42 (LSB)

From this passage, many churches derive four foundational pillars:

1. **Teaching** — The apostles' doctrine (Scripture)
2. **Fellowship** — Authentic community
3. **Worship** — Breaking of bread (communion, worship)
4. **Prayer** — Consistent, fervent communication with God

These aren't the only valid pillars, but they represent biblically-grounded categories that have shaped churches for two thousand years.

---

## Common Pillar Frameworks

Different churches articulate their pillars in different ways. Here are several examples:

### The Acts 2 Model

| Pillar | Focus |
|--------|-------|
| Teaching | Scripture, doctrine, discipleship |
| Fellowship | Community, relationships, care |
| Worship | Praise, communion, adoration |
| Prayer | Individual and corporate prayer |

### The Strategic Model

| Pillar | Focus |
|--------|-------|
| Invite | Evangelism, outreach |
| Connect | Assimilation, community |
| Disciple | Growth, maturity |
| Send | Multiplication, mission |

### The Proclamation Model

| Pillar | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Unapologetic Preaching | Proclaiming the authority of God's Word without apology |
| Unashamed Worship | Lifting high the name of Jesus through worship |
| Unceasing Prayer | Believing firmly in the power of prayer |
| Unafraid Witness | Sharing the good news of Jesus with boldness |

### The Reformation Model (Five Solas)

| Pillar | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| Scripture Alone | The Bible as sole authority |
| Christ Alone | Salvation through Christ only |
| Grace Alone | Saved by grace, not works |
| Faith Alone | Justified through faith |
| Glory to God Alone | All for God's glory |

<Callout type="tip">
  Don't feel pressured to be original. If an existing framework captures your convictions, adopt it. The goal is clarity and faithfulness, not creativity.
</Callout>

---

## If You're Planting Within a Network

If you're planting as part of a church network or from a sending church, your pillars may already be defined. This is actually an advantage:

**Benefits of inherited pillars:**
- Proven and refined over time
- Shared language with partner churches
- Built-in accountability and alignment
- Resources and training already developed

**Your responsibility:**
- Understand them deeply (not just memorize them)
- Be able to articulate why each pillar matters
- Commit to them genuinely, not just formally
- Teach them clearly to your Core Group

<Callout type="important">
  If you can't wholeheartedly embrace your network's pillars, that's a serious conversation to have before planting. Misalignment on fundamentals creates problems later.
</Callout>

---

## Defining Your Own Pillars

If you're planting independently or your network gives flexibility, you'll need to define your own pillars. Here's a process:

### Step 1: Start with Scripture

Begin with biblical texts that capture the essence of the church. Key passages include:

- **Acts 2:42-47** — The early church's practices
- **Matthew 28:18-20** — The Great Commission
- **Ephesians 4:11-16** — Equipping for ministry
- **1 Peter 2:9** — The identity of God's people

What themes emerge? What does Scripture emphasize about the church's purpose and practice?

### Step 2: Identify Non-Negotiables

Ask yourself:
- What must this church always be about?
- What would we never compromise, regardless of pressure?
- What distinguishes a healthy church from an unhealthy one?
- What burns in my heart for this congregation?

Write down everything that comes to mind, then look for patterns and themes.

### Step 3: Consolidate into 3-5 Pillars

Too many pillars become impossible to remember and communicate. Aim for 3-5 core commitments that are:

- **Biblical** — Rooted in Scripture
- **Memorable** — Easy to recall and repeat
- **Comprehensive** — Covering the essential dimensions of church life
- **Distinctive** — Reflecting your specific convictions and calling

### Step 4: Articulate Clearly

For each pillar, be able to answer:
- What does this mean?
- Why does it matter?
- What does it look like in practice?
- What Scripture supports it?

### Step 5: Test and Refine

Share your pillars with:
- Your spouse
- Trusted mentors
- Your coach (if you have one)
- Potential Core Group members

Listen to feedback. Refine the language. Make sure they communicate clearly.

---

## How Pillars Shape Your Church

Once defined, pillars should influence everything:

| Area | How Pillars Apply |
|------|-------------------|
| **Preaching** | Teaching reinforces and applies pillar values |
| **Programs** | Ministries align with and advance pillar commitments |
| **Decisions** | Opportunities evaluated against pillar priorities |
| **Hiring** | Staff must embody and champion the pillars |
| **Membership** | New members taught and expected to embrace pillars |
| **Budget** | Resources allocated according to pillar priorities |

<Callout type="warning">
  Pillars on paper mean nothing. They must be lived, taught, and reinforced constantly. If your actual priorities don't match your stated pillars, people will notice.
</Callout>

---

## Teaching Pillars to Your Core Group

Your Core Group must deeply understand and embrace your pillars. Plan to:

1. **Introduce them early** — From the first Vision Meeting
2. **Explain them thoroughly** — Don't assume understanding
3. **Illustrate them concretely** — Show what they look like in practice
4. **Reinforce them constantly** — Reference them in teaching and decisions
5. **Model them personally** — Live what you teach

The goal is a Core Group that can articulate the pillars and explain why they matter—not just recite them.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And they were continually devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers."* — Acts 2:42 (LSB)
</Callout>

Your pillars define what you're building. Take time to get them right. A church built on solid pillars will stand firm through any storm.
articles.excerpt: Learn what church pillars are, why they matter for your plant, and how to identify or adopt the foundational values that will shape your church's identity.
articles.title: Understanding the 4 Pillars

articles.content:
Not all church plants succeed equally. Some launch strong and bear fruit for decades. Others struggle from day one and never gain traction. What makes the difference?

After observing numerous church plants, 8 critical success factors consistently distinguish healthy, fruitful launches from those that struggle.

---

## The 8 Factors

### 1. Vision Casting

**The ability and passion of the Senior Pastor to cast the vision in such a way that transforms interested individuals into COMMITTED, COMPELLED, CONTAGIOUS, and COURAGEOUS Core Group members.**

Vision casting isn't just describing what you want to build. It's painting a picture so compelling that people can't help but want to be part of it. It's helping them see what could be and inspiring them to sacrifice for it.

<Callout type="insight">
  People don't join organizations—they join movements. Your vision casting must
  make them feel the weight of what God is doing and the privilege of
  participating in it.
</Callout>

**Key questions:**
- Can people articulate the vision after hearing you share it?
- Do they feel compelled to tell others?
- Are they willing to sacrifice to make it happen?

---

### 2. Shared Ownership

**Core Group members own the responsibility equally with the Senior Pastor for growing the Core Group.**

The Senior Pastor cannot build the Core Group alone. If growth depends entirely on one person's networking and invitations, you'll plateau quickly.

Shared ownership means every Core Group member:
- Feels personally responsible for growth
- Actively invites people to Vision Meetings
- Owns the success or failure of the plant

<Callout type="warning">
  If only the Senior Pastor is inviting people, you have a club, not a movement.
  Shared ownership is non-negotiable.
</Callout>

---

### 3. Critical Mass

**Core Group grows to this methodology's benchmark of 50 COMMITTED, COMPELLED, CONTAGIOUS, and COURAGEOUS adults, with 100 as the target.**

Numbers matter—not for vanity, but for sustainability. A church plant needs enough people to:
- Staff all ministry teams effectively
- Create energy in worship gatherings
- Provide financial sustainability
- Weather normal attrition without crisis

| Core Group Size | Reality |
|----------------|---------|
| Under 30 | High risk—likely underpowered for launch |
| 30-50 | Minimum viable—every person is critical |
| 50-75 | Solid foundation—room for some attrition |
| 75-100 | Strong position—multiple people for each role |
| 100+ | Excellent—positioned for growth from day one |

---

### 4. Unity

**A deep work of God's Spirit to grow the Core Group in unity and cohesiveness.**

Unity isn't just the absence of conflict—it's the presence of genuine love, shared vision, and mutual commitment. A unified Core Group can weather any storm. A divided one will fracture under pressure.

Unity requires:
- Time together (you can't rush community)
- Shared experiences (victories and challenges)
- Healthy conflict resolution (disagreements handled well)
- Common values (alignment on what matters most)

---

### 5. Prayer

**A commitment to consistent, fervent prayer which permeates the Core Group.**

Church planting is a spiritual battle. Only God can change hearts, open doors, and build His church. Prayer isn't an add-on to your strategy—it is your strategy.

<Callout type="important">
  A prayerless church plant is a powerless church plant. Make prayer central,
  not peripheral.
</Callout>

Prayer should be:
- **Consistent** — Regular rhythms, not sporadic bursts
- **Fervent** — Earnest and passionate, not routine
- **Permeating** — Woven through everything, not isolated to meetings

---

### 6. Generosity

**A sacrificial spirit of generosity evidenced among the Core Group to adequately launch the church.**

Launching a church costs money. Equipment, facilities, marketing, and operations all require funding. The primary source of that funding is the Core Group itself.

Generosity in the Core Group:
- Demonstrates commitment (people invest in what they believe in)
- Funds necessary purchases
- Models for future members what giving looks like
- Creates shared ownership through shared sacrifice

---

### 7. Emerging Leadership

**Leadership emerges from the Core Group to comprehensively own the 8 primary responsibilities of the launch.**

The Senior Pastor cannot do everything. For a healthy launch, leaders must emerge to own:

| Responsibility | Leader Needed |
|---------------|---------------|
| Worship | Worship Leader |
| Children's Ministry | Children's Ministry Leader |
| Facilities | Facilities Leader |
| Assimilation | Assimilation Leader |
| Small Groups | Small Group Leader |
| Promotion | Promotion Leader |
| Technology | Technology Leader |
| Project Management | Launch Coordinator |

<Callout type="tip">
  Identify potential leaders early. Give them increasing responsibility. By
  launch, they should fully own their areas with minimal supervision.
</Callout>

---

### 8. Comprehensive Training

**Training of the Core Group in the ministry model and the key responsibilities of the launch.**

Enthusiasm isn't enough. Your team needs to know how to execute their responsibilities with excellence. Training should cover:

- The ministry model and philosophy
- Specific role responsibilities
- Practical skills for execution
- Problem-solving for common issues

Untrained volunteers create chaos. Trained volunteers create excellence.

---

## How the Factors Work Together

These 8 factors aren't isolated—they reinforce each other:

```
VISION CASTING → attracts people with 4 C's
        ↓
SHARED OWNERSHIP → multiplies recruitment
        ↓
CRITICAL MASS → enables ministry teams
        ↓
UNITY → creates cohesive culture
        ↓
PRAYER → sustains spiritual vitality
        ↓
GENEROSITY → funds necessary resources
        ↓
EMERGING LEADERSHIP → distributes responsibility
        ↓
COMPREHENSIVE TRAINING → enables excellent execution
```

Weakness in any factor creates a bottleneck. Strength across all factors creates momentum.

---

## Self-Assessment

Regularly evaluate your church plant against these 8 factors:

| Factor | Strong | Adequate | Needs Work |
|--------|--------|----------|------------|
| Vision Casting | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |
| Shared Ownership | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |
| Critical Mass | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |
| Unity | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |
| Prayer | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |
| Generosity | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |
| Emerging Leadership | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |
| Comprehensive Training | ◯ | ◯ | ◯ |

Identify your weakest factor and make it your focus. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Unless Yahweh builds the house, They labor in vain who build it;"* — Psalm 127:1 (LSB)
</Callout>

These 8 factors position you for success, but ultimately God builds the church. Stay dependent on Him while faithfully executing what He's called you to do.
articles.excerpt: An overview of the 8 critical success factors that determine whether a church plant launches healthy and bears fruit.
articles.title: 8 Critical Success Factors Overview

articles.content:
Not all meetings are created equal. Many church plant gatherings become aimless—nice fellowship without clear purpose. To maximize every gathering, structure them around three key objectives: **Inspire**, **Instill**, and **Inform**.

---

## The Three Objectives

Every Core Group and Launch Team meeting should accomplish at least one of these objectives—ideally all three:

| Objective | Focus | Key Question |
|-----------|-------|--------------|
| **Inspire** | Vision and worship | "Are hearts stirred for what God is doing?" |
| **Instill** | Culture and values | "Are we deepening alignment with who we are?" |
| **Inform** | Training and updates | "Are people equipped to take action?" |

<Callout type="insight">
  These aren't separate meeting types—they're layers that should be present in every gathering. The best meetings inspire hearts, instill values, and inform minds in a single session.
</Callout>

---

## Objective 1: INSPIRE — Cast Vision

**Inspire gatherings renew people's vision of the Living God and remind them why you're planting the church.**

People leak vision. The excitement from last month fades. The pressures of daily life crowd out the calling. Regular inspiration counteracts this natural drift.

### What Inspiration Accomplishes

- Renews people's awareness of God's greatness
- Reminds them of the privilege of participating in His work
- Rekindles passion when energy wanes
- Creates unity around shared purpose
- Provides spiritual fuel for the hard work ahead

### How to Inspire

**Through worship:**
- Begin gatherings with worship and prayer
- Don't rush this—let people genuinely connect with God
- Worship reminds everyone who they're serving

**Through Scripture:**
- Share devotional thoughts that connect to the mission
- Let God's Word speak to hearts
- Ground the work in eternal truth

**Through stories:**
- Share what God is doing locally, nationally, and globally
- Celebrate answered prayers and milestones
- Tell stories of lives being changed

**Through vision casting:**
- Paint a picture of what the future church will look like
- Help people see beyond today's challenges to tomorrow's fruit
- Connect current sacrifice to future impact

<Callout type="tip">
  Great leaders continually cast vision. Don't assume people remember the vision just because you shared it once. Repeat it regularly, from different angles, with fresh illustrations.
</Callout>

---

## Objective 2: INSTILL — Enculturate the Team

**Instill gatherings thoroughly enculturate members in values, distinctives, and DNA.**

Culture isn't taught once—it's absorbed over time through repeated exposure. Instill meetings create that exposure, ensuring everyone deeply understands and embraces what makes your church distinctive.

### What Instilling Accomplishes

- Deepens understanding of core values
- Creates alignment on what matters most
- Builds shared language and understanding
- Develops ownership of the church's identity
- Prevents drift from foundational commitments

### How to Instill

**Through teaching:**
- Systematically teach through your 4 Pillars
- Explain the Worship/Walk/Work model
- Unpack your ministry philosophy and distinctives
- Don't assume—make implicit values explicit

**Through modeling:**
- Let people see values lived out, not just taught
- Share how you're applying values in real decisions
- Demonstrate the culture you want to create

**Through experience:**
- Visit established churches that embody your values
- Attend training events together
- Create shared experiences that reinforce culture

**Through discussion:**
- Process values together, not just lecture
- Let people ask questions and wrestle
- Build understanding through dialogue

<Callout type="important">
  Alignment creates power. When everyone deeply understands and resonates with your values, enormous energy, joy, and momentum are produced. Misalignment creates friction and confusion.
</Callout>

### What to Instill

| Area | Content |
|------|---------|
| **Theology** | Doctrinal commitments, statement of faith |
| **Philosophy** | Why you do ministry the way you do |
| **Values** | The 4 Pillars and core commitments |
| **Model** | Worship/Walk/Work ministry funnel |
| **Distinctives** | What makes this church unique |
| **Expectations** | What you're asking of Core Group members |

---

## Objective 3: INFORM — Train the Team

**Inform gatherings equip people with the knowledge and skills they need to take action.**

Inspiration without information leaves people stirred but stuck. They want to help but don't know how. Inform meetings bridge the gap between motivation and execution.

### What Informing Accomplishes

- Transfers practical knowledge and skills
- Prepares people for their specific roles
- Provides updates on progress and next steps
- Enables confident action
- Reduces anxiety about the unknown

### How to Inform

**Through training:**
- Ministry-specific skills development
- Role-based preparation
- Hands-on practice and rehearsal
- Outside training events and resources

**Through updates:**
- Progress reports on key milestones
- Timeline and deadline communication
- Changes and adjustments to plans
- Celebration of what's been accomplished

**Through next steps:**
- Clear action items for individuals and teams
- Specific assignments with deadlines
- Resources needed for completion
- Follow-up and accountability structures

<Callout type="tip">
  Information overload kills action. Focus each meeting on the most important information people need right now. Save the rest for later.
</Callout>

---

## Balancing the Three Objectives

### Early Core Group Phase

**Emphasis: Inspire + Instill**

Early on, focus primarily on vision casting and cultural formation. People need to fall in love with the vision and deeply absorb the values. Training can wait until you're closer to launch.

| Objective | Approximate Time |
|-----------|-----------------|
| Inspire | 30-40% |
| Instill | 40-50% |
| Inform | 10-20% |

### Launch Team Phase

**Emphasis: All Three**

Once you transition to Launch Team with a set date, training becomes critical. Now you need all three objectives in balance.

| Objective | Approximate Time |
|-----------|-----------------|
| Inspire | 25-30% |
| Instill | 25-30% |
| Inform | 40-50% |

### Pre-Launch Phase

**Emphasis: Inform + Inspire**

In the final weeks, training intensifies. But don't neglect inspiration—people need spiritual fuel for the sprint to launch.

| Objective | Approximate Time |
|-----------|-----------------|
| Inspire | 20-25% |
| Instill | 15-20% |
| Inform | 55-65% |

---

## Structuring a Meeting

Here's a typical meeting structure that incorporates all three objectives:

| Time | Activity | Objective |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 0:00-0:15 | Worship and prayer | Inspire |
| 0:15-0:25 | Devotional/Scripture | Inspire |
| 0:25-0:35 | Vision updates and stories | Inspire |
| 0:35-0:55 | Teaching on values/model | Instill |
| 0:55-1:15 | Training content | Inform |
| 1:15-1:25 | Updates and next steps | Inform |
| 1:25-1:30 | Prayer and dismissal | Inspire |

<Callout type="warning">
  Don't skip the Inspire portion to save time. You can have the most informed team in the world, but without inspiration, they'll burn out or drift away.
</Callout>

---

## Common Mistakes

### All Inspire, No Inform

**Symptom:** People feel excited but don't know what to do.

**Solution:** Add practical training and clear next steps to every meeting.

### All Inform, No Inspire

**Symptom:** Meetings feel like work sessions; passion fades.

**Solution:** Always begin with worship and vision. Connect tasks to the bigger picture.

### Neglecting Instill

**Symptom:** People are busy but not aligned; confusion about values and direction.

**Solution:** Systematically teach your distinctives. Don't assume—make values explicit.

### One-Size-Fits-All

**Symptom:** Same meeting format regardless of phase or need.

**Solution:** Adjust emphasis based on where you are in the launch process.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And let us consider how to stimulate one another to love and good deeds, not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day drawing near."* — Hebrews 10:24-25 (LSB)
</Callout>

Every meeting is an opportunity. When you intentionally inspire hearts, instill values, and inform minds, gatherings become transformative rather than transactional. Make every meeting count.
articles.excerpt: The three objectives that should shape every Core Group and Launch Team gathering—inspiring vision, instilling culture, and informing for action.
articles.title: Meeting Objectives: Inspire, Instill, Inform

articles.content:
Not everyone who expresses interest in your church plant should join your Core Group. Church planting is too demanding, too costly, and too important to fill your team with people who aren't fully ready.

The 4 C's define the character and commitment required. Every Core Group member must be **COMMITTED**, **COMPELLED**, **CONTAGIOUS**, and **COURAGEOUS**.

---

## Why the 4 C's Matter

Church planting is hard. You'll face:
- Financial pressure
- Spiritual opposition
- Relational conflict
- Exhaustion and discouragement
- Setbacks and disappointments

A Core Group filled with the right people will endure these challenges and emerge stronger. A Core Group with the wrong people will fracture under pressure, creating division and discouragement at the worst possible time.

<Callout type="important">
  The 4 C's aren't optional nice-to-haves. They're essential requirements. Be
  willing to grow slowly with the right people rather than quickly with the
  wrong ones.
</Callout>

---

## The 4 C's Explained

### 1. COMMITTED

**Fully dedicated to the vision, mission, and distinctives of the church plant.**

Commitment means more than casual interest. It means:

| Surface Interest | True Commitment |
|-----------------|-----------------|
| "This sounds interesting" | "I'm all in" |
| "I'll come when I can" | "This is my priority" |
| "I hope it works out" | "I'll sacrifice to make it work" |
| "Let me know if you need help" | "What do you need me to do?" |

**Signs of commitment:**
- Regular attendance at Vision Meetings and Core Group gatherings
- Willingness to rearrange schedules for church plant activities
- Financial giving that demonstrates sacrifice
- Following through on commitments and responsibilities

**Red flags:**
- Chronic absence or last-minute cancellations
- Unwillingness to adjust personal priorities
- Excuses for why they can't contribute
- Enthusiasm without follow-through

<Callout type="tip">
  Commitment is revealed over time. Don't rush people into the Core Group.
  Watch for consistent patterns of dedication before formalizing their role.
</Callout>

---

### 2. COMPELLED

**Driven by conviction to participate in this specific church plant.**

Compelled people don't need to be convinced—they feel an internal drive to be part of what God is doing. This isn't obligation or guilt; it's genuine passion.

**Signs of being compelled:**
- They articulate why this church plant matters to them personally
- They initiate conversations about the vision with others
- They bring ideas and energy, not just attendance
- They feel genuine excitement about the future

**Questions that reveal compulsion:**
- "Why do you want to be part of this?"
- "What excites you most about this church plant?"
- "How does this connect to what God is doing in your life?"

People who are truly compelled have answers that come from the heart, not rehearsed responses.

---

### 3. CONTAGIOUS

**Enthusiasm that spreads to others.**

Contagious people don't just hold the vision—they spread it. Their excitement is infectious. When they talk about the church plant, others want to know more.

**Characteristics of contagious people:**
- Natural evangelists for the vision
- Invite others to Vision Meetings without being asked
- Speak positively about the church plant in everyday conversations
- Their networks become aware of the church plant through organic sharing

<Callout type="insight">
  Contagious Core Group members are your best recruiting tool. One truly
  contagious person can bring more guests to Vision Meetings than all your
  marketing efforts combined.
</Callout>

**How to identify contagious people:**
- Who brought guests to the last Vision Meeting?
- Who talks about the church plant on social media?
- Who introduces you to their friends and family?
- Who asks for invitation cards to distribute?

If someone is excited but never shares that excitement with others, they may be committed but not contagious.

---

### 4. COURAGEOUS

**Willing to take risks and step out in faith.**

Church planting requires courage. The Core Group must be willing to:

- Leave comfortable church situations
- Invest time and money with uncertain outcomes
- Face opposition and criticism
- Persevere when things get difficult
- Try new things that might fail

**Signs of courage:**
- Willingness to have hard conversations
- Stepping up for difficult responsibilities
- Maintaining commitment during setbacks
- Speaking up when something needs to be said
- Taking initiative rather than waiting to be told

**Signs of insufficient courage:**
- Waiting to see if the plant will succeed before fully committing
- Hedging bets by maintaining backup options
- Avoiding any responsibility that involves risk
- Shrinking back when challenged or criticized

<Callout type="warning">
  Courageous doesn't mean reckless. Look for people who count the cost and still
  say yes—not people who blindly agree without understanding the sacrifice.
</Callout>

---

## Evaluating Potential Core Group Members

When someone expresses interest in joining the Core Group, evaluate them against all 4 C's:

| Quality | Questions to Consider |
|---------|----------------------|
| **Committed** | Are they consistently showing up? Following through? Prioritizing the plant? |
| **Compelled** | Do they have genuine internal motivation? Can they articulate why this matters to them? |
| **Contagious** | Are they spreading the vision? Bringing guests? Talking about the plant? |
| **Courageous** | Are they willing to sacrifice? Take risks? Persevere through difficulty? |

### The Interview Process

Before formalizing someone's place in the Core Group, have a direct conversation:

1. **Share expectations clearly** — Make sure they understand what's required
2. **Ask probing questions** — Don't accept surface answers
3. **Look for evidence** — Past behavior predicts future behavior
4. **Give them an out** — Make it easy to say no if they're not ready

It's better to have an awkward conversation now than a dysfunctional team member later.

---

## What If Someone Lacks One of the 4 C's?

Not everyone starts with all 4 C's fully developed. Consider:

| Situation | Approach |
|-----------|----------|
| **Missing one quality** | Coach them specifically in that area; revisit in 60-90 days |
| **Missing two qualities** | They're not ready; maintain relationship but don't include in Core Group |
| **Strong in all four** | Welcome them enthusiastically to the Core Group |

Some people can be developed. Others aren't ready for this particular role at this particular time. Discernment is required.

<Callout type="tip">
  When in doubt, wait. It's easier to add someone to the Core Group later than
  to remove them after they've joined.
</Callout>

---

## Cultivating the 4 C's in Your Core Group

The 4 C's aren't just recruitment criteria—they're ongoing development targets. Regularly cultivate these qualities:

**For Commitment:**
- Clearly communicate expectations
- Celebrate those who follow through
- Address lack of commitment directly

**For Compulsion:**
- Continually cast vision
- Share stories of God's work
- Connect individual roles to the larger mission

**For Contagiousness:**
- Train and equip for invitation
- Celebrate every guest brought
- Create easy on-ramps for inviting others

**For Courage:**
- Model courage yourself
- Normalize taking risks
- Support those who step out in faith

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith."* — 2 Timothy 4:7 (LSB)
</Callout>

Building a Core Group of COMMITTED, COMPELLED, CONTAGIOUS, and COURAGEOUS people takes time and discernment. Don't rush it. The quality of your Core Group determines the trajectory of your church plant.
articles.excerpt: Understanding the 4 essential qualities every Core Group member must possess for a successful church plant.
articles.title: The 4 C's: Committed, Compelled, Contagious, Courageous

articles.content:
Every healthy church is built on foundational pillars—non-negotiable, biblically-rooted values that define who you are and what you're about. These aren't programs or preferences. They're the unchanging commitments that shape every decision, ministry, and priority.

---

## What Are Church Pillars?

**Church pillars are the fundamental, non-negotiable, and biblically-based core values that define a congregation's identity, culture, and strategic direction.**

Think of them as the load-bearing walls of your church. Programs can change. Styles can evolve. Methods can adapt. But pillars remain constant. They answer the essential question: *What will this church always be about, regardless of circumstances?*

<Callout type="insight">
  Pillars aren't what you do—they're why you do it. They're not your activities—they're your convictions.
</Callout>

---

## Why Pillars Matter

Without clear pillars, churches drift. Decisions become arbitrary. Unity fragments. New members never understand what makes this church distinctive.

| Function | How Pillars Help |
|----------|-----------------|
| **Identity** | Define who you are as a church |
| **Decision-making** | Provide criteria for evaluating opportunities |
| **Unity** | Create alignment among leaders and members |
| **Accountability** | Establish standards for evaluating faithfulness |
| **Communication** | Give language for explaining your church |

---

## The Biblical Foundation

The concept of church pillars is rooted in Scripture. Acts 2:42 (LSB) provides the foundational model:

> *"And they were continually devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers."*

From this passage, four pillars emerge:

### 1. Teaching (The Word)

**The apostles' doctrine—Scripture as the foundation.**

This pillar commits the church to:
- Preaching and teaching God's Word faithfully
- Grounding all ministry in biblical truth
- Making disciples through scriptural instruction
- Holding doctrine as non-negotiable

**In practice:** Expository preaching, Bible studies, theological training, scriptural decision-making.

---

### 2. Fellowship (Community)

**Authentic community—life shared together.**

This pillar commits the church to:
- Genuine relationships, not surface connections
- Mutual care and accountability
- Shared life beyond Sunday gatherings
- Unity in diversity

**In practice:** Small groups, shared meals, life-on-life discipleship, care ministries.

---

### 3. Worship (Breaking of Bread)

**Corporate worship—gathering to honor God.**

This pillar commits the church to:
- Regular, vibrant corporate worship
- The Lord's Supper as central practice
- Lifestyle worship beyond Sunday
- God-centered rather than consumer-driven gatherings

**In practice:** Sunday services, communion, prayer meetings, worship nights.

---

### 4. Prayer

**Consistent, fervent prayer—dependence on God.**

This pillar commits the church to:
- Individual and corporate prayer as priority
- Dependence on God rather than self-effort
- Prayer permeating all ministries
- Spiritual warfare through intercession

**In practice:** Prayer teams, prayer meetings, prayer emphasis in services, fasting.

<Callout type="important">
  These four pillars from Acts 2 aren't the only valid framework, but they represent biblically-grounded categories that have shaped healthy churches for two thousand years.
</Callout>

---

## Alternative Pillar Frameworks

Different churches articulate their pillars in different ways while maintaining biblical fidelity. Here are several proven frameworks:

### The Proclamation Model

| Pillar | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Unapologetic Preaching** | Proclaiming God's Word without compromise |
| **Unashamed Worship** | Lifting high the name of Jesus |
| **Unceasing Prayer** | Believing firmly in the power of prayer |
| **Unafraid Witness** | Sharing the good news with boldness |

### The Strategic Model

| Pillar | Focus |
|--------|-------|
| **Invite** | Evangelism and outreach |
| **Connect** | Assimilation and community |
| **Disciple** | Growth and maturity |
| **Send** | Multiplication and mission |

### The Five Solas (Reformation Model)

| Pillar | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Scripture Alone** | The Bible as sole authority |
| **Christ Alone** | Salvation through Christ only |
| **Grace Alone** | Saved by grace, not works |
| **Faith Alone** | Justified through faith |
| **Glory to God Alone** | All for God's glory |

<Callout type="tip">
  Don't feel pressured to be original. If an existing framework captures your convictions, adopt it. The goal is clarity and faithfulness, not creativity.
</Callout>

---

## How Pillars Shape Everything

Once defined, pillars should influence every area of church life:

### Preaching and Teaching

Teaching reinforces pillar values. If prayer is a pillar, preach on prayer. If fellowship is a pillar, teach on community. Don't let pillars become slogans—keep them alive through consistent teaching.

### Ministry Programs

Every ministry should advance at least one pillar. If a program doesn't connect to your pillars, question whether it belongs. Resources are limited—invest in what matters most.

### Decision-Making

When opportunities arise, evaluate them against your pillars:
- Does this advance our core commitments?
- Does it align with who we are?
- Does it strengthen or distract from our pillars?

### Budget Allocation

Money reveals priorities. Your budget should reflect your pillars. If discipleship is a pillar but receives minimal funding, your stated values don't match your actual values.

### Staff and Leadership

Leaders must embody and champion the pillars. In hiring, evaluate candidates against pillar alignment. In development, train leaders to think through a pillar lens.

### Membership Expectations

New members should understand and embrace the pillars. Include pillar teaching in membership classes. Make clear that joining means committing to these values.

<Callout type="warning">
  Pillars on paper mean nothing. They must be lived, taught, and reinforced constantly. If your actual priorities don't match your stated pillars, people will notice—and trust will erode.
</Callout>

---

## Pillars in Church Planting

For church plants, pillars serve additional functions:

### They Attract the Right People

When you clearly communicate your pillars, people self-select. Those who resonate will engage; those who don't will look elsewhere. This is healthy—you want a unified Core Group, not a random collection.

### They Provide Consistency

In the chaos of planting, pillars keep you anchored. When you're overwhelmed with decisions, return to your pillars. They simplify choices and prevent drift.

### They Enable Delegation

As leadership emerges, pillars provide guardrails. Leaders can make decisions confidently when they understand the non-negotiables.

### They Create Culture

Culture is "how we do things here." Pillars define that. A church committed to prayer will develop a prayer culture. A church committed to biblical teaching will develop a learning culture. Pillars shape culture from day one.

---

## Teaching Pillars to Your Core Group

Your Core Group must deeply understand and embrace your pillars:

1. **Introduce early** — From the first Vision Meeting
2. **Explain thoroughly** — Don't assume understanding
3. **Illustrate concretely** — Show what they look like in practice
4. **Reinforce constantly** — Reference them in teaching and decisions
5. **Model personally** — Live what you teach

**The test:** Can your Core Group members articulate the pillars and explain why each matters? If not, keep teaching.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And they were continually devoting themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers."* — Acts 2:42 (LSB)
</Callout>

Your pillars define what you're building. Take time to get them right, teach them clearly, and live them consistently. A church built on solid pillars will stand firm through any storm.
articles.excerpt: Understanding church pillars—the foundational, non-negotiable values that define your congregation's identity and shape every decision.
articles.title: The 4 Pillars

articles.content:
Not everyone who attends a Vision Meeting and expresses interest is a good fit for your Core Group. Church planting is too demanding and too important to fill your team with people who aren't ready. The 5 Interview Criteria help you evaluate fit before formalizing commitment.

---

## Why Careful Evaluation Matters

It's tempting to accept anyone who shows enthusiasm. More people means more help, right?

Not necessarily.

The wrong people in your Core Group can:
- Drain energy instead of contributing it
- Create conflict and division
- Undermine culture and values
- Require excessive pastoral care at the wrong time
- Leave at critical moments, causing disruption

<Callout type="important">
  It's better to grow slowly with the right people than quickly with the wrong ones. A small, aligned Core Group outperforms a large, misaligned one every time.
</Callout>

---

## The 5 Criteria

When evaluating potential Core Group members, assess them across these five dimensions:

| Criterion | Key Question |
|-----------|--------------|
| **Maturity** | Are they spiritually and emotionally mature? |
| **Gifted** | Do they bring needed skills and abilities? |
| **Chemistry** | Is there good relational fit? |
| **Right Reasons** | Are they joining for healthy motivations? |
| **Season of Life** | Are they in a stable season? |

---

## Criterion 1: MATURITY

**Are they spiritually and emotionally mature?**

Church planting is spiritually intense. Your Core Group will face challenges that expose character weaknesses. Immature believers will struggle—and their struggles will become your problems.

### Spiritual Maturity Indicators

- Consistent personal devotional life
- Evidence of the fruit of the Spirit
- History of faithful church involvement
- Ability to handle disagreement graciously
- Teachable spirit
- Self-awareness of weaknesses

### Emotional Maturity Indicators

- Handles conflict constructively
- Takes responsibility rather than blaming
- Manages stress without destructive behavior
- Maintains appropriate boundaries
- Demonstrates resilience through difficulty
- Shows empathy and consideration for others

### Red Flags

- Chronic drama or conflict in relationships
- Inability to receive correction
- History of church hopping
- Unresolved major issues (addiction, marriage crisis)
- Excessive need for attention or validation
- Patterns of blaming others

<Callout type="tip">
  Maturity isn't about age or years as a Christian. Some young believers are remarkably mature; some longtime Christians never grow up. Look at fruit, not tenure.
</Callout>

---

## Criterion 2: GIFTED

**Do they bring needed skills and abilities?**

Every church plant needs specific skills to launch effectively. Evaluate what gifts a potential member brings and whether those gifts address current gaps.

### Gifts to Consider

| Area | Skills Needed |
|------|---------------|
| **Worship** | Musicians, vocalists, tech operators |
| **Children's Ministry** | Teachers, childcare, curriculum |
| **Hospitality** | Greeters, hosts, food preparation |
| **Administration** | Organization, finance, project management |
