| **Technology** | AV, website, social media |
| **Facilities** | Setup, logistics, maintenance |

### Questions to Ask

- What spiritual gifts has this person demonstrated?
- What skills do they bring from their profession or experience?
- Does this address a current gap in our team?
- Are they willing to serve in their area of giftedness?

### Balance Giftedness with Other Criteria

Gifts matter, but they're not sufficient alone. A gifted musician with relational immaturity will cause more problems than they solve. A skilled administrator with wrong motivations will undermine culture.

<Callout type="warning">
  Don't overlook character flaws because someone fills a skill gap. Character problems don't improve under the pressure of church planting—they intensify.
</Callout>

---

## Criterion 3: CHEMISTRY

**Is there good relational fit?**

Church planting requires deep partnership. You'll spend significant time together under pressure. If the relational chemistry isn't there, that tension will compound over time.

### Chemistry Considerations

- Do you enjoy being around this person?
- Can you envision doing ministry together long-term?
- Do they fit with the existing Core Group dynamics?
- Is communication natural or forced?
- Do they share your sense of humor and approach to life?

### What Chemistry Is Not

Chemistry isn't about finding people exactly like you. Diversity strengthens teams. But there needs to be baseline relational compatibility—a sense that you can work together well.

### Trust Your Instincts

If something feels off relationally, pay attention. You don't need to diagnose exactly what's wrong. Sometimes chemistry simply isn't there, and that's okay.

---

## Criterion 4: RIGHT REASONS

**Are they joining for healthy motivations?**

People join church plants for various reasons. Some are healthy; others are not. Unhealthy motivations eventually surface and cause problems.

### Healthy Motivations

- Genuine sense of calling to this specific work
- Desire to build something for God's glory
- Excitement about the vision and values
- Wanting to grow and be stretched
- Longing to reach people for Christ

### Unhealthy Motivations

| Warning Sign | What It Reveals |
|--------------|-----------------|
| Fleeing a previous church conflict | Unresolved issues will follow them |
| Seeking position or title | Ego-driven, not mission-driven |
| Looking for a project to fix | May become controlling |
| Wanting to implement their agenda | Not aligned with your vision |
| Escaping accountability | Running from growth opportunities |
| Attracted to the novelty | Will leave when it gets hard |

### How to Discern Motivations

Ask directly:
- "Why do you want to be part of this church plant?"
- "What excites you about this?"
- "What are you hoping to find or experience?"
- "How did you leave your previous church?"

Listen carefully. Surface answers may mask deeper motivations. Follow up with probing questions.

<Callout type="insight">
  People rarely articulate their true motivations clearly, even to themselves. Watch behavior over time. Consistent patterns reveal genuine motivations.
</Callout>

---

## Criterion 5: SEASON OF LIFE

**Are they in a stable season?**

Church planting requires margin—time, energy, and emotional capacity to give. People in unstable life seasons often lack that margin, even with the best intentions.

### Seasons That May Indicate Readiness

- Established in career or vocation
- Stable marriage and family life
- Settled geographically (not planning to move)
- Manageable life responsibilities
- Past major life transitions (new baby, job change)

### Seasons That May Indicate Caution

| Situation | Concern |
|-----------|---------|
| Newlyweds (under 1 year) | Marriage needs priority attention |
| New parents (infant at home) | Sleep deprivation, limited capacity |
| Major career transition | Energy absorbed elsewhere |
| Health crisis (self or family) | Limited margin |
| Recent major move | Still establishing roots |
| Active conflict or crisis | Needs to be resolved first |

### The Conversation

Don't assume—ask directly:
- "What does your current life season look like?"
- "What major commitments are competing for your time?"
- "Do you have the margin to invest significantly in this?"
- "Are there any major life changes on the horizon?"

<Callout type="tip">
  A "not now" doesn't have to mean "not ever." If someone isn't ready due to life season, maintain the relationship. Their season will change, and they may be perfect for your church later.
</Callout>

---

## Conducting the Interview

### Before the Conversation

- Review your observations from Vision Meetings
- Note any concerns or questions
- Pray for discernment
- Prepare specific questions

### During the Conversation

1. **Create safety** — Make clear this is exploratory, not a test
2. **Share expectations** — Be clear about what Core Group membership requires
3. **Ask open questions** — Let them share; don't lead
4. **Listen more than talk** — Watch for what's beneath the surface
5. **Address concerns directly** — If you have questions, ask them
6. **Give them an out** — Make it easy to say no if they're not ready

### After the Conversation

- Debrief with your spouse or co-leader
- Pray before deciding
- If uncertain, wait—time reveals truth
- If clear, communicate your decision warmly

---

## When Someone Doesn't Fit

Not everyone will meet all five criteria. Handle these situations graciously:

- **Be honest** — Don't give false hope or vague answers
- **Be kind** — Rejection hurts; show compassion
- **Be specific** — If appropriate, share what needs to change
- **Keep the door open** — Circumstances change; people grow
- **Point them somewhere** — Help them find a good church home

<Callout type="warning">
  Avoiding hard conversations now creates bigger problems later. It's kinder to be honest upfront than to manage a bad fit for months.
</Callout>

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers; for what partnership have righteousness and lawlessness, or what fellowship has light with darkness?"* — 2 Corinthians 6:14 (LSB)
</Callout>

Careful evaluation isn't unloving—it's wise stewardship. The quality of your Core Group determines the trajectory of your church plant. Take the time to evaluate well, and you'll build on a solid foundation.
articles.excerpt: The five criteria for evaluating whether someone is a good fit for your Core Group—Maturity, Gifted, Chemistry, Right Reasons, and Season of Life.
articles.title: The 5 Interview Criteria

Every church needs a clear pathway for discipleship—a system that moves people from wherever they are toward deeper engagement and spiritual maturity. The **Ministry Funnel** provides this pathway, guiding people from their first visit through to active service.

---

## What is the Ministry Funnel?

The Ministry Funnel is a visual framework showing how people progress through increasing levels of engagement with the church. Like any funnel, it's widest at the top (easiest entry) and narrows as commitment deepens.

```
       ┌─────────────────────┐
       │      WORSHIP        │  ← Entry Point (widest)
       │  Corporate Gatherings │
       └──────────┬──────────┘
                  ↓
          ┌──────────────┐
          │     WALK     │  ← Deeper Connection
          │  Small Groups │
          └──────┬───────┘
                 ↓
            ┌─────────┐
            │  WORK   │  ← Active Service (narrowest)
            │ Ministry │
            │  Teams   │
            └─────────┘
```

<Callout type="insight">
  The funnel isn't about hierarchy or status. It's about depth of engagement. Someone serving in ministry (Work) should still be worshiping and walking in community—they've simply added another dimension to their discipleship.
</Callout>

---

## The Three Stages

### Stage 1: WORSHIP — The Entry Point

**Corporate worship gatherings are where most people first encounter the church.**

Sunday services serve as the wide opening of the funnel. They're:
- Accessible to anyone
- Low commitment to attend
- The primary first impression
- Where vision and values are communicated

**Goals at this stage:**
- Welcome guests warmly
- Provide meaningful worship experiences
- Communicate vision clearly
- Create easy next steps

| Metric | What to Track |
|--------|---------------|
| Attendance | How many people are showing up? |
| Guest retention | Are first-time guests returning? |
| Connection | Are people taking next steps? |

<Callout type="tip">
  Don't skip the funnel. Some churches try to get people serving immediately. But without the foundation of community (Walk), service becomes unsustainable. Let people progress naturally through the stages.
</Callout>

---

### Stage 2: WALK — Deeper Connection

**Small groups are where acquaintances become family.**

Corporate worship gathers the crowd, but small groups build the community. This is where people:
- Build authentic relationships
- Study Scripture together
- Share life's joys and struggles
- Experience care and accountability
- Develop spiritual friendships

**Goals at this stage:**
- Connect every regular attender to a small group
- Foster genuine relationships, not just meetings
- Create environments where people are known and know others
- Develop leaders within groups

| Metric | What to Track |
|--------|---------------|
| Small group participation | What percentage of attenders are in groups? |
| Group health | Are groups growing spiritually and relationally? |
| Leader development | Are new leaders emerging from groups? |

**The critical transition:**

Moving from Worship to Walk is the most important transition in the funnel. People who attend services but never connect in community:
- Remain anonymous
- Feel like spectators
- Are highly likely to drift away
- Never develop lasting commitment

<Callout type="important">
  Churches don't have a back door problem—they have a front door to side door problem. People leave because they never connected relationally. Small groups solve this.
</Callout>

---

### Stage 3: WORK — Active Service

**Ministry teams are where consumers become contributors.**

As people grow in worship and community, they're ready to serve. Work encompasses:
- Serving on ministry teams
- Using spiritual gifts for the body
- Taking ownership of the church's mission
- Investing in others' growth

**Goals at this stage:**
- Help people discover their gifts
- Place people in meaningful service roles
- Develop increasing responsibility over time
- Cultivate future leaders

| Metric | What to Track |
|--------|---------------|
| Volunteer engagement | What percentage of attenders are serving? |
| Team health | Are teams functioning well? |
| Leadership pipeline | Are servants becoming leaders? |

**Service roles include:**
- Facilities (setup, teardown, parking)
- Hospitality (greeting, guest services)
- Children's ministry
- Worship and production
- Small group leadership
- Assimilation
- Administration
- Prayer teams

---

## Why the Funnel Matters for Church Planting

### It Guides Your Priorities

You can't build everything at once. The funnel tells you what to focus on and when:

| Phase | Priority |
|-------|----------|
| **Core Group** | Establish Walk (small group community first) |
| **Launch** | Execute Worship (compelling corporate gatherings) |
| **Post-Launch** | Develop Work (ministry team engagement) |

### It Shapes Your Metrics

Instead of just counting attendance, you measure health at each stage:
- Are people worshiping? (attendance, engagement)
- Are people walking? (small group connection)
- Are people working? (service involvement)

A church with strong attendance but weak small groups will struggle to retain people. A church with active servers but no community will burn people out.

### It Informs Your Assimilation Strategy

The funnel shows you where to focus your assimilation efforts:
- Guest follow-up moves people from "visitor" to "attender" (Worship)
- Small group connection moves people from "attender" to "member" (Walk)
- Service opportunities move people from "member" to "minister" (Work)

---

## Common Funnel Failures

### Failure 1: No Clear Pathway

**Symptom:** People attend for months but never connect deeper.

**Solution:** Create obvious, easy next steps at each stage. Don't assume people know what to do next—tell them explicitly and make it simple.

### Failure 2: Pushing Too Fast

**Symptom:** New attenders are pressured to serve immediately; they burn out or leave.

**Solution:** Let people progress naturally. Build relationship before requesting commitment. Service should be the overflow of connection, not the price of entry.

### Failure 3: Leaking Funnel

**Symptom:** People move through stages but fall out along the way.

**Solution:** Track transitions. Who attended last month but not this month? Who visited a small group but didn't return? Follow up intentionally at each stage.

### Failure 4: Stuck at One Stage

**Symptom:** People plateau—they worship but never join a group, or they're in a group but never serve.

**Solution:** Regularly cast vision for the next stage. Create easy on-ramps. Address barriers honestly.

<Callout type="warning">
  A full sanctuary with empty small groups is a church waiting to decline. Numbers at the top of the funnel mean nothing if people aren't progressing through it.
</Callout>

---

## Implementing the Funnel from Day One

Even before launch, you can establish the funnel:

**During Core Group phase:**
- Your Core Group is already at Walk (small group community)
- Add Work by assigning responsibilities
- Vision Meetings function as proto-Worship gatherings

**At launch:**
- Worship gatherings become your entry point
- Small groups are ready to receive new people
- Ministry teams are staffed and functioning

**Post-launch:**
- Track movement through each stage
- Remove barriers to progression
- Celebrate stories of people moving deeper

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And He Himself gave some as apostles, and some as prophets, and some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints for the work of service, to the building up of the body of Christ,"* — Ephesians 4:11-12 (LSB)
</Callout>

The Ministry Funnel isn't just organizational structure—it's a discipleship pathway. Build it intentionally from the start, and you'll create a church where people don't just attend but belong, grow, and serve.
articles.excerpt: How the ministry funnel moves people from first-time guests to fully engaged disciples through Worship, Walk, and Work.
articles.title: The Ministry Funnel
