articles.title: Promotion Channels Guide

articles.content:
With Launch Sunday **3-4 weeks away**, you've entered the final stretch. This isn't the time for new initiatives—it's the time to integrate, refine, and polish everything you've been building.

Your training should be 90-100% complete. Your teams should know their roles. Now it's about bringing all the pieces together into a unified, well-rehearsed operation.

---

## The Mindset Shift

Up until now, you've been building—recruiting Core Group members, forming teams, acquiring equipment, and training leaders. The final 3-4 weeks require a different mindset:

**From building to refining.**

Think of this window like a dress rehearsal for a major production. The script is written, the actors know their lines, the sets are built. Now you practice until everything flows seamlessly.

<Callout type="insight">
  This window is about integration, not introduction. You're not teaching new 
  concepts—you're helping teams work together as a unified whole.
</Callout>

---

## Three Primary Priorities

The final 3-4 weeks focus on three critical areas:

### 1. Operations

All set-up equipment needed for launch must arrive in this window. Your facilities team conducts intensive hands-on training. The goal: every person knows their role, every piece of equipment has a place, and set-up/tear-down becomes second nature.

[Learn more about Operations](/wiki/pre-launch/operations-setup-teardown)

### 2. Launch Team Preparation

The spiritual dimension intensifies. This is the time for focused prayer, fasting, and drawing near to the Lord together. You'll also conduct Pre-Launch Services—full rehearsals that let every team practice in real conditions.

[Learn more about Spiritual Preparation](/wiki/pre-launch/launch-team-spiritual-preparation)

### 3. Promotion Plan

Three to four weeks out triggers the full launch of your promotion plan. Get the word out to as many people as possible using every channel available to you.

[Learn more about the Promotion Plan](/wiki/pre-launch/the-promotion-plan)

---

## The Weekly Rhythm

Here's how these final weeks typically flow:

| Week | Focus |
|------|-------|
| **Week 4** | Equipment arrives, In-Service Training Day, promotion launches |
| **Week 3** | First Pre-Launch Service, refine operations, prayer intensifies |
| **Week 2** | Second Pre-Launch Service, work out issues, continue promotion |
| **Week 1** | Final Pre-Launch Service, final checklist review, celebration and prayer |

<Callout type="warning">
  Don't try to cram new training into these final weeks. If a team isn't ready 
  by now, simplify their responsibilities rather than rushing their preparation.
</Callout>

---

## What Should Be Complete

By the time you enter this window, these elements should already be in place:

### Training
- [ ] Peak Performance series completed by all Launch Team members
- [ ] Ministry-specific training completed for each team
- [ ] Small Group 101 completed for small group leaders
- [ ] Boot Camp completed for emerging leaders

### Teams
- [ ] All ministry team leaders identified and trained
- [ ] Team rosters finalized with clear role assignments
- [ ] Communication channels established for each team

### Equipment & Facilities
- [ ] Worship center secured and contract signed
- [ ] Major equipment ordered (arrival expected in this window)
- [ ] Storage solution arranged
- [ ] Office space secured (if applicable)

### Systems
- [ ] Assimilation software selected and configured
- [ ] Check-in system tested
- [ ] Database ready for guest information
- [ ] Follow-up processes documented

---

## What Happens in This Window

### Equipment & Setup

All portable church equipment arrives and is inspected. Your In-Service Training Day teaches everyone the proper way to set up, tear down, and care for equipment.

### Pre-Launch Services

Three services (typically Sunday evenings) give every team real practice:
- Set-up and tear-down teams work together
- Worship team leads actual services
- Children's ministry runs their full program
- Assimilation processes are tested
- Senior Pastor delivers Peak Performance teaching

### Prayer & Fasting

Schedule one day per week for fasting, ending with corporate worship and prayer followed by a shared meal. The Senior Pastor leads this spiritual emphasis.

### Promotion Execution

Your promotion plan goes live. Social media, invitation cards, personal invitations—everything launches to build awareness and anticipation.

---

## Keys to Success

### Stay Calm

Things will go wrong during Pre-Launch Services. That's the point—find the problems now, not on Launch Sunday. Approach issues with curiosity, not panic.

### Communicate Constantly

Over-communicate during this window. Send weekly updates. Hold brief team leader check-ins. Make sure everyone knows what's happening and what's expected.

### Protect Your Senior Pastor

The Senior Pastor needs margin during these weeks for sermon preparation, prayer, and leadership. Don't let administrative details consume all their time and energy.

### Celebrate Progress

Take moments to acknowledge how far you've come. Celebrate the team. Express gratitude to God. This builds momentum and morale heading into launch.

<Callout type="tip">
  Keep a running list of every issue that surfaces during Pre-Launch Services. 
  Address each one before the next rehearsal. By Launch Sunday, you'll have 
  worked through most potential problems.
</Callout>

---

## The Final Week

The week before Launch Sunday is special. By now, you've done everything you can to prepare. The final week is about:

1. **Final checklist review** — Every team confirms readiness
2. **Rest** — Encourage the team to get adequate sleep
3. **Prayer** — Intense intercession for Launch Sunday
4. **Celebration** — Acknowledge the journey and thank God together

[See the Final Checklist Review](/wiki/pre-launch/final-checklist-review)

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Unless Yahweh builds the house, They labor in vain who build it; Unless Yahweh watches the city, The watchman keeps awake in vain."* — Psalm 127:1 (LSB)
</Callout>

You've prepared diligently. Now trust the One who called you. He is faithful, and He will do it.
articles.excerpt: An overview of the critical final weeks before Launch Sunday and how to maximize this window for a successful church launch.
articles.title: The Final 3-4 Weeks

articles.content:
Three to four weeks before Launch Sunday triggers the full launch of your promotion plan. This is when you get the word out to as many people as possible using every channel available.

Promotion isn't about hype or marketing tricks. It's about ensuring that people who need what your church offers actually know you exist.

---

## The Goal of Promotion

Effective promotion accomplishes one primary goal: **awareness that leads to attendance**.

You want people to:
1. Know your church exists
2. Know when and where you meet
3. Feel invited and welcome to attend
4. Remember you when they're ready to try church

<Callout type="insight">
  Most people need to encounter a message 7+ times before they act on it. 
  Multi-channel promotion increases the likelihood that your church breaks 
  through the noise of daily life.
</Callout>

---

## Developing Your Promotion Plan

### Start with Your Budget

Be realistic about what you can afford. Effective promotion doesn't require a massive budget, but it does require intentional allocation of resources.

| Budget Level | Recommended Focus |
|--------------|-------------------|
| **Minimal** | Personal invitations, social media, yard signs |
| **Moderate** | Add door hangers, invitation cards, local ads |
| **Substantial** | Add direct mail, radio, billboards |

### Prioritize High-Impact Channels

Not all promotion is equal. Some channels consistently outperform others:

**Highest Impact:**
- Personal invitations from Launch Team members
- Social media (targeted, organic, and paid)
- Door hangers in target neighborhoods

**Moderate Impact:**
- Direct mail postcards
- Local newspaper/media coverage
- Partner church announcements

**Variable Impact:**
- Radio advertising
- Billboard advertising
- Online advertising

<Callout type="warning">
  The most effective promotion is always personal invitation. No amount of 
  advertising can substitute for a genuine invitation from someone who cares.
</Callout>

---

## The Promotion Timeline

### 4 Weeks Out

- Finalize all promotional materials (design, print, production)
- Brief Launch Team on personal invitation goals
- Schedule social media content
- Order yard signs and outdoor signage

### 3 Weeks Out

- Begin social media campaign
- Distribute invitation cards to Launch Team
- Place yard signs in strategic locations
- Send press release to local media

### 2 Weeks Out

- Begin door hanger distribution
- Launch paid advertising (if using)
- Mail direct mail pieces (if using)
- Increase social media frequency

### 1 Week Out

- Final push on all channels
- Personal invitation follow-ups
- Partner church announcements
- Launch Team reminder to invite

---

## Personal Invitation Strategy

Personal invitations are your most powerful promotional tool. Every Launch Team member should be actively inviting.

### Set Clear Goals

Challenge each Launch Team member to:
- Identify 10-15 people to personally invite
- Have face-to-face or phone conversations (not just texts)
- Follow up with those who express interest
- Bring at least one person or family to Launch Sunday

### Equip with Tools

Provide Launch Team members with:
- Invitation cards to hand out
- Key information (time, location, what to expect)
- Answers to common questions
- Permission to be enthusiastic

### Track and Encourage

Check in weekly on invitation progress:
- How many conversations have you had?
- What responses are you getting?
- How can we pray for your contacts?

---

## Promotional Materials

### Essential Items

| Item | Purpose | Quantity |
|------|---------|----------|
| Invitation cards | Personal handouts | 500-1000 |
| Door hangers | Neighborhood saturation | Based on target area |
| Yard signs | Visibility in community | 25-50 |
| Social media graphics | Online presence | Multiple sizes/versions |
| Website | Information hub | 1, optimized |

### Optional Items

| Item | When to Use |
|------|-------------|
| Direct mail postcards | Budget allows, target area defined |
| Video content | Strong videography capability |
| Radio ads | Budget allows, target demographic matches |
| Billboard | High-traffic location available |
| Newspaper ads | Local paper has strong readership |

### Design Principles

All promotional materials should:
- Be visually consistent (same colors, fonts, feel)
- Clearly communicate time and location
- Include website and/or QR code for more information
- Feel welcoming and professional
- Avoid insider language

---

## Digital Promotion

### Website

Your website is your digital front door. Ensure it:
- Loads quickly on mobile devices
- Clearly states when and where you meet
- Explains what to expect for first-time guests
- Provides easy contact information
- Has a clear path to learn more

### Social Media

Focus your energy where your target audience spends time:

| Platform | Best For |
|----------|----------|
| Facebook | Families, community events, groups |
| Instagram | Visual content, younger audiences |
| YouTube | Video content, sermon previews |

**Content ideas:**
- Behind-the-scenes preparation
- Team member testimonials
- Countdown posts
- Event information
- Community engagement

### Paid Advertising

If budget allows, consider:
- Facebook/Instagram ads targeted to your geographic area
- Google Ads for relevant search terms
- Boosted posts for high-performing organic content

<Callout type="tip">
  Start with a small paid advertising budget to test what works. Scale up 
  spending on ads that perform well, and cut what doesn't.
</Callout>

---

## Community Outreach

### Local Media

Send a press release to local newspapers and news stations. "New Church Launches" can be legitimate local news, especially in smaller communities.

Include:
- Who: Church name, Senior Pastor name
- What: Church launch
- When: Launch Sunday date and time
- Where: Location
- Why: Brief vision statement
- Contact information for follow-up

### Community Presence

Look for opportunities to be visibly present in the community:
- Community events and festivals
- Service projects
- Local business partnerships
- Neighborhood gatherings

---

## Partner Church Support

Your network of partner churches can amplify your launch:

### Announcements

The week before Launch Sunday, provide partner churches with:
- A PowerPoint slide (Senior Pastor photo, church name, launch date)
- Brief announcement copy for their bulletin or screen
- Website information to share

### Prayer

Ask partner churches to pray for your launch in their services. This builds connection and spiritual covering.

### Referrals

Partner churches may have members who live in your area. Ask if they'll share information with those who might benefit from a church closer to home.

---

## Measuring Effectiveness

Track what you can to learn for the future:

| Metric | How to Track |
|--------|--------------|
| Personal invitations made | Launch Team self-reporting |
| Social media reach | Platform analytics |
| Website visits | Google Analytics |
| "How did you hear about us?" | Connection card question |

The most important metric is the last one. Ask every Launch Sunday guest how they heard about you. This data shapes future promotion strategy.

---

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. **Starting too late** — Promotion needs lead time. Don't wait until the last week.
2. **Relying only on advertising** — Advertising supports personal invitation; it doesn't replace it.
3. **Inconsistent messaging** — All materials should tell the same story with the same details.
4. **Ignoring digital** — Most people will check your website before visiting. Make it count.
5. **Underspending on printing** — Running out of invitation cards is a missed opportunity.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"How then will they call on Him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in Him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?"* — Romans 10:14 (LSB)
</Callout>

Promotion helps people find a church where they can hear the gospel preached and connect with the community of faith. Go and tell them.

articles.title: The Promotion Plan

articles.content:
Peak Performance covers the foundations. Boot Camp goes deeper. This intensive discipleship program is designed for emerging leaders—those who will carry significant responsibility in the life of your church.

Boot Camp isn't for everyone. It's for those ready to be stretched, challenged, and developed into the leaders your church needs.

---

## What is Boot Camp?

Boot Camp is an intensive discipleship experience that goes beyond membership training to develop character, conviction, and competence in future leaders.

| Peak Performance | Boot Camp |
|-----------------|-----------|
| Membership foundations | Leadership development |
| All members | Emerging leaders |
| 3 sessions | Extended commitment |
| What we believe | How we live and lead |
| Information | Transformation |

<Callout type="insight">
  Peak Performance asks, "Do you understand our church?" Boot Camp asks, 
  "Are you ready to lead in our church?"
</Callout>

---

## Why Boot Camp Matters

Every healthy church needs a pipeline of developing leaders. Without intentional leadership development, you'll face a perpetual shortage of qualified people to serve in key roles.

### Boot Camp Accomplishes

1. **Deepened Discipleship** — Participants grow in spiritual maturity
2. **Identified Leaders** — You discover who's ready for greater responsibility
3. **Shared DNA** — Leaders are thoroughly enculturated in your values
4. **Relational Bonds** — Participants form lasting connections
5. **Equipped Servants** — Leaders gain practical ministry skills

---

## Who Should Attend?

Boot Camp is for **emerging leaders**—people who show potential for significant ministry responsibility. They may be:

- Future ministry team leaders
- Future small group leaders
- Future staff members
- Key volunteers ready for more

### Selection Criteria

Look for the **3 C's**:

| Criteria | What to Look For |
|----------|-----------------|
| **Character** | Integrity, humility, teachability, spiritual maturity |
| **Competence** | Skills, gifts, ability to learn and grow |
| **Chemistry** | Alignment with vision, ability to work well with others |

<Callout type="warning">
  Boot Camp isn't a reward for enthusiasm. Select participants based on 
  potential and readiness, not just willingness. Not everyone who wants to 
  lead is ready to lead.
</Callout>

---

## Boot Camp Curriculum

Boot Camp content should cover three domains: **Being**, **Knowing**, and **Doing**.

### Domain 1: Being (Character Development)

Who we are matters more than what we do. Boot Camp prioritizes character formation.

| Topic | Focus |
|-------|-------|
| **Spiritual Disciplines** | Prayer, Scripture, fasting, solitude |
| **Personal Holiness** | Purity, integrity, self-control |
| **Humility and Teachability** | Receiving correction, admitting weakness |
| **Emotional Health** | Self-awareness, healthy relationships |
| **Servant Leadership** | Leading by serving, not position |

### Domain 2: Knowing (Theological Foundations)

Leaders need deeper theological grounding than the average member.

| Topic | Focus |
|-------|-------|
| **Gospel Fluency** | Articulating the gospel clearly |
| **Biblical Theology** | How the Bible fits together |
| **Ecclesiology** | Theology of the local church |
| **Apologetics** | Defending the faith graciously |
| **Church History** | Learning from those who came before |

### Domain 3: Doing (Ministry Skills)

Theory without practice produces ineffective leaders.

| Topic | Focus |
|-------|-------|
| **Leadership Principles** | Vision, delegation, decision-making |
| **Teaching and Communication** | Clear, compelling delivery |
| **Pastoral Care** | Shepherding people through challenges |
| **Conflict Resolution** | Handling disagreements biblically |
| **Team Building** | Recruiting, training, releasing |

---

## Boot Camp Format Options

### Option 1: Weekly Cohort

| Element | Details |
|---------|---------|
| **Duration** | 12-16 weeks |
| **Frequency** | Weekly, 2 hours |
| **Size** | 8-12 participants |
| **Format** | Teaching + discussion + application |

**Pros:** Sustained development, time to process and apply
**Cons:** Long commitment, harder to maintain momentum

### Option 2: Intensive Retreat

| Element | Details |
|---------|---------|
| **Duration** | Weekend retreat |
| **Setting** | Off-site location |
| **Format** | Immersive teaching, worship, community |

**Pros:** Deep relational bonding, focused attention
**Cons:** Covers less material, less time for application

### Option 3: Hybrid Approach

Combine a retreat weekend with follow-up sessions:

1. **Kickoff Retreat** — Intensive weekend together
2. **Weekly Sessions** — 8-10 weeks of continued development
3. **Graduation** — Commissioning into leadership roles

<Callout type="tip">
  The hybrid approach often works best. The retreat builds community and 
  creates momentum; the weekly sessions provide space for deeper learning 
  and accountability.
</Callout>

---

## Leading Boot Camp

### Who Should Lead?

The Senior Pastor should be directly involved in Boot Camp leadership. This is where you pour into your future leaders—it can't be fully delegated.

Consider involving:
- Senior Pastor (primary leader)
- Experienced elders or leaders
- Guest speakers for specific topics

### Creating the Right Environment

Boot Camp should feel different from other church training:

| Element | Why It Matters |
|---------|---------------|
| **Smaller group** | Allows for deeper relationship |
| **Higher expectations** | Communicates this is serious |
| **Vulnerability** | Leaders model transparency |
| **Accountability** | Participants challenge each other |
| **Application** | Learning is tested in real ministry |

---

## Before Launch: Boot Camp Timing

For your Launch Team, consider offering a condensed Boot Camp during Phase 3 to develop your initial leadership core.

### Pre-Launch Boot Camp

| Approach | Timing |
|----------|--------|
| **Intensive** | Full weekend, 3-6 weeks before launch |
| **Condensed** | 4-6 weekly sessions during Phase 3 |
| **Combined** | Weekend retreat + 3-4 follow-up sessions |

### Who to Include Pre-Launch

Prioritize those who will hold key roles:
- Ministry team leaders
- Small group leaders
- Those with clear leadership gifting

<Callout type="important">
  You can't train everyone in Boot Camp before launch. Focus on your key 
  leaders first. Establish an ongoing Boot Camp rhythm after launch for 
  continued development.
</Callout>

---

## After Launch: Ongoing Boot Camp

Make Boot Camp a regular part of your leadership development pipeline:

| Frequency | Format |
|-----------|--------|
| **Annual** | Once per year, new cohort each time |
| **Bi-annual** | Spring and Fall cohorts |
| **Continuous** | Rolling enrollment, ongoing sessions |

### Boot Camp → Leadership Pipeline

Boot Camp should feed into leadership roles:

```
Boot Camp Graduate
      ↓
Ministry Team Leader / Small Group Leader
      ↓
Ministry Director / Small Group Coach
      ↓
Elder Candidate / Staff
```

---

## Measuring Success

How do you know if Boot Camp is working?

| Indicator | What to Look For |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Spiritual Growth** | Participants demonstrate deepened maturity |
| **Leadership Emergence** | Graduates step into roles of greater responsibility |
| **Multiplication** | Leaders develop other leaders |
| **Retention** | Boot Camp graduates remain engaged long-term |
| **Church Health** | Overall leadership capacity increases |

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And the things which you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also."* — 2 Timothy 2:2 (LSB)
</Callout>

Boot Camp is 2 Timothy 2:2 in action: entrusting truth to faithful people who will entrust it to others. Invest deeply in your emerging leaders, and they'll multiply your impact for generations.
articles.excerpt: An intensive discipleship program designed to develop emerging leaders and deepen spiritual maturity.
articles.title: Boot Camp Overview

articles.content:
Training without clear goals is aimless activity. Before you begin Phase 3, you need to know exactly what "ready" looks like. This article outlines the specific goals your Launch Team must achieve by Launch Sunday.

These aren't aspirational targets—they're minimum requirements for a healthy launch.

---

## The Five Readiness Areas

By Launch Sunday, your church must be ready in five critical areas:

| Area | What It Means |
|------|---------------|
| **High Impact Service** | Every element of Sunday morning is prepared and rehearsed |
| **Assimilation** | Processes are in place to connect guests to the church |
| **Small Groups** | Groups are ready to launch shortly after Launch Sunday |
| **Active Service** | Ministry teams are trained and positioned |
| **Leadership Development** | Pipeline for developing future leaders is established |

<Callout type="important">
  A weak launch in any of these five areas creates problems that compound 
  over time. Take the time to achieve readiness across all five.
</Callout>

---

## High Impact Service

Your first Sunday service sets the tone for everything that follows. Guests form lasting impressions within minutes. The goal is a service that honors God and serves people excellently.

### Requirements

| Role | Readiness Standard |
|------|-------------------|
| **Senior Pastor** | Prepared to preach with clarity and passion |
| **Worship Leader** | Worship team rehearsed and ready to lead |
| **Children's Ministry** | Age-appropriate environments fully set up |
| **Facilities** | Venue transformed into a welcoming worship space |
| **Administration** | Systems in place for offering, communication, and records |

### Key Questions

- Is your preaching calendar established for the first sermon series?
- Has the worship team rehearsed together multiple times?
- Is every children's room equipped with curriculum, supplies, and trained volunteers?
- Have you conducted full run-throughs of the service flow?

---

## Assimilation

Getting guests through the door is only half the battle. The other half is connecting them to the life of the church. Your assimilation process should be designed and ready before Launch Sunday.

### Requirements

- Guest registration process established (Friendship Registers, connection cards)
- Database software selected and configured
- Follow-up process documented (who contacts, when, how)
- Guest reception area planned
- Party with the Pastor scheduled for shortly after launch

### Key Questions

- Do you have a clear path for moving someone from first-time guest to connected member?
- Is your database ready to capture and track guest information?
- Do you have trained people assigned to guest follow-up?
- Is your follow-up timeline defined (24-hour call, 48-hour letter, etc.)?

<Callout type="tip">
  Test your assimilation process during Pre-Launch Services. Have Launch Team 
  members role-play as guests to identify gaps in the system.
</Callout>

---

## Small Groups

Small groups are where discipleship happens. While groups may not launch on the same day as Sunday services, they should be **fully ready** to launch within weeks of Launch Sunday.

### Requirements

| Element | Readiness Standard |
|---------|-------------------|
| **Philosophy** | Small group model clearly defined and communicated |
| **Leaders** | Group leaders identified, trained, and assigned |
| **Curriculum** | First study selected and materials obtained |
| **Roll-out Plan** | Launch date and sign-up process determined |
| **Coaching Structure** | Small group coaches identified (if applicable) |

### Key Questions

- Do you have enough trained leaders to launch the number of groups you need?
- Have leaders completed Small Group 101 training?
- Is the sign-up and assignment process defined?
- Do you have an apprentice development plan for future leaders?

---

## Active Service

Launch Sunday requires people serving in every ministry area. These teams must be recruited, trained, and positioned before the big day.

### Ministry Teams to Establish

| Team | Primary Responsibilities |
|------|-------------------------|
| **Facilities** | Set-up, tear-down, parking, signage |
| **Children's Ministry** | Teaching, check-in, safety, room management |
| **Assimilation** | Greeting, ushering, guest follow-up |
| **Small Groups** | Leading and shepherding group members |
| **Worship & Production** | Music, audio, video, lighting |
| **Promotion** | Marketing, communication, social media |
| **Prayer** | Intercessory prayer before and during services |
| **Technology** | Website, presentation software, equipment |
| **Administration** | Finance, records, communication |

### Key Questions

- Does every team have a designated leader?
- Has each team received ministry-specific training?
- Do teams have written checklists for their responsibilities?
- Have teams practiced their roles during Pre-Launch Services?

---

## Leadership Development

A healthy church develops leaders continuously. By Launch Sunday, you should have systems in place to identify and develop future leaders.

### Requirements

- **Boot Camp** — Intensive discipleship program ready to launch
- **Potential Leaders** — Emerging leaders identified and targeted for development
- **Apprentice Model** — Plan for developing leaders within each ministry team
- **Leadership Pipeline** — Clear pathway from new believer to ministry leader

### Key Questions

- Have you identified the top 10-20 emerging leaders in your Launch Team?
- Is Boot Camp scheduled to begin shortly after launch?
- Does each ministry team leader have an apprentice in development?

<Callout type="insight">
  The leaders you develop in year one become the foundation for growth in 
  years two and three. Start the pipeline early.
</Callout>

---

## The Readiness Checklist

Use this checklist to assess your Launch Sunday readiness:

### High Impact Service
- [ ] Senior Pastor sermon prepared
- [ ] Worship team rehearsed and ready
- [ ] Service flow documented and practiced
- [ ] Children's Ministry environments ready
- [ ] All equipment tested and operational

### Assimilation
- [ ] Guest registration process in place
- [ ] Database configured and tested
- [ ] Follow-up process documented
- [ ] Follow-up team trained and assigned
- [ ] Guest reception area planned

### Small Groups
- [ ] Small group model defined
- [ ] Leaders trained (Small Group 101 complete)
- [ ] Curriculum selected
- [ ] Launch date determined
- [ ] Sign-up process ready

### Active Service
- [ ] All ministry teams have designated leaders
- [ ] Ministry-specific training complete
- [ ] Team checklists written
- [ ] Teams have practiced during Pre-Launch Services

### Leadership Development
- [ ] Boot Camp curriculum ready
- [ ] Emerging leaders identified
- [ ] Apprentice model communicated to team leaders

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"For which one of you, when he wants to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost to see if he has enough to complete it?"* — Luke 14:28 (LSB)
</Callout>

Calculate the cost. Set clear goals. Then pursue them with excellence. Launch Sunday readiness doesn't happen by accident—it happens by intention.

articles.title: Goals by Launch Sunday

articles.content:
When your Core Group transitions to a Launch Team, your meetings change. They become more frequent, more focused, and more intentional. Every gathering should accomplish three primary objectives: **Inspire**, **Instill**, and **Inform**.

Miss any of these, and your team arrives at Launch Sunday either unmotivated, misaligned, or unprepared.

---

## The Three Objectives

| Objective | Purpose | Method |
|-----------|---------|--------|
| **Inspire** | Keep the vision alive | Worship, devotional, prayer, updates |
| **Instill** | Enculturate the team | Teaching on values, distinctives, DNA |
| **Inform** | Train for responsibilities | Corporate training, ministry team training |

<Callout type="insight">
  These three objectives map to head, heart, and hands. Inspire touches the 
  heart. Instill shapes the mind. Inform equips the hands.
</Callout>

---

## Objective 1: Inspire (Cast Vision)

**Purpose:** Keep people connected to why they're doing this.

The long months of preparation can drain enthusiasm. Weekly meetings, training sessions, and logistical details can make people forget the bigger picture. Your job as a leader is to continually fan the flame of vision.

### How to Inspire

| Element | What It Accomplishes |
|---------|---------------------|
| **Worship** | Renews focus on God and His greatness |
| **Devotional** | Grounds the team in Scripture |
| **Prayer** | Cultivates dependence on God |
| **Updates** | Shows what God is doing locally and beyond |

### Practical Application

- Open every meeting with worship—even if it's just a few songs
- Share a brief devotional that connects to the mission
- Pray specifically for the launch, for the community, for each other
- Celebrate wins: new people joining, resources provided, prayers answered

<Callout type="tip">
  Share stories from other church plants. Hearing how God is moving elsewhere 
  reminds your team that they're part of something bigger.
</Callout>

### Warning Signs

If your team shows signs of discouragement, cynicism, or going-through-the-motions, you may be under-investing in inspiration. Double down on vision casting before fatigue sets in.

---

## Objective 2: Instill (Enculturate Team)

**Purpose:** Build deep alignment around values, distinctives, and DNA.

A team that shares the same values works together smoothly. A team with conflicting assumptions creates friction. Instillation is the process of thoroughly enculturating your Launch Team in what makes your church distinct.

### What to Instill

| Topic | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|
| **4 Pillars** | The theological foundation of your church |
| **Worship/Walk/Work** | The discipleship model that shapes ministry |
| **Ministry Funnel** | How people move from guests to servants |
| **Core Values** | The non-negotiables that guide decisions |
| **Distinctives** | What makes your church unique |

### How to Instill

- **Teaching** — Dedicated time in meetings for values-based teaching
- **Visiting** — Take the team to visit established partner churches
- **Training Events** — Attend regional or network training together
- **Discussion** — Create space for questions and dialogue

### Practical Application

- Dedicate 15-20 minutes of each meeting to teaching on DNA
- Assign reading from foundational documents
- Schedule at least one observation visit to a partner church
- Use case studies: "How would our values apply in this situation?"

<Callout type="important">
  Don't assume people absorbed everything from Vision Meetings. Instillation 
  requires repetition. Teach the same truths from different angles until 
  they're second nature.
</Callout>

---

## Objective 3: Inform (Train the Team)

**Purpose:** Equip people with the knowledge and skills they need.

This is where the practical work happens. Training turns willing people into capable servants.

### Training Layers

| Layer | Description | Examples |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| **Corporate Training** | Whole-team learning | Peak Performance Series, Boot Camp |
| **Ministry Team Training** | Role-specific learning | Children's Ministry protocols, Worship team rehearsals |
| **Outside Training** | Learning from others | Network conferences, ministry workshops |
| **Hands-on Observation** | Learning by watching | Visiting partner churches, shadowing leaders |

### How to Inform

- Schedule dedicated training blocks within meetings
- Break into ministry teams for specialized training
- Bring in experienced leaders to teach specific topics
- Create opportunities for practice (Pre-Launch Services)

### Practical Application

- Complete Peak Performance Series with the whole team
- Give ministry team leaders time to train their teams
- Schedule observation visits where teams shadow their counterparts at established churches
- Use Pre-Launch Services as full dress rehearsals

---

## Meeting Structure Example

Here's how a typical Launch Team meeting might incorporate all three objectives:

| Time | Activity | Objective |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 6:30 - 6:45 | Arrival and fellowship | — |
| 6:45 - 7:00 | Worship (2-3 songs) | Inspire |
| 7:00 - 7:15 | Devotional and prayer | Inspire |
| 7:15 - 7:30 | Updates and celebration | Inspire |
| 7:30 - 8:00 | Teaching: Core values/distinctives | Instill |
| 8:00 - 8:45 | Training: Ministry team breakouts | Inform |
| 8:45 - 9:00 | Closing announcements and prayer | — |

Adjust the balance based on where you are in the timeline. Early in Phase 3, lean heavier on Instill and Inform. As launch approaches, increase the Inspire component to build momentum.

---

## Meeting Frequency

As you progress through Phase 3, meeting frequency should increase:

| Phase | Frequency | Focus |
|-------|-----------|-------|
| **Early Phase 3** | Bi-weekly | Foundation building |
| **Mid Phase 3** | Weekly | Training intensification |
| **Final Month** | Weekly + ministry meetings | Integration and practice |

<Callout type="warning">
  Don't peak too early. Maintain a sustainable pace early on, then intensify 
  as Launch Sunday approaches. Burning out your team before launch defeats 
  the purpose.
</Callout>

---

## Balancing the Three

All three objectives matter, but the balance shifts over time:

| Timing | Primary Focus |
|--------|---------------|
| **Months out** | Instill (build alignment) |
| **Weeks out** | Inform (complete training) |
| **Days out** | Inspire (build momentum) |

Never drop any objective entirely. Even on your most training-heavy night, start with worship and prayer. Even on your most inspirational night, include practical updates.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And let us consider how to stimulate one another to love and good deeds, not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day drawing near."* — Hebrews 10:24-25 (LSB)
</Callout>

Your meetings are more than logistics. They're the furnace where your team is forged. Inspire them, instill truth in them, and inform them—and they'll be ready for whatever Launch Sunday brings.

articles.content:
Corporate training builds shared understanding. Ministry-specific training builds specialized competence. Each ministry team needs customized training that prepares them for their unique responsibilities.

This article outlines the training requirements for each key ministry area.

---

## The Training Principle

Every ministry team needs training in three areas:

| Area | Question Answered |
|------|------------------|
| **Philosophy** | Why do we do this ministry? |
| **Procedures** | How do we execute our responsibilities? |
| **Practice** | Have we rehearsed until we're confident? |

Skip any of these, and teams arrive at Launch Sunday either unmotivated (missing philosophy), confused (missing procedures), or unprepared (missing practice).

<Callout type="important">
  Ministry-specific training should be 90-100% complete by the time you 
  reach the final 3-4 weeks before launch. That final window is for 
  integration, not foundational training.
</Callout>

---

## Worship & Production Team

The worship and production team owns the entire Sunday morning experience from a technical and artistic standpoint.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Theology of Worship** | Why we worship, what worship accomplishes |
| **Service Philosophy** | What we're trying to create on Sunday morning |
| **Excellence and Accessibility** | High quality without being intimidating |
| **Team Character** | Humility, preparation, servant hearts |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Service Flow** | Order of service, transitions, timing |
| **Rehearsal Protocol** | When, how long, what to cover |
| **Sound Setup** | Board configuration, mic placement, mixing |
| **Video/Lighting** | Projection, slides, lighting cues |
| **Stage Setup** | Instrument placement, cables, stands |
| **Communication** | In-ear cues, hand signals, contingency plans |

### Practice Requirements

- Multiple full rehearsals with all elements
- Pre-Launch Services as dress rehearsals
- Walk-through of set-up and tear-down procedures
- Practice handling equipment failures and contingencies

---

## Children's Ministry Team

Children's Ministry requires extensive training due to safety requirements and the specialized nature of teaching children.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Why Children's Ministry Matters** | Impact on families, discipleship begins early |
| **Ministry Philosophy** | How we approach teaching and caring for children |
| **Age-Appropriate Faith Development** | What kids can understand at each stage |
| **Partnership with Parents** | Supporting, not replacing, parental discipleship |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Check-In Process** | Registration, name tags, security codes |
| **Safety Protocols** | Adult-to-child ratios, bathroom procedures, never alone |
| **Classroom Management** | Handling behavior, engaging activities |
| **Curriculum Execution** | How to teach the lesson effectively |
| **Allergy and Medical** | Identifying allergies, medication policies |
| **Emergency Procedures** | Fire, medical emergency, security threat |
| **Parent Communication** | Pickup procedures, incident reports |

### Practice Requirements

- Full walk-through of check-in process
- Role-play of common scenarios (crying child, bathroom needs, behavior issues)
- Practice with all equipment (check-in system, pagers, etc.)
- Pre-Launch Service with real children

<Callout type="warning">
  Children's Ministry training is non-negotiable. Every volunteer must 
  complete background checks and safety training before serving. No exceptions.
</Callout>

---

## Facilities Team

The facilities team transforms a rented space into a welcoming worship environment and returns it to its original state every week.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **First Impressions** | The building speaks before anyone does |
| **Stewardship** | Caring for what we've been given |
| **Relationship with Facility Owner** | Being excellent tenants |
| **Team Culture** | Serving together, having fun |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Set-Up Sequence** | What gets set up first, workflow optimization |
| **Room Configuration** | Seating arrangement, stage setup, signage |
| **Equipment Handling** | Proper care of sound, video, lighting gear |
| **Storage Procedures** | How to load, organize, and secure equipment |
| **Tear-Down Sequence** | Efficient breakdown, facility restoration |
| **Parking and Signage** | Directing guests, outdoor setup |
| **Trailer Loading** | Maximizing space, securing equipment |

### Practice Requirements

- Full set-up and tear-down rehearsal (timed)
- In-Service Training Day with all equipment
- Walk-through of every storage and setup location
- Pre-Launch Services as full practice

---

## Assimilation Team

The assimilation team owns the guest experience from arrival through follow-up.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Why Guests Matter** | Every guest is someone God brought |
| **The Guest Experience** | Seeing Sunday through a newcomer's eyes |
| **From Guest to Family** | The pathway from first visit to belonging |
| **Warmth Without Weirdness** | Being friendly without being overwhelming |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Greeter Positioning** | Where to stand, what to say |
| **Guest Identification** | Spotting first-time guests |
| **Registration Process** | Connection cards, Friendship Registers |
| **Guest Reception Area** | What it is, how it works |
| **Usher Responsibilities** | Seating, offering, assistance |
| **Database Entry** | Entering guest information accurately |
| **Follow-Up Process** | Who contacts, when, how |

### Practice Requirements

- Role-play of greeting scenarios
- Practice with registration systems
- Walk-through of entire guest pathway
- Pre-Launch Service with team members acting as guests

<Callout type="tip">
  Have team members visit another church anonymously and report on their 
  experience. Nothing teaches the guest perspective like being a guest.
</Callout>

---

## Small Group Team

Small group leaders receive dedicated training through Small Group 101, but the broader small group team also needs coordination training.

### Coordination Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Group Launch Strategy** | How and when groups will launch |
| **Sign-Up Process** | How people join groups |
| **Assignment Process** | How people are placed in groups |
| **Leader Support** | How coaches support leaders |
| **Reporting and Communication** | Attendance, concerns, needs |

### See Also

- [Small Group 101](/wiki/training/small-group-101) for leader-specific training

---

## Promotion Team

The promotion team owns marketing and communication before, during, and after launch.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Why Promotion Matters** | Getting the word out to reach people |
| **Brand and Message** | What we communicate and how |
| **Excellence in Communication** | Quality reflects the message |
| **Stewardship of Resources** | Maximum impact, appropriate spending |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Pre-Launch Promotion** | Timeline and channels |
| **Launch Day Documentation** | Photo and video capture |
| **Social Media** | Platforms, posting schedule, voice |
| **Print Materials** | Design, production, distribution |
| **Website Management** | Updates, content, accuracy |
| **Email Communication** | Lists, frequency, content |

### Practice Requirements

- Dry run of all promotion channels
- Test all digital systems (website, email, social)
- Practice video/photo capture during Pre-Launch Services

---

## Prayer Team

The prayer team undergirds everything with intercession.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Theology of Prayer** | Why prayer matters, how it works |
| **Corporate Prayer** | Praying together as a body |
| **Intercessory Prayer** | Standing in the gap for others |
| **Prayer and the Launch** | Covering the launch in prayer |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Pre-Service Prayer** | When, where, who |
| **Prayer During Service** | Designated prayer space, rotation |
| **Prayer Requests** | Collection, confidentiality, follow-up |
| **Corporate Prayer Gatherings** | Format, frequency, leadership |
| **Communication** | Sharing requests, updates, answers |

---

## Technology Team

The technology team handles digital infrastructure and technical support.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Technology as Tool** | Serving the mission, not showing off |
| **Reliability** | Systems that work every time |
| **Appropriate Investment** | Wise use of resources |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Website Management** | Updates, content management |
| **Presentation Software** | Slides, lyrics, announcements |
| **Database Systems** | Guest management, reporting |
| **Troubleshooting** | Common problems and solutions |
| **Backup Plans** | What to do when systems fail |

---

## Administration Team

The administration team handles finance and church operations.

### Philosophy Training

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Biblical Stewardship** | Managing God's resources faithfully |
| **Financial Integrity** | Above reproach in all things |
| **Confidentiality** | Protecting sensitive information |

### Procedures Training

| Area | What to Cover |
|------|---------------|
| **Offering Collection** | Secure handling of cash and checks |
| **Counting Procedures** | Two-person rule, documentation |
| **Recording and Reporting** | Database entry, reports |
| **Disbursements** | Approval process, check signing |
| **Contribution Statements** | Frequency, accuracy |

<Callout type="important">
  Financial procedures must be established and followed from day one. 
  Sloppy financial practices early create problems that compound over time.
</Callout>

---

## Training Delivery

### Who Trains Each Team?

| Team | Primary Trainer |
|------|-----------------|
| Worship & Production | Worship Leader |
| Children's Ministry | Children's Ministry Leader |
| Facilities | Facilities Leader |
| Assimilation | Assimilation Leader + Senior Pastor |
| Small Groups | Small Group Leader + Senior Pastor |
| Promotion | Promotion Leader |
| Prayer | Prayer Leader + Senior Pastor |
| Technology | Technology Leader |
| Administration | Senior Pastor + Financial Leader |

### Training Schedule

Build ministry training into your Phase 3 calendar:

1. **Early Phase 3** — Philosophy training for all teams
2. **Mid Phase 3** — Procedures training by team
3. **Late Phase 3** — Practice through Pre-Launch Services
4. **Final Weeks** — Refinement and integration

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Whatever you do, do your work heartily, as for the Lord rather than for men,"* — Colossians 3:23 (LSB)
</Callout>

Every ministry team serves the Lord, not just the church. Train them to serve with excellence, and they'll honor Him in everything they do.
articles.excerpt: Detailed training requirements for each ministry team to ensure they're fully prepared for Launch Sunday.
articles.title: Ministry-Specific Training

articles.content:
Peak Performance is a three-session training series that serves as your church's membership class. Every Launch Team member should complete this series before Launch Sunday—and it becomes the pathway for new members after launch.

The series accomplishes two critical goals: it ensures alignment around your church's DNA, and it creates a clear pathway for commitment.

---

## Why Peak Performance?

New churches often assume alignment exists because enthusiasm is high. But enthusiasm without understanding leads to confusion and conflict later. Peak Performance creates **informed commitment**.

<Callout type="insight">
  People can't commit to what they don't understand. Peak Performance gives 
  them the clarity needed to commit wholeheartedly—or to recognize they're 
  not the right fit.
</Callout>

### What Peak Performance Accomplishes

| Session | Outcome |
|---------|---------|
| **Peak Performance I** | Understanding of vision and values |
| **Peak Performance II** | Alignment on beliefs and doctrine |
| **Peak Performance III** | Clarity on commitment and next steps |

---

## Peak Performance I: Vision, Mission, and Values

**Purpose:** Help participants understand what this church is about and where it's going.

This session answers the fundamental questions: *Why does this church exist? What makes it distinct? Where is it headed?*

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **The Story** | How this church plant came to be |
| **Vision** | The preferred future you're pursuing |
| **Mission** | The specific work God has called you to |
| **Core Values** | The non-negotiables that guide decisions |
| **The 4 Pillars** | Your theological foundation |
| **Worship/Walk/Work** | Your discipleship model |

### Session Flow

1. **Welcome and introductions** — Create a warm, inviting environment
2. **The Story** — Share the journey that led to this church plant
3. **Vision and Mission** — Cast a clear picture of what you're building
4. **Core Values** — Explain each value with practical examples
5. **4 Pillars Overview** — Introduce the theological foundation
6. **Discipleship Model** — Explain Worship/Walk/Work
7. **Q&A** — Address questions and concerns
8. **Preview of Session II** — Set expectations for next week

<Callout type="tip">
  Use visuals. PowerPoint, handouts, and banners help people grasp and 
  remember key concepts. The 4 Pillars and Worship/Walk/Work especially 
  benefit from visual representation.
</Callout>

---

## Peak Performance II: Beliefs and Doctrine

**Purpose:** Ensure alignment on what this church believes and teaches.

Doctrinal clarity prevents future conflict. This session walks through your statement of faith and explains how your beliefs shape ministry practice.

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Statement of Faith** | Walk through each doctrinal point |
| **The Gospel** | Clear articulation of the good news |
| **The Bible** | Your view of Scripture's authority |
| **The Church** | Theology of the local church |
| **Baptism and Communion** | Your practice of the ordinances |
| **Church Government** | Elder leadership and how decisions are made |
| **Distinctives** | What sets this church apart doctrinally |

### Session Flow

1. **Review** — Brief recap of Session I
2. **Why Doctrine Matters** — Connect beliefs to everyday life
3. **Statement of Faith** — Systematic walk-through
4. **Gospel Presentation** — Ensure everyone can articulate the gospel
5. **Church Practices** — Explain baptism, communion, membership
6. **Government Structure** — How the church is led and governed
7. **Q&A** — Address theological questions
8. **Preview of Session III** — Set expectations for commitment discussion

<Callout type="important">
  This session may surface disagreements. That's healthy. Better to discover 
  misalignment now than after someone is serving in leadership.
</Callout>

---

## Peak Performance III: Commitment and Next Steps

**Purpose:** Call participants to clear commitment and explain what membership involves.

This session moves from information to invitation. After two sessions of learning, participants are asked to decide: *Will you commit?*

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **The Call to Commitment** | Why formal commitment matters |
| **Membership Expectations** | What's expected of members |
| **Serving Opportunities** | Ministry teams and how to get involved |
| **Giving** | The role of generosity in the life of a believer |
| **Small Groups** | The importance of community |
| **Next Steps** | How to formalize membership |
| **Commitment Card** | Walking through and signing the commitment |

### Session Flow

1. **Review** — Brief recap of Sessions I and II
2. **The Call** — Biblical basis for church commitment
3. **Expectations** — Clear explanation of what membership involves
4. **Serving** — Overview of ministry teams and spiritual gifts
5. **Generosity** — Teaching on biblical stewardship
6. **Community** — The role of small groups
7. **Commitment Time** — Invitation to sign commitment cards
8. **Celebration** — Welcome new members, pray over them
9. **Next Steps** — What happens after commitment

<Callout type="tip">
  Don't rush the commitment moment. Give people time to read, reflect, and 
  ask questions. Pressured commitment creates shallow members.
</Callout>

---

## Logistics and Format

### Session Length

Plan for 90 minutes per session:
- 60 minutes of content
- 15 minutes for Q&A
- 15 minutes for fellowship and follow-up

### Scheduling Options

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| **Three consecutive weeks** | Momentum, easy to track | Requires three-week commitment |
| **One intensive day** | Complete in one sitting | Long day, less reflection time |
| **Monthly rotation** | Flexible entry points | Takes longer to complete |

For the Launch Team, three consecutive weeks works best. After launch, consider a monthly rotation for ongoing membership.

### Materials Needed

- [ ] PowerPoint or slides for each session
- [ ] Handouts summarizing key content
- [ ] Statement of faith document
- [ ] Commitment cards
- [ ] Ministry team descriptions and sign-up sheets
- [ ] Small group information
- [ ] Name tags and sign-in sheets

---

## Running Peak Performance for Your Launch Team

For your Launch Team, Peak Performance serves as both training and commitment formalization. Schedule the series early enough in Phase 3 that everyone completes it well before launch.

### Recommendations

1. **Require attendance** — Make clear this is expected of all Launch Team members
2. **Provide make-up options** — Offer alternative times for those who miss sessions
3. **Use it as alignment check** — Pay attention to questions and concerns raised
4. **Celebrate completion** — Recognize those who complete the series

<Callout type="warning">
  If someone in your Launch Team resists completing Peak Performance, that's 
  a signal worth exploring. Commitment to the process reflects commitment to 
  the mission.
</Callout>

---

## After Launch

Peak Performance becomes your ongoing membership pathway. New guests who want to join complete the series and sign commitment cards just like your Launch Team did.

### Ongoing Schedule

Most churches offer Peak Performance:
- Monthly (one session per month, rotating)
- Quarterly (three-week intensive each quarter)
- On demand (when enough new people are ready)

Choose the rhythm that fits your context and growth pace.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"Him we proclaim, admonishing every man and teaching every man with all wisdom, so that we may present every man complete in Christ."* — Colossians 1:28 (LSB)
</Callout>

Peak Performance isn't just orientation—it's the beginning of presenting people complete in Christ. Start well, and they'll grow well.
articles.excerpt: A three-session membership class that establishes the foundational DNA of your church for every Launch Team member.
articles.title: Peak Performance Training Series

articles.content:
Small groups are where discipleship happens. Sunday services gather the church, but small groups grow the church. Every healthy church plant needs trained small group leaders ready to shepherd people in community.

Small Group 101 is your training course for equipping those leaders.

---

## Why Small Groups Matter

Small groups accomplish what Sunday services cannot:

| Sunday Service | Small Group |
|----------------|-------------|
| Inspires many at once | Develops individuals deeply |
| One-way communication | Interactive discussion |
| Anonymous attendance possible | Accountability and relationship |
| Surface-level connection | Genuine community |

<Callout type="insight">
  Sunday services can draw a crowd, but small groups build a church. 
  Without healthy small groups, growth becomes a mile wide and an inch deep.
</Callout>

A church of 100 without small groups has 100 loosely connected individuals. A church of 100 with strong small groups has 10 families deeply invested in each other's lives.

---

## Small Group 101 Objectives

By the end of this training, leaders should be able to:

1. **Articulate** the philosophy and purpose of small groups
2. **Facilitate** engaging group discussions
3. **Shepherd** group members through life's challenges
4. **Multiply** by developing apprentice leaders
5. **Execute** the logistical requirements of leading a group

---

## Session 1: Philosophy and Purpose

**Goal:** Leaders understand *why* small groups exist and how they fit into the church's discipleship model.

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Biblical Foundation** | Acts 2:42-47, one-anothers, early church model |
| **Discipleship Model** | Where groups fit in Worship/Walk/Work |
| **The Ministry Funnel** | How people move from guest to group |
| **Group Purpose** | Community, growth, care, mission |
| **Expectations** | What's expected of leaders and members |

### Key Concepts

**The "Walk" in Worship/Walk/Work**

Small groups are the "Walk" component—where believers walk together in community, growing in Christlikeness through relationship.

**The Three Purposes of Small Groups**

1. **Connect** — Build authentic relationships
2. **Grow** — Study Scripture and apply it together
3. **Serve** — Care for one another and reach outward

<Callout type="tip">
  Help leaders see that their group isn't just a Bible study—it's a 
  community with a mission. Groups that only study together eventually 
  stagnate. Groups that serve together thrive.
</Callout>

---

## Session 2: Facilitation Skills

**Goal:** Leaders can guide engaging, transformative group discussions.

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Facilitator vs. Teacher** | Drawing out vs. pouring in |
| **Question Types** | Open, closed, application, personal |
| **Discussion Dynamics** | Handling talkers, drawing out quiet members |
| **Creating Safety** | Confidentiality, vulnerability, grace |
| **Time Management** | Balancing fellowship, study, and prayer |

### The Art of Asking Questions

Good facilitators ask questions that open conversation, not shut it down.

| Instead of... | Ask... |
|---------------|--------|
| "The answer is grace, right?" | "What stands out to you in this passage?" |
| "Don't you agree that...?" | "How have you seen this play out in your life?" |
| "Does anyone have questions?" | "What questions does this raise for you?" |

### Handling Common Challenges

| Challenge | Response |
|-----------|----------|
| **The talker** | "Great insight. Let's hear from someone who hasn't shared yet." |
| **The silent member** | "Sarah, I'd love to hear your perspective on this." |
| **The tangent** | "That's interesting. Let's table that for after group." |
| **The debater** | "Good question. What do others think?" |
| **The advice-giver** | "Instead of solutions, let's just listen and pray." |

<Callout type="warning">
  New leaders often over-prepare content and under-prepare for group 
  dynamics. The best content means nothing if the discussion falls flat. 
  Spend as much time preparing to facilitate as preparing the material.
</Callout>

---

## Session 3: Shepherding Skills

**Goal:** Leaders can care for group members through life's challenges.

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Shepherd's Heart** | Caring for people, not just managing meetings |
| **One-on-One Connection** | Meeting with members outside of group |
| **Crisis Response** | How to respond when life falls apart |
| **Appropriate Referral** | Knowing when to involve pastors or professionals |
| **Prayer Ministry** | Praying for and with group members |

### The Shepherding Rhythm

Effective small group leaders maintain connection between meetings:

| Frequency | Activity |
|-----------|----------|
| **Weekly** | Check-in texts or calls |
| **Monthly** | One-on-one coffee or meal with a member |
| **As needed** | Crisis response and hospital visits |
| **Ongoing** | Prayer for each member by name |

### Knowing Your Limits

Small group leaders are not counselors, therapists, or pastors. Train leaders to recognize when situations require referral:

- Mental health crises
- Marriage counseling needs
- Addiction issues
- Abuse situations
- Complex theological questions

<Callout type="important">
  The goal is not to equip leaders to handle every situation—it's to equip 
  them to recognize what they can handle and what requires the Senior Pastor 
  or professional help.
</Callout>

---

## Session 4: Multiplication and Apprenticeship

**Goal:** Leaders understand how to develop future leaders and multiply their group.

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Why Multiply** | Kingdom growth, leadership development, fresh energy |
| **The Apprentice Model** | Identifying and developing potential leaders |
| **Multiplication Pathway** | How groups grow and birth new groups |
| **Overcoming Resistance** | Addressing fear of change |
| **Healthy Endings** | Celebrating and transitioning well |

### The Apprentice Pathway

1. **Identify** — Look for the "3 C's": Character, Competence, Chemistry
2. **Invite** — Ask them to consider leadership
3. **Include** — Bring them into planning and decision-making
4. **Instruct** — Teach them through explanation and observation
5. **Release** — Gradually hand over responsibilities
6. **Launch** — Send them to lead their own group

### When to Multiply

Groups should consider multiplication when:
- Size consistently exceeds 12-15 people
- An apprentice is ready to lead
- The group has been together 12-18 months
- Energy is high and momentum is strong

<Callout type="tip">
  Multiplication is easier when it's expected from the beginning. Tell new 
  groups on day one: "Our goal is to grow and multiply so more people can 
  experience this kind of community."
</Callout>

---

## Session 5: Logistics and Execution

**Goal:** Leaders understand the practical requirements of running a group.

### Content to Cover

| Topic | Key Points |
|-------|------------|
| **Group Launch** | First meeting essentials |
| **Rhythm and Schedule** | Weekly, bi-weekly, semester-based |
| **Location and Hospitality** | Creating a welcoming environment |
| **Curriculum Selection** | Choosing and preparing studies |
| **Communication** | Keeping members informed |
| **Reporting** | Attendance, pastoral concerns, needs |

### First Meeting Essentials

- [ ] Introductions and icebreakers
- [ ] Establish group expectations (time, confidentiality, participation)
- [ ] Share contact information
- [ ] Preview the curriculum/study
- [ ] Pray together
- [ ] Confirm next meeting details

### Ongoing Administration

| Task | Frequency |
|------|-----------|
| Prepare for meeting | Weekly |
| Send reminders | Weekly |
| Report attendance | Weekly |
| Connect with absent members | After each absence |
| Communicate with coach/pastor | Bi-weekly or as needed |
| Evaluate group health | Quarterly |

---

## Training Format Options

| Format | Duration | Best For |
|--------|----------|----------|
| **Intensive** | Full Saturday (8 hours) | Launch Team training pre-launch |
| **Weekly** | 5 weeks, 90 min each | Ongoing leader development |
| **Cohort** | Monthly over 5 months | New leaders after launch |

For pre-launch, the intensive format works best to get all leaders trained quickly.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And let us consider how to stimulate one another to love and good deeds, not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day drawing near."* — Hebrews 10:24-25 (LSB)
</Callout>

Small groups are where "one another" happens. Train your leaders well, and you'll build a church where no one walks alone.
articles.excerpt: Training for small group leaders covering philosophy, mechanics, and leadership skills for healthy group ministry.
articles.title: Small Group 101

articles.content:
Once your Core Group transitions to a Launch Team with an established launch date, the mission shifts. Vision Meetings continue, but the primary focus becomes **training and preparation** for Launch Sunday.

This phase is where your team transforms from enthusiastic supporters into equipped servants ready to execute every aspect of a high-impact church launch.

---

## Why Training Matters

A church plant can have the right people, adequate funding, and a great location—but without proper training, Launch Sunday becomes chaotic instead of celebratory. Training accomplishes three essential outcomes:

1. **Competence** — Team members know what to do and how to do it well
2. **Confidence** — Trained teams serve with assurance rather than anxiety
3. **Cohesion** — Training builds teamwork and shared understanding

<Callout type="insight">
  Training doesn't just prepare individuals—it transforms a group of committed 
  people into a unified team that can execute together under pressure.
</Callout>

---

## The Training Framework

Phase 3 training operates on three levels, each serving a distinct purpose:

### Corporate Training

Training delivered to the entire Launch Team together. This builds shared understanding and team unity.

| Program | Purpose | Audience |
|---------|---------|----------|
| Peak Performance Series | Membership and discipleship foundations | All Launch Team members |
| Boot Camp | Intensive discipleship and leadership development | Emerging leaders |

### Ministry Team Training

Specialized training for each ministry area. This builds competence in specific responsibilities.

| Ministry | Training Focus |
|----------|----------------|
| Worship & Production | Service flow, equipment, transitions |
| Children's Ministry | Curriculum, check-in, safety protocols |
| Facilities | Set-up, tear-down, storage procedures |
| Assimilation | Guest process, database, follow-up |
| Small Groups | Leader training, group dynamics, curriculum |

### Observation & Practice

Learning by watching established churches and practicing in your own context.

- Visit partner churches to observe their operations
- Conduct Pre-Launch Services as full rehearsals
- Practice set-up and tear-down until it becomes second nature

---

## Training Programs at a Glance

### Peak Performance Training Series

A three-session membership class that covers the foundational DNA of your church. Every Launch Team member should complete this series.

**Sessions:**
- Peak Performance I — Vision, mission, and values
- Peak Performance II — Beliefs and doctrine
- Peak Performance III — Commitment and next steps

[Learn more about Peak Performance](/wiki/training/peak-performance-training-series)

### Small Group 101

Training for small group leaders that covers the philosophy, mechanics, and leadership skills needed to launch and sustain healthy small groups.

[Learn more about Small Group 101](/wiki/training/small-group-101)

### Boot Camp

An intensive discipleship experience for emerging leaders. Boot Camp goes deeper than Peak Performance, developing the character and skills needed for ministry leadership.

[Learn more about Boot Camp](/wiki/training/boot-camp-overview)

### Ministry-Specific Training

Customized training for each ministry team covering their unique responsibilities, procedures, and standards.

[Learn more about Ministry-Specific Training](/wiki/training/ministry-specific-training)

---

## Training Timeline

Training should be **90-100% complete** by the time you reach the final 3-4 weeks before launch. That final window is for integration and refinement—not foundational training.

| Timeframe | Focus |
|-----------|-------|
| **Early Phase 3** | Corporate training (Peak Performance, Boot Camp) |
| **Mid Phase 3** | Ministry team training begins |
| **Late Phase 3** | Practice, observation visits, refinement |
| **Final 3-4 Weeks** | Pre-Launch Services, integration, final prep |

<Callout type="warning">
  Don't wait until the last minute to train. Rushed training produces anxious 
  teams. Give your people time to learn, practice, and gain confidence.
</Callout>

---

## The Three Meeting Objectives

As your Launch Team meetings become more frequent, they serve three primary objectives:

1. **Inspire** — Continue casting vision through worship, devotional, and prayer
2. **Instill** — Enculturate the team in values, distinctives, and DNA
3. **Inform** — Train the team in their specific responsibilities

[Learn more about Launch Team Meeting Objectives](/wiki/training/launch-team-meeting-objectives)

---

## Training is Discipleship

Never forget that training is ultimately about discipleship. You're not just teaching skills—you're developing people who will serve the Lord and His church for years to come.

The goal isn't a perfect launch. The goal is mature believers equipped for works of service. Launch Sunday is simply the first opportunity to put that equipping into practice.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"And He Himself gave some as apostles, and some as prophets, and some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints for the work of service, to the building up of the body of Christ,"* — Ephesians 4:11-12 (LSB)
</Callout>

Your job is to equip. Their job is to serve. Together, you build the body of Christ.
articles.excerpt: An overview of the training programs that prepare your Launch Team for a successful church launch.
articles.title: Training Programs Overview

articles.content:
Your first gifts may arrive before your first public service. Decide how you will record and acknowledge them before a donor asks for a statement at tax time.

A clear receipt tells a donor what your church received and what, if anything, you provided in return. This guide covers U.S. federal receipt rules and a practical statement process. A receipt does not establish that every donor can deduct a gift. Leave the donor's tax return to the donor and their tax adviser.

---

## Assign the receipt process

Ask your Financial Leader to name the person who prepares receipts and another authorized person who reviews them. Follow your existing separation of duties. Keep individual giving records with those who need them for financial work; the Senior Pastor should not prepare donor statements or receive individual giving totals.

Use your church's accounting or giving system for this work. Establish a contact address for corrections and keep a copy of every statement you send. If a sending church receives gifts for your plant, agree with its Financial Leader about which organization acknowledges those gifts. Do not have both organizations issue receipts that describe the same donor payment as a gift received by each.

---

## Know which rule applies

The IRS distinguishes the donor's records from the charity's disclosure duties.

| Situation | What to provide or explain |
|---|---|
| Monetary gift of any amount | The donor needs a bank record or church communication showing the organization's name, gift date and amount. |
| Single contribution of $250 or more | The donor needs a timely written acknowledgment from the receiving charity, including the goods-or-services statement. |
| Payment over $75, partly a gift and partly for goods or services | The charity must give a written disclosure of the benefit's estimated value and the limit on the deductible portion, unless an exception applies. |

Apply the $250 test to each contribution. Several smaller gifts do not become a single contribution because their annual total is $250 or more. Still offer every identified donor an accurate statement.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance checked October 15, 2026. Before issuing statements, confirm the current $250 acknowledgment and over-$75 disclosure thresholds with the IRS, using Publication 1771 and its charitable contribution guidance. Ask your accountant about rules for the gift year you are reporting.
</Callout>

---

## Include the acknowledgment details

Use the receiving organization's name. Include the donor's name and the date and amount of each monetary gift. For donated property, describe the property without assigning its tax value.

Address what the donor received in exchange. State that you provided no goods or services if that is true. Otherwise, describe the goods or services and give a good faith estimate of their value. If the only return was intangible religious benefits, say so instead.

Intangible religious benefits include admission to a religious ceremony and generally are not sold commercially outside a gift context. They do not include consumer goods, travel services or education leading to a recognized degree. Have your accountant check wording when the distinction is unclear.

For an ordinary monetary gift with nothing provided in return, a receipt could read:

> Riverbend Church acknowledges a monetary gift of $320 from Jordan Lee on October 4, 2026. The church provided no goods or services in exchange for this gift.

Use wording that matches the actual transaction. Add your contact information so the donor can report an error.

---

## Send it while it can help

A donor must obtain the acknowledgment by the earlier of the date they file their original return for the gift year or that return's due date, including extensions. An acknowledgment sent after the donor files may be too late.

Send acknowledgments promptly throughout the year. A single annual statement can cover several qualifying gifts. List the individual dates and amounts, and include the required acknowledgment language. A paper letter or an email can serve as written acknowledgment.

Use January 31 after the gift year as an internal delivery target, and honor earlier requests. Publication 1771 describes that date as typical charity practice. The controlling deadline for the donor is the earlier-of rule above.

<Callout type="tip">
Send a sample statement to your reviewer before the year ends. Check the organization's name, individual gift entries and acknowledgment language, then test how the donor will open and save it.
</Callout>

---

## Disclose goods and services

A fundraising meal or item offered in return for a payment needs separate attention. The over-$75 disclosure test uses the whole payment, including the benefit's value.

For example, suppose someone pays $120 at a fundraiser and receives a meal with a fair market value of $35. The potential charitable portion is $85. Your written disclosure must explain that only the payment exceeding the benefit's value may be deductible and give the $35 good faith estimate. These figures illustrate the calculation; they are not IRS thresholds.

Provide the disclosure when soliciting or receiving the payment. Do not postpone it until the annual statement. Keep the basis for your valuation with the event records.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not put a blanket no-goods-or-services statement on fundraiser payments when donors received a benefit. Exceptions exist for certain small benefits and intangible religious benefits. Confirm an exception before relying on it; the IRS adjusts some small-benefit limits for inflation.
</Callout>

---

## Handle unusual gifts separately

For donated equipment, acknowledge the item and receipt date, and address any goods or services provided in return. Keep the property description separate from the monetary gift total. The donor handles valuation and any required appraisal. An authorized church signature on Form 8283 acknowledges receipt; it does not endorse the donor's appraised value.

Volunteer time and services are not deductible contributions. Thank volunteers without assigning a deductible amount to their hours. Certain unreimbursed expenses may qualify under separate rules. Have your accountant review the acknowledgment needed for those expenses.

Refer vehicles, securities, retirement-account distributions and gifts through a donor-advised fund for review before applying your ordinary receipt template. This guide does not supply their specialized tax documentation.

---

## Prepare the annual statement

Before sending statements:

- [ ] Reconcile recorded gifts with counting, deposit and online payment records.
- [ ] Review duplicate donor records and confirm the intended recipient and delivery address.
- [ ] Resolve returned payments and unexplained differences before stating a total.
- [ ] List each monetary contribution's date and amount, then verify the annual total.
- [ ] Separate property gifts and payments involving benefits from ordinary monetary gifts.
- [ ] Check acknowledgment wording against what each donor actually received.
- [ ] Have the authorized reviewer check the statements and keep the approved copies.
- [ ] Send statements privately, record delivery and follow up on failed emails or returned mail.

Keep pledges separate from gifts actually made. For year-end transactions, use the IRS contribution-timing rules rather than assigning every gift the date it reached your bank. Ask your accountant to resolve uncertain dates.

---

## Correct mistakes openly

Give donors a named contact for questions. Compare a disputed entry with the underlying records. Explain the correction, send a clearly dated replacement and retain the earlier version with the reason for changing it. Do not backdate a receipt or promise that a late correction will repair the donor's tax position.

Common mistakes include counting a pledge as a payment, sending one donor another donor's statement, omitting acknowledgment language and describing an annual total without individual gift details. Review these points before each statement run.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"In this case, moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful."* — 1 Corinthians 4:2 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Set up donor acknowledgments, distinguish IRS receipt rules and prepare accurate annual giving statements for your church.
articles.title: Donor Receipts and Giving Statements

articles.content:
