You can rehearse the music, finish the lyric slides, and test the stream while still missing permission for what you plan to share. Settle those permissions before your first public service so volunteers know what belongs on the screen and online.

This guide covers U.S. copyright basics for worship music and films. Use it to prepare questions for a licensing provider or copyright attorney. It does not determine whether a particular use is lawful.

---

## Understand the religious-service exemption

Under 17 U.S.C. 110(3), the following is exempt from copyright infringement:

> performance of a nondramatic literary or musical work or of a dramatico-musical work of a religious nature, or display of a work, in the course of services at a place of worship or other religious assembly;

That covers qualifying performances and displays during a religious service. It does not grant permission to make copies. Creating lyric slides or printing song sheets raises a separate reproduction question, even when the display during worship qualifies for the exemption.

The House report explains that the exemption does not extend to transmissions to the public or to showing motion pictures in sequence. It also excludes social, educational, fundraising, and entertainment activities from this particular exemption. Other exceptions may apply, but being a church does not settle every use.

<Callout type="warning">
A worship service in a rented auditorium can qualify. Do not assume the building's license covers your church, or that your service exemption covers a concert, movie night, or public stream.
</Callout>

---

## Map what you will actually use

Make a list before buying a license. Start with the service plan, then include rehearsals, the lobby, and anything you will post later.

| Planned use | What to check |
|---|---|
| Live congregational singing | Whether the service exemption applies |
| Lyric slides or printed songs | Permission to reproduce the exact song |
| Music performed by your team online | Streaming and archive permissions |
| Backing tracks or an artist's recording online | Song and recording coverage |
| Film scene or movie night | Title, venue, audience, and exhibition permission |
| Worship clip in a promotional video | Permission for that separate use |

A song and a particular recording of it are different works. Check both when using recorded music. Put anything uncertain on a question list rather than treating a successful download as permission.

---

## Cover lyrics and music copies

CCLI's Church Copyright License permits specified copying of covered songs for congregational singing, including digital projection. Its terms require song validation, reporting when required, and copyright credits. It does not authorize copying every score, choir arrangement, or instrumental work.

ONE LICENSE offers reprint permissions for covered congregational music in bulletins and projections. Its reprint license excludes music for choirs, ensembles, accompanists, and instrumentalists. Check the publisher and the particular material before making copies.

For your music team, identify the edition you intend to use and ask whether that use is covered. Buy authorized copies or obtain permission for excluded material. Keep the credit information with the slides and handouts so volunteers do not have to reconstruct it on Sunday.

---

## Separate streaming from recording rights

CCLI's Streaming License extends its Church Copyright License to covered songs performed live by church musicians online. Streaming Plus adds coverage for authorized master recordings, backing tracks, and multitracks. Validate the song and recording rather than assuming every track you own qualifies.

ONE LICENSE's Podcast / Streaming options distinguish streaming alone from a bundle that includes reprint rights. Its Limited option does not permit sharing lyrics or melody lines with viewers. Its separate Recorded Audio License can cover specified recordings when paired with Podcast / Streaming permission. Ask the provider to confirm your exact combination and tracks.

Check archived services as well as the live broadcast. Ask what must happen to existing videos if coverage ends. ONE LICENSE requires removal of material licensed under its Podcast / Streaming options when you do not renew.

<Callout type="important">
License descriptions were checked October 15, 2026. Before purchasing or renewing, confirm current terms, fees, catalog coverage, reporting, and archive rules with CCLI, ONE LICENSE, CVLI, or Swank, as applicable. Confirm U.S. law with the U.S. Copyright Office. Provider pages can change.
</Callout>

---

## Treat films as a separate permission

A film's religious theme does not bring its screening within the religious-service exemption. Check permission for a sermon scene and for a full movie before scheduling either.

CVLI's Church Video License covers participating content subject to its terms. Verify the title, any current exclusions, and the licensed location. CVLI says its license does not cover movie content in services streamed to the general public. Its support page describes limited closed or gated streaming permissions, so ask about the precise audience and platform rather than assuming a password is sufficient.

Swank also licenses films for religious organizations. Request permission for your specific event and follow its instructions for obtaining a legal copy. Tell the provider about publicity, admission, location, and online viewing before committing to the event.

---

## Choose coverage around your service plan

Compare coverage against the songs and media you actually intend to use. CCLI and ONE LICENSE are options to investigate, not automatic substitutes for each other. A license is useful only where its catalog and permitted activities match your needs.

Ask a provider to confirm coverage in writing for any doubtful item. Give the song title, writer, publisher, recording version, and intended use. For a film, give the title, event details, and audience.

<Callout type="tip">
Give one person responsibility for the permission list and a backup person access to it. Keep confirmations, license details, renewal dates, and reporting instructions together for the Worship Leader and production volunteers.
</Callout>

Before budgeting, request a current quote for your church and planned uses. Ask whether a sending church's or venue's agreement includes your plant. Record the answer instead of carrying over another organization's license number.

---

## Check the service before going live

Use a checklist with the final service plan:

- [ ] Verify each song, score, recording, and video against its permission.
- [ ] Add the credits and license notices required for slides, handouts, and streams.
- [ ] Check music before and after the service, including any lobby audio reaching the stream.
- [ ] Remove or replace material whose permission you cannot confirm.
- [ ] Test the online feed separately from the room's sound and screens.
- [ ] Record actual use and submit the provider's required reports.
- [ ] Check the posted recording and note its archive and renewal obligations.

YouTube warns that licensed content can still interrupt a live stream if the rights holder has not added the channel to its Content ID allowlist. Ask your provider about handling claims before the service. Keep a plan for continuing without the disputed material.

---

## Avoid shortcuts that leave gaps

Credit is not a substitute for permission. Owning a copy does not give you every reproduction or public-performance right. A music license also does not settle permission for every photo, Bible translation, video, or other item in a service.

Do not assume a short film clip is automatically fair use. U.S. law calls for weighing the purpose, nature, amount used, and market effect. Ask a copyright attorney when relying on that exception for a doubtful use.

Keep a dated record of the use you checked and the answer you received. Recheck when the repertoire, recording source, venue, or distribution changes. The next volunteer should be able to see why an item is cleared without repeating the research.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Whether, then, you eat or drink or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God."* — 1 Corinthians 10:31 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Check the permissions for worship music, lyric copies, streaming, recordings, and films before your church goes live.
articles.title: Copyright Licenses for Worship and Streaming

articles.content:
A guest receives an invitation to your church and searches for the address. Make that search part of your launch preparation. Check what appears under your church's name, who can correct it, and where the map sends someone.

Work through the listings with your Technology Leader or Promotion Leader. Your goal is an accurate public presence with access your church can retain when responsibilities change. Keep the website as the place to explain service times, parking, and what a guest should expect.

---

## Prepare your public information

Make a reference sheet before you open accounts. Use it to check each listing against your website and signs.

| Record | Prepare |
|--------|---------|
| Church identity | Public name, short description, logo |
| Guest contact | Church phone, monitored email, website |
| Meeting location | Approved public address, entrance, parking instructions |
| Schedule | Current service times and any separate office hours |
| Access record | Profile URL, responsible leader, backup, claim status |

Keep passwords and recovery codes in a password manager, separate from this sheet. Use a church-controlled email address for organizational accounts where the platform permits it. Keep personal logins personal when a platform assigns access to individuals.

<Callout type="important">
Platform guidance checked October 15, 2026. Before acting, confirm current eligibility, verification options, and account controls with Google Business Profile Help, Apple Support, Yelp for Business, and Meta Help. Apple now calls Business Connect Apple Business. Screens and requirements can change.
</Callout>

---

## Find and claim your Google profile

Search Google Maps for your church's name and city. Check the address before selecting a result, especially if another church has a similar name.

- [ ] If your church has an unverified profile, select "Claim this business" and follow "Manage now."
- [ ] If another account has verified it, use Google's ownership-request process.
- [ ] If no profile exists and your church is eligible, start at `business.google.com/add`.
- [ ] Complete the verification options Google offers, then check the public result.

Google determines the available verification methods. Do not plan around receiving a particular method or finishing by a promised date. Add another authorized leader through the profile's "People and access" controls. Each person should use their own Google Account.

Use your actual church name. Keep marketing taglines and extra service or location descriptions out of the name field. Select the category that accurately describes your church.

---

## Check eligibility at your meeting location

A rented venue needs care. Google excludes an ongoing meeting at a location you neither own nor have authority to represent. Confirm your authority with the venue and check Google's eligibility guidance before creating a profile. Do not claim the school's or host church's listing as your own.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not substitute a P.O. box or remote mailbox for an eligible Google location. If your meeting arrangement is unclear, ask Google support before proceeding. Keep an accurate invitation and directions on your website while you resolve it.
</Callout>

Keep worship schedules separate from ordinary opening hours. Google's guidance says some organizations with varied activity schedules, including worship services, should not provide business hours. Check the rule against your actual arrangement rather than copying the service time into every hours field.

---

## Update your Apple Maps location

Use Apple Business, formerly Apple Business Connect, to manage your church's Apple Maps location. In Apple's current guide, the location workflow begins at "Brands" then "Locations." Choose "Add Location" and "Add single location," then search for your church.

Select the existing location if it appears. Add a new location only after checking for a match. Review the map marker, address, category, phone, website, and applicable hours. Follow Apple's organization or location verification prompts. Phone verification is available only in some circumstances.

If another organization manages the location, use Apple's transfer-request process and provide the supporting documentation it requests. Record whether the claim is pending or complete in your access record. Check Apple Maps itself after approval.

---

## Claim your Yelp page

Start at `biz.yelp.com/claim` and search for the church. Select its existing page, or use "Add to Yelp for free" if it is absent. Create a Yelp for Business account with an email you monitor, then follow the verification prompts.

Yelp describes claiming as free and separate from advertising. Keep any advertising proposal as a separate spending decision for your church.

Once you have access, check the address, phone, website, photos, and applicable hours. Use a recognizable exterior or entrance photo to help guests identify the meeting place. If the existing page belongs to a different church, leave it alone and resolve the mismatch with Yelp support.

---

## Establish Facebook and Instagram accounts

Search for existing church accounts first. If a former volunteer manages one, ask for an access handoff before creating another account with a similar name.

Use a Facebook Page for your church's public presence. If you need a new Page, follow Meta's Page creation guide. Add your church's identifying information and website. Facebook lets people with full control manage other people's Page access. Have an authorized leader grant access to the people responsible for the Page.

For Instagram, create or recover the church account, choose a recognizable available username, and add the church website and a clear description. Check that the account's email and recovery phone still reach an authorized person. Instagram's help guidance warns that losing access to the signup email can limit account recovery.

<Callout type="tip">
Link the church's social accounts from your official website. Instagram identifies this as a way to show authenticity without a verified badge. Record the exact profile URLs so your team shares the right accounts.
</Callout>

---

## Protect access before you hand it off

Use strong, unique passwords and a password manager. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever available, including the email accounts used for recovery. CISA recommends these protections for online accounts.

Plan a handoff while the outgoing volunteer is available. Ask the incoming leader to sign in with their own authorized access and confirm they can perform their assigned work. Use platform roles where offered, and give people the access their responsibilities require. Limit who can change access for everyone else.

Record the responsible leader, backup, and recovery process in a restricted church record. Store recovery codes securely. When someone leaves the role, review their access and update recovery details before closing the handoff. Do not put passwords into an ordinary task checklist or group message.

---

## Check the result as a guest

Ask someone outside the setup team to check the public pages on a phone.

- [ ] Search the church's name and city on Google Maps and Apple Maps.
- [ ] Confirm the map points to the intended meeting place.
- [ ] Open the website link and find the next service time.
- [ ] Test the public phone and contact method.
- [ ] Open each social link from the website.
- [ ] Flag old addresses, duplicate-looking results, and unanswered messages for follow-up.

Assign a leader to repeat this check after a venue, schedule, or leadership change. Put a recurring review on that leader's calendar. Finish by recording unresolved claims and who will follow them up.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"A good name is to be chosen over great wealth, Favor is better than silver and gold."* — Proverbs 22:1 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Claim and check your church's map listings and social accounts, protect access, and keep guest information current.
articles.title: Claiming Your Church's Online Presence

articles.content:
You can learn a great deal about an area before buying a demographic report. The harder part is keeping track of which place, population and time period each number describes.

This guide walks you through U.S. Census Bureau data, USPS delivery routes and local planning resources. You will finish with a short area brief that another leader can check and update.

---

## 1. Name the area you are studying

Write down the question first. Are you describing a city, comparing nearby areas or checking the streets around a possible meeting location? Record the state, county and exact place name before searching.

Start with a named Census geography, such as a city or census tract. If you use several tracts, list each one and retain a map. Label this as your chosen study area. Do not present it as an official neighborhood boundary unless you have checked that boundary with the local agency.

Census ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, called ZCTAs, approximate the distribution of postal ZIP Codes. They are not delivery routes, and some valid postal ZIP Codes have no corresponding ZCTA. Keep those labels separate in your notes.

---

## 2. Choose the right Census product

The American Community Survey, or ACS, describes social, economic, housing and demographic characteristics. Its figures are survey estimates. For population totals, the Census Bureau recommends the decennial census or its Population Estimates Program instead.

| Your question | Starting point |
|---|---|
| What are the area's characteristics? | ACS data profiles |
| What does a small area look like? | ACS five-year estimates |
| What is the population total? | Decennial census or Population Estimates Program |

Standard ACS one-year estimates cover areas with at least 65,000 people. Five-year estimates cover smaller areas, including census tracts. A five-year estimate combines observations across that period. Its ending year does not make it a snapshot of that single year.

<Callout type="important">
Tool instructions and availability were checked October 15, 2026. Before using a figure, confirm the current release, geography and period with the U.S. Census Bureau. Confirm current routes and any mailing requirements with USPS before planning a mailing.
</Callout>

---

## 3. Retrieve the ACS profiles

Open data.census.gov. Search for your place and a table ID, or use its filters to select the geography and survey product. Filters are useful for tracts with complex names. Check the selected geography again whenever you change tables.

The Census Bureau identifies these profile tables:

| Table ID | Profile subject |
|---|---|
| DP02 | Social characteristics |
| DP03 | Economic characteristics |
| DP04 | Housing characteristics |
| DP05 | Demographic and housing estimates |

- [ ] Select your geography and the ACS one-year or five-year product.
- [ ] Choose the period and open the profile you need.
- [ ] Read the row labels, population covered and table notes before copying figures.
- [ ] Keep margins of error visible.
- [ ] Download the table and save its source information.

The Download control offers Excel, CSV and ZIP formats. Excel includes an Information worksheet with source details, the population covered and table notes. CSV has less explanatory information, so save those details separately if you choose CSV. A download can preserve hidden columns or removed margins of error. Check the file you saved.

---

## 4. Check uncertainty before comparing

The Census Bureau publishes a margin of error for every ACS estimate to help you assess reliability. Read it alongside the estimate. If uncertainty is large relative to the figure, mark the result as uncertain before using it in a planning discussion.

For comparisons, use the same product and check that the geography and definition still match. Compare one-year estimates with one-year estimates, or five-year estimates with five-year estimates. Follow Census guidance to compare non-overlapping five-year periods. Adjacent releases share observations and should not be treated as independent annual measurements.

<Callout type="warning">
A difference between two displayed estimates does not by itself establish a real change. Check margins of error and the Census Bureau's comparison guidance before describing an area as growing, shrinking or changing.
</Callout>

If a comparison matters to a major decision, ask a Census data specialist or local planning analyst to help interpret it. Keep their explanation with the tables.

---

## 5. Look at USPS delivery routes

USPS provides the Every Door Direct Mail Online Tool, often called EDDM. Search by address, city and state, or ZIP Code. Use Show Table to inspect neighborhood routes. The tool includes demographic filters such as age, household size and income.

Record the route identifiers and the date you looked them up. Keep any route counts under their displayed labels. Do not relabel delivery addresses as people, or substitute a route total for an ACS population estimate.

Use this step to understand postal coverage. Stop before ordering or paying if you are only researching. Mailing design, postage and campaign decisions require their own current checks.

---

## 6. Ask local planning for context

Search your city or county's official website for its planning department, population reports and open-data resources. Ask which published geography best matches the area you mean.

For a concrete example, New York City's Department of City Planning maintains Population FactFinder. Its documentation describes selecting study areas to produce population profiles. That is an example of a local resource, not a tool covering every city.

Ask your local office these questions:

- Which report or map should I use for this area?
- What period does it describe, and when was it updated?
- Is a figure an observed count, a survey estimate or a projection?
- Have boundaries or definitions changed since the earlier report?

Save the report title and the answer you receive. Do not assume a local dashboard uses newer data just because its page looks recent.

---

## 7. Keep the limits in the brief

The Census Bureau's faith-community guidance explains that the decennial census does not collect religious affiliation. Do not use these profiles to count church attenders or label households as believers or nonbelievers.

Also avoid assigning an area's average characteristics to an individual resident. If a report describes a tract, label your finding as a tract finding. Keep conclusions about a person's circumstances out of the spreadsheet.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"He who responds with a word before he hears, It is folly and shame to him."* — Proverbs 18:13 (LSB)
</Callout>

Keep questions raised by the data in a separate part of your notes. A question to investigate is different from a finding supported by a table.

---

## 8. Save a brief someone else can check

Attach your map and original downloads. For every figure you keep, record the publisher, table ID, row label, geography, period, estimate, margin of error if supplied, source location and access date.

<Callout type="tip">
Start your brief with the area definition and data period. A reader should be able to tell what the figures describe before reaching the first number.
</Callout>

- [ ] Keep Census areas and postal routes clearly labeled.
- [ ] Separate source findings from questions and local observations.
- [ ] Flag missing information and uncertain comparisons.
- [ ] Record who will check the sources again before the brief informs a decision.

Share the brief and its files together. Another leader should be able to locate the same tables, understand the limits and correct a figure without repeating your whole search.
articles.excerpt: Find Census profiles, inspect USPS routes and check local planning sources. Save an area brief with clear boundaries, dates and limits.
articles.title: Finding Demographic Data for Your Area

articles.content:
Your church needs an Employer Identification Number, or EIN, even if you have no employees. The IRS uses this nine-digit number to identify your organization for tax filing and reporting, and you can use it when opening a church bank account.

You can apply directly through the IRS for free. This guide walks through preparing the information, submitting an application, and keeping the confirmation. It covers the EIN process for a U.S. church.

---

## Know what the number does

An EIN identifies your organization. Receiving one does not establish its federal tax-exempt status. It is also different from a state sales-tax exemption number.

Keep the EIN application separate from questions about recognition of exemption. If you apply for IRS recognition, you need an EIN for that application, but the number itself says nothing about your church's tax status.

<Callout type="important">
IRS procedures and processing information in this guide were checked October 15, 2026. Before applying, confirm the current Form SS-4, instructions, online availability, fees, limits, and processing information with the IRS. The IRS currently charges no fee for an EIN.
</Callout>

---

## Form the church and check for an existing EIN

Wait until your organization is legally formed before applying. If you are creating a corporation, complete state formation first. Use the organization's legal name from its formation documents.

Before starting a new application, check whether your church already has an EIN. Look for the IRS assignment notice, check past tax returns, or ask the bank holding the church's account. If you still cannot find it, an authorized person can ask the IRS to recover the number after identity verification.

A single entity should have only one EIN. If you discover multiple numbers and do not know which to use, contact the IRS Business and Specialty Tax Line for help.

---

## Identify the responsible party

The IRS requires the name and taxpayer identification number of the responsible party. This is the person who ultimately controls the organization and its funds or assets. For a tax-exempt organization, it is generally the principal officer.

For a church, the responsible party must be a person, rather than another organization. Identify that person before filing. A nominee with only limited authority during formation cannot apply for the EIN or be listed as the responsible party.

If an authorized third party will apply, obtain the signed authorization the IRS requires. On a paper application, complete the Third Party Designee section and the signature area. That authorization ends when the IRS assigns and releases the EIN to the designee.

---

## Prepare your application information

Use Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number, and its instructions to prepare. Gather the details before beginning the online session.

| Detail | What to prepare |
|---|---|
| Legal and trade names | Legal name from the formation documents, plus a different trade name if applicable |
| Addresses | Mailing address and a different physical address if applicable; no P.O. box for the physical address |
| Person | Full name and Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number |
| Entity type | The church-specific option, called "Church or church-controlled organization" on Form SS-4 |
| Reason and dates | Reason for applying, starting date, and closing month of the accounting year |
| Activity and employees | Description of the church's activities and expected employee counts for the next 12 months |
| Previous application | Whether this same entity has already received an EIN |

For Form SS-4, select the church option on line 9a. The instructions reserve "Other nonprofit organization" for organizations other than churches or church-controlled organizations.

Answer the employment questions from your actual plans. If you expect no employees, enter zero in the employee-count boxes and skip line 14 as instructed. The IRS may use your answers to determine which federal tax returns you must file.

---

## Apply online through the IRS

The online tool is for domestic organizations formed in the United States or U.S. territories whose principal place of business is there. You must be the responsible party or an authorized representative and have the responsible party's SSN or ITIN.

- [ ] Open the IRS website's "Get an employer identification number" page and use its application button.
- [ ] Enter the church's information and answer the application questions.
- [ ] Submit the application in the same session.
- [ ] If approved, print the EIN confirmation letter for your records.

The IRS issues the number immediately online when it approves the application. The session cannot be saved for later and expires after 15 minutes of inactivity.

<Callout type="warning">
Use only one application method for the same entity. Do not send another application by fax or mail after applying online. The IRS limits EIN issuance to one per responsible party per day across all application methods.
</Callout>

---

## Use an alternative when needed

If you cannot apply online, complete Form SS-4 and use the IRS fax or mail instructions. Sign and date the application, and use the current destination for your location.

For a fax application, provide a return fax number. The SS-4 instructions say you can generally receive the EIN by fax within four business days. For mail, they say to complete the form at least four to five weeks before you need the number and expect it in approximately four weeks.

Treat those periods as estimates. The IRS warns that processing delays can occur. Telephone applications are available only to international applicants, so a domestic church should use the online, fax, or mail route.

---

## Save the confirmation and know when to use it

Print the online confirmation letter and keep a copy of Form SS-4 for your records. The online application also offers the option to save the assignment notice at the end of the session.

You can use your EIN immediately for most business needs, including opening a bank account. The IRS says to wait up to two weeks for electronic tax filing, electronic tax deposits or payments, and its Taxpayer Identification Number Matching Program.

<Callout type="tip">
If you need confirmation later, an authorized caller can request IRS Letter 147C, EIN Previously Assigned, through the Business and Specialty Tax Line. Recover or confirm the existing number rather than applying again because the original notice is missing.
</Callout>

---

## Keep the record current

Use Form 8822-B to report a change of address, location, or responsible party. Report a change of responsible party to the IRS within 60 days of the change.

You do not need a new EIN simply because your church changes its name, address, or responsible party. Changes in ownership or structure generally require a new number, so consult the IRS guidance when the entity itself changes.

Before submitting, check for these avoidable mistakes:

- [ ] Applying before legal formation is complete.
- [ ] Naming a formation nominee as the responsible party.
- [ ] Choosing the generic nonprofit category instead of the church category.
- [ ] Filing duplicate applications for the same entity.
- [ ] Treating an EIN confirmation as proof of tax exemption.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Prepare your church's EIN application, identify the responsible party, and keep the IRS confirmation without duplicating an existing number.
articles.title: Getting Your Church's EIN

articles.content:
USPS offers lower nonprofit prices for eligible USPS Marketing Mail. If you plan to send church flyers or newsletters, check both your church's authorization and the mailing itself before using those prices.

An IRS exemption does not automatically qualify you for nonprofit postage. USPS makes its own eligibility decision, and nonprofit prices apply only to domestic mail.

---

## Check whether your church qualifies

Religious organizations are an eligible category. USPS includes nonprofit organizations whose primary purpose is conducting religious worship, supporting qualifying religious worship organizations, or teaching a particular religious faith.

Your organizing documents and actual activities must support a qualifying primary purpose. The organization must be nonprofit, and its net income must not benefit a private stockholder or individual. Incidental religious activities alone do not qualify an organization.

You apply using PS Form 3624, Application to Mail at Nonprofit USPS Marketing Mail Prices. Select the category that describes your organization's primary purpose.

---

## Check whether the mailing fits

USPS Marketing Mail is bulk mail. Each mailing must contain at least 200 addressed pieces or 50 pounds of addressed pieces. Individual pieces must weigh less than 16 ounces. There is no single-piece USPS Marketing Mail price.

Flyers, newsletters and bulletins are examples of material sent as USPS Marketing Mail, provided the contents do not require another mail class. Check the complete mailing with your Business Mail Entry Unit, especially if it includes advertising.

<Callout type="important">
These requirements were checked with USPS on October 15, 2026. Before printing or paying postage, confirm current eligibility, preparation rules, prices and fees with USPS. Use its current Notice 123 price list and Business Mail Entry Unit for the mailing you plan to send.
</Callout>

---

## Gather the application documents

Prepare evidence of both your nonprofit status and your qualifying purpose. Publication 417 explains the supporting documents; PS Form 3624 includes the application instructions.

| What USPS needs | What to gather |
|---|---|
| Papers | Your articles of incorporation, constitution or other organizing instrument, including amendments |
| Status | Your IRS exemption letter, or, if unavailable, a complete financial statement from an independent auditor substantiating nonprofit status |
| Work | Bulletins, meeting minutes, brochures or other materials showing your activities, with available financial and budget information |

A statement from a member of your organization is not an acceptable substitute for the independent financial statement. Federal income tax exemption itself is not required to qualify for the postal prices, but you still need the required evidence of eligibility.

Use the organization's complete name consistently on the application and supporting documents. Have a responsible church official sign it. A printer or mailing agent cannot sign for your church.

<Callout type="tip">
Ask your postmaster or Business Mail Entry Unit about documentation questions. A postal specialist may request additional supporting information during review.
</Callout>

---

## Submit and wait for authorization

Submit the completed application and supporting documents to the Post Office where you intend to deposit the mail. Request a date-stamped copy for your records. USPS also describes an online application option through its Business Customer Gateway.

Until USPS authorizes nonprofit prices, pay the applicable regular USPS Marketing Mail postage for a Marketing Mail mailing. If you want to preserve a possible refund while the application is pending, arrange this with the postmaster before mailing. Approval can allow a refund of the eligible difference, subject to USPS rules. First-Class Mail postage is not refundable under this process.

When approved, save the authorization letter. USPS issues a national nonprofit authorization number, which belongs in the appropriate space on each nonprofit mailing's postage statement.

---

## Separate authorization from mailing costs

There is no fee to apply for nonprofit authorization. Mailing permits, annual mailing fees and postage are separate matters.

A mailing permit gives permission to use a particular postage payment method. A permit imprint has an application fee; applying to mail with precanceled stamps or a postage meter has no application fee. Ask USPS which permits and fees apply to your planned payment method and mailing location. USPS describes annual-fee waivers for qualifying full-service automation mailings, so confirm whether a waiver applies.

Your national nonprofit authorization can be used at Post Offices that accept presorted mailings. At a location without PostalOne! access, file PS Form 3623 to confirm authorization before using nonprofit prices there. Ask the receiving office to confirm the arrangements before taking your mail to a new location.

---

## Prepare the mailpiece correctly

Nonprofit mail follows the sorting and preparation rules for regular USPS Marketing Mail. It also needs the proper nonprofit marking, such as NONPROFIT ORG, in the location appropriate to your postage payment method.

Show the authorized organization's name and address on the outside or prominently in the contents. If you include a return address, use the authorized organization's name and complete return address. Ask USPS about a different church name before using it; a doing-business-as name must appear on the authorization.

- [ ] Check the content, piece count and weight against the applicable mailing standards.
- [ ] Confirm the nonprofit marking and organization identification.
- [ ] Prepare the required sorting and postage statement.
- [ ] Enter the national nonprofit authorization number on that statement.

---

## Do not borrow another organization's authorization

Your authorization covers your organization's own mail. It cannot be lent or rented to another organization. A supporting church's authorization does not automatically cover a separate church plant's mail.

Cooperative mailings have their own eligibility rules, including a limited fundraising exception. If another organization shares the mailing's cost, risk or benefit, ask USPS to review the arrangement before claiming nonprofit prices.

<Callout type="warning">
Authorization does not approve every product or advertisement you might include. Have your Business Mail Entry Unit review advertising while you are designing the piece. Check Publication 417 before committing to a print run with promotional inserts.
</Callout>

---

## Keep the authorization and mailing records

Keep your application copy, approval letter and postage statements together. They document the application, authorization and mailings, and postage statements support a refund request when one is available.

USPS revokes nonprofit authorization for nonuse if the authorized organization makes no nonprofit-price mailings during a two-year period. Keep track of your mailing dates, and confirm your authorization before restarting after a long pause.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Apply for USPS nonprofit mailing authorization and check the costs, content and preparation rules before sending your church’s mail.
articles.title: Nonprofit Postage Rates

articles.content:
Your church needs records that support its tax-exempt status and any federal returns it must file. IRS guidance includes governing documents, minutes, accounting records and property records, even when a church has not applied for formal recognition of exemption.

Start a corporate records binder with those documents, and keep a clear index to related files. Use the filing arrangement below as a practical starting point, then check the rules that apply to your church.

---

## Choose a usable filing system

The IRS does not prescribe a specific recordkeeping format for churches. Choose a system suited to your activities, with records that support the income and expenses in your books.

For this setup, use a binder for permanent corporate documents and an index to financial and property files stored elsewhere. Give each index entry a document category and its storage location. Keep the same categories in your electronic folders so you can find the supporting records when needed.

<Callout type="tip">
This binder layout is an organizing suggestion. The IRS requires adequate records, not a particular binder, set of tabs or software product.
</Callout>

---

## Gather the permanent documents

IRS Publication 4221-PC recommends keeping organizing documents, amendments and board minutes permanently. It also includes the application for recognition of exemption and the determination letter among permanent records.

Create these tabs or folders:

- Articles of incorporation or other organizing document, with amendments.
- Bylaws, with amendments.
- Board meeting minutes.
- Exemption application and IRS determination letter, if your church has them.

Keep earlier amendments with the permanent documents. Mark the current governing documents clearly so a reader can distinguish them from older versions.

The IRS church guide says recordkeeping applies whether or not the IRS has officially recognized your exemption. If your church has no determination letter, continue collecting the records that support its claim to exemption.

---

## File decisions as they happen

The IRS encourages governing bodies and authorized committees to document meetings and written actions contemporaneously. File the resulting minutes and written decisions with the governance records.

Check your own state's nonprofit corporation law for the records it requires. For example, Washington's corporate-records statute covers meeting minutes, unanimous written consents and actions by board committees. It also calls for current governing documents, a current director and officer list, and the latest annual report delivered to the secretary of state.

Use that example to prepare questions for your state filing office or attorney. Confirm which records your legal structure must maintain, rather than treating another state's checklist as your own.

---

## Keep the supporting records

Your accounting books need supporting documents. IRS examples include invoices, paid bills, receipts, deposit slips and canceled checks. Organize those files by year and type of receipt or expense, and put their locations in the binder index.

Retain documents showing the amounts and sources of receipts, including donor correspondence and pledge documents when applicable. For expenses, keep evidence of the amount paid and the purpose of the expense, including relevant contracts and invoices.

For property, keep acquisition and disposition records. Include purchase and sale documents, improvement costs and financing documents where applicable. File them by asset so the purchase history remains connected to the eventual disposition record.

---

## Set retention periods carefully

Use the IRS guidance below as a starting point for your written retention schedule. These are different categories with different starting events, not a single discard date for everything in the binder.

| Record category | IRS guidance |
|---|---|
| Organizing documents, bylaws and amendments; board minutes; exemption application and determination letter | Keep permanently, under Publication 4221-PC guidance. |
| Revenue and expense records, including payroll records | Publication 1828 says at least four years after filing the returns to which they relate. |
| Records of property acquisition and disposition, including investments | Publication 1828 says at least four years after filing the return for the year in which disposition occurs. |
| Employment tax records | The IRS employment-tax page says at least four years after filing the fourth quarter for the year. Special tax-credit records can require longer. |

The revenue and expense guidance is tied to the relevant return's filing. The property guidance is tied to the return for the disposition year. If no relevant return is required, ask your tax adviser how to set the retention period; do not invent a filing date.

<Callout type="important">
Retention guidance checked October 15, 2026. Before disposing of records, confirm the current guidance with the IRS and check applicable state requirements. Publication 4221-PC notes that a grantor, insurer, creditor or state agency may require longer retention.
</Callout>

---

## Protect paper and electronic files

Keep sensitive paper records in a locked cabinet or room. Limit access to people who need the information for their responsibilities, following the FTC's practical data-security guidance.

Apply that approach to payroll and other files containing personal information. Use the binder index to point to restricted files rather than putting every sensitive document into a widely shared binder.

Electronic records still need to meet the basic recordkeeping requirements that apply to paper records. The IRS encourages a written retention policy that addresses electronic files, backups, archiving and regular checks of system reliability.

<Callout type="warning">
A scanned file still needs protection and a usable backup process. Include backup and reliability checks in your records policy, and check access to sensitive files rather than assuming everyone with the binder needs those files too.
</Callout>

---

## Write down how records are handled

Adopt a written policy covering document integrity, retention and destruction, as the IRS encourages. Identify the categories you keep, their locations, the applicable retention periods and how you will dispose of sensitive records securely when they are no longer needed.

Include the electronic-file procedures and backup checks. Review access when people's responsibilities change so access continues to match their work.

Before approving destruction, check both tax and non-tax needs. Reaching the end of an IRS period does not settle a longer requirement from another applicable source.

---

## Check the binder against the files

Use this setup checklist:

- [ ] Gather organizing documents, bylaws, amendments and board minutes.
- [ ] Add exemption application records and the determination letter if applicable.
- [ ] Check state requirements for corporate records and current officer information.
- [ ] Index the accounting support and property records by storage location.
- [ ] Record retention periods and the events that start them.
- [ ] Restrict sensitive files and document backup and disposal procedures.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Organize your church’s governing documents, minutes and supporting records, with IRS retention guidance and a practical setup checklist.
articles.title: Keeping a Corporate Records Binder

articles.content:
Open a bank account for your church when you are ready to receive and spend church funds. Use a dedicated organizational account to keep those transactions separate from your personal finances.

Before you apply, gather the church's legal documents and EIN, compare account terms, and involve your Financial Leader. Follow the church's existing financial-accountability policy when choosing who will use the account.

---

## Start with the church's financial controls

Read [Principles of Financial Accountability](/wiki/administrative/financial/principles-of-financial-accountability) before naming signers or requesting online access. It assigns financial operations to a Financial Leader under the elders' direction and keeps the Senior Pastor out of handling money, writing checks, and bank account access.

Ask the Financial Leader to carry those responsibilities into the account setup. Use the existing policy for separation of duties and spending approvals. Do not give someone transaction access simply because the application asks for information about that person.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"for we respect what is good, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men."* — 2 Corinthians 8:21 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Compare the account's actual costs

Ask prospective banks for the current account terms and fee schedule. The Small Business Administration recommends comparing transaction fees, minimum-balance fees, and early-termination fees rather than choosing your personal bank automatically.

Use this list when you speak with a banker:

| Ask about | What to confirm |
|---|---|
| Monthly costs | Maintenance fees and conditions for avoiding them |
| Balance requirements | Opening deposit and any ongoing minimum balance |
| Deposits and payments | Included transactions and charges after the allowance |
| Cash deposits | How the bank measures its allowance and charges for additional deposits |
| Online access | Separate user accounts and the permissions available |

A nonprofit account can have transaction and cash-deposit allowances even when it has no monthly maintenance fee. Ask the banker to explain both the headline offer and its disclosures before you choose.

<Callout type="important">
Bank terms and federal guidance were checked on October 15, 2026. Confirm current costs and application requirements with your bank, EIN confirmation options with the IRS, customer-identification guidance with FinCEN, and deposit-insurance limits with the FDIC before relying on them.
</Callout>

---

## Get the bank's document checklist

Tell the banker your church's legal structure before requesting a checklist. Requirements for a corporation can differ from those for an unincorporated association. Ask which documents establish the church's existence and which people must participate in opening the account.

Prepare the documents your bank requests:

- [ ] The church's EIN and any required IRS confirmation.
- [ ] Formation documents, such as articles of incorporation, a charter, or articles of association, as applicable.
- [ ] Government-issued identification and personal information for authorized signers.
- [ ] Any required assumed-name documentation if the church uses a different public name.
- [ ] Any additional evidence of current officers or authority requested for the church's structure.

For example, Chase's unincorporated-association checklist includes organizational documents and may require meeting minutes listing current officers. Treat that as a bank-specific example, not a universal church checklist.

---

## Bring the right EIN evidence

The IRS says you can use a newly assigned EIN immediately to open a bank account. Ask your bank what written confirmation it accepts.

If you need confirmation, the IRS lists an entity transcript, a digital CP575 for eligible Business Tax Account users, and Letter 147C, EIN Previously Assigned. Request Letter 147C through the IRS business and specialty tax line. The digital CP575 can substitute for the original CP575A-J notice series and Letter 147C.

When preparing the application, compare the church name on the EIN record with its formation documents. The IRS instructs applicants to use the name on their registration or formation documents when applying for an EIN.

<Callout type="tip">
If you already have an EIN, use the IRS confirmation process when documentation is missing. Do not apply for another EIN just to replace a missing notice.
</Callout>

---

## Expect questions about the people involved

FinCEN distinguishes nonprofit ownership from control. A nonprofit or nonstock corporation, or similar entity validly organized with the appropriate state authority, is excluded from the ownership part of the customer-due-diligence requirement. That exclusion does not depend on federal tax-exempt status. For a church organized as a nonprofit or nonstock corporation, the bank still collects information under the control part.

For such a corporation, expect to identify a person with significant responsibility for managing or directing the organization. FinCEN's examples include a treasurer. Its guidance calls for identifying information such as name, date of birth, address, and Social Security number or another applicable government identification number.

FinCEN does not treat an unincorporated association as a legal entity customer, so this beneficial-ownership requirement does not apply. The bank still identifies signers and may ask for current officers under its own procedures. Explain the church's actual structure rather than inventing ownership percentages. Ask the banker to distinguish identity information from account permissions, and continue to follow the church's signer policy.

---

## Check how deposit insurance applies

For a qualifying corporation, partnership, or unincorporated association, FDIC coverage is up to $250,000 at the same insured bank. The organization must engage in an independent activity, meaning a legitimate purpose rather than existing solely to increase deposit-insurance coverage. Corporations and partnerships must also be validly formed under applicable state law.

The FDIC combines accounts owned by the same nonprofit corporation at the same bank. Calling one account an operating account and another a building fund does not give each its own insurance limit.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not count a separate insurance allowance for every account or fund name. If the church expects deposits beyond the applicable coverage, ask the FDIC and your bank to confirm how the church's ownership and account arrangement affect coverage.
</Callout>

---

## Complete the application with the banker

Confirm who must attend or complete identification steps before scheduling the appointment. Bring the requested documents and the required opening deposit. Review the information you submit against those documents.

Be prepared to describe the church's activities and expected account use. Bank applications may ask about the nature of the organization and the types and volume of transactions you expect. Give the banker the church's own information, including any additional details requested for its legal structure.

---

## Set up access for the approved roles

Ask the bank to show your Financial Leader how to configure each approved user's access. For example, U.S. Bank's Shared Access provides individual usernames and passwords, view-only access, and transaction access. Its administrators can add or remove users.

Check each permission against your church's financial-accountability policy before assigning it. Review who can see statements and who can move money. Follow [Disbursements and Approvals](/wiki/administrative/financial/disbursements-and-approvals) for the church's payment process, including its separation between initiating and approving online payments.

Use your bank's access reports to review users, permissions, and limits. Update access when authorized responsibilities change, and keep the church's payment documentation in its accounting records.
articles.excerpt: Prepare the church’s bank documents, confirm EIN and identity requirements, compare account terms, and set up access under your financial controls.
articles.title: Opening the Church Bank Account

articles.content:
When you hire church staff, your church takes on employer responsibilities. Federal income-tax exemption does not remove the need to handle employment taxes correctly.

Start by separating ordinary employee payroll from clergy tax treatment. IRS Publication 517 explains why a minister can be an employee for income-tax purposes while paying self-employment tax on ministerial earnings.

---

## Identify the employer and payroll owner

Before hiring employees, confirm that your church has an Employer Identification Number, or EIN. Use the church's EIN on employment-tax filings and payments, rather than a staff member's Social Security number.

Assign someone to monitor payroll tax payments and IRS correspondence even if you hire a payroll service. The IRS holds the employer responsible when a payroll service fails to deposit its taxes. Keep the church's address on its IRS account so tax notices reach you directly.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"The laborer is worthy of his wages."* — 1 Timothy 5:18 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Classify the work before entering payroll

Under the IRS common-law rule, a worker is generally your employee when you have the right to control what they do and how they do it. Giving someone freedom in daily work does not remove that right of control.

Review the actual working relationship before choosing employee or contractor reporting. Publication 15 directs employers to the worker-classification guidance in Publication 15-A. For wages paid to employees, use Form W-2 rather than a Form 1099.

Part-time employees and employees hired for short periods receive the same federal employment-tax treatment as full-time employees. Review a part-time administrator's status using the work arrangement, rather than assuming a small schedule makes the person a contractor.

---

## Set clergy tax treatment separately

Ask your CPA or payroll provider to review the minister's credentials and duties against Publication 517. Its definition includes duly ordained, commissioned or licensed ministers and describes the religious functions they must be authorized to perform.

| Situation | Federal treatment to review |
|---|---|
| Minister employed by the congregation and paid a salary | Generally an employee with wages for income-tax purposes |
| Earnings for ministerial services | Generally subject to self-employment tax under SECA, rather than FICA, unless an applicable exception applies |
| Church employee outside the clergy categories in Publication 517 | Wages generally subject to Social Security and Medicare under FICA, subject to exceptions such as a qualifying church's Form 8274 election |

A qualifying minister's salary for ministerial services is not subject to mandatory federal income-tax withholding. A minister who is a common-law employee may agree with the church to voluntary withholding to cover income and self-employment taxes. Otherwise, estimated tax payments may be needed. Have the minister and tax adviser settle that arrangement before setting withholding.

<Callout type="warning">
Use a payroll provider or CPA familiar with Publication 517 to review clergy settings. Self-employment tax treatment of ministerial earnings does not, by itself, make the minister an independent contractor for income-tax purposes. Review any claimed exemption against the IRS requirements before changing coverage.
</Callout>

---

## Document a housing allowance before payment

If you include a ministerial housing allowance, the employing church must officially designate a definite amount before paying it. The church cannot decide the amount after the payment. Keep the designation in an employment contract, church minutes, budget or another official action taken before payment.

Designation alone does not make the entire allowance excludable. For a minister who owns a home, Publication 517 limits the income-tax exclusion to the smallest of the amount actually used to provide a home, the officially designated amount, or the home's fair rental value including furnishings and utilities. The allowance must also stay within reasonable compensation for the services.

The housing exclusion applies to income tax, not self-employment tax. Have the CPA check eligibility and the exclusion calculation rather than marking every housing payment tax-free.

---

## Complete the hiring paperwork

Use this checklist when you bring an employee onto payroll:

- [ ] Record the employee's name and Social Security number correctly for wage reporting.
- [ ] Report new and rehired employees to the state where they work within 20 days of hire. Federal law requires every employer to do this; some states require it sooner.
- [ ] For employees subject to federal income-tax withholding, ask for a signed Form W-4 when work starts and apply it to the first wage payment.
- [ ] Have the employee complete and sign Section 1 of Form I-9 no later than the first day of employment.
- [ ] Complete Section 2 within three business days after that first day. For employment lasting less than three business days, complete it no later than the first day.
- [ ] Provide the I-9 instructions and Lists of Acceptable Documents. Let the employee choose which acceptable documentation to present.

Keep the completed I-9; do not mail it to USCIS. Follow its instructions for document examination and any applicable reverification.

---

## Check state requirements independently

Ask your state revenue and labor agencies which employer registrations, withholding rules and employment programs apply to your church. Include the employee's work location and residence in that inquiry. Do not assume the federal payroll settings answer the state questions.

New Jersey illustrates the separate steps. Its registration guidance includes Form NJ-REG for tax and employer registration. Its withholding guidance addresses resident employees and nonresidents working in the state, with exceptions. In New Jersey, federal and state law require employers to report newly hired and rehired employees to the state directory. Use your own state's agency instructions for the reporting method and deadline.

Federal unemployment tax is another distinct question. Organizations exempt under section 501(c)(3) are exempt from FUTA. Check state unemployment obligations separately with the state agency.

---

## Prepare each pay run and filing calendar

For staff subject to ordinary withholding, use Form W-4 and the IRS withholding methods to calculate federal income tax. Account for the employee and employer portions of Social Security and Medicare where applicable. Apply the separately reviewed clergy treatment to ministerial earnings.

Determine the church's federal deposit schedule under Publication 15. Deposit timing follows tax-liability rules, not how often you pay staff. Federal tax deposits must be electronic; filing a return is a separate responsibility.

Generally, report federal income-tax withholding and FICA on quarterly Form 941. Use annual Form 944 only after receiving the IRS's written notice authorizing that filing. Plan for wage statements and SSA reporting too.

<Callout type="important">
Tax guidance checked October 15, 2026. The IRS's general deadline to file 2026 Forms W-2 and W-3 with the SSA and furnish employee W-2 copies is February 1, 2027. Confirm the current deadline, withholding figures and deposit rules with the IRS, and state requirements with the relevant state agencies, before processing payroll.
</Callout>

---

## Keep records and verify the service's work

Retain employment-tax records for at least four years. Publication 15 calls for wage amounts and dates, employee information, withholding certificates, tax-deposit details and copies of returns with confirmation numbers. Keep records of fringe benefits and expense reimbursements, including substantiation.

Reconcile annual wage reporting with the employment-tax returns using the IRS instructions. The reconciliation compares income tax withheld, Social Security and Medicare wages, and those taxes; employer and employee tax portions need different treatment in that comparison.

<Callout type="tip">
Ask your payroll service how you can verify federal deposits yourself through EFTPS. The IRS recommends that employers retain their own access and periodically check payments. Follow up immediately on a missed or late deposit rather than waiting for year-end forms.
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Set up staff payroll with clear clergy tax treatment, hiring forms, state checks, deposit oversight and employment-tax records.
articles.title: Setting Up Payroll for Church Staff

articles.content:
Your church can face claims involving injuries, damaged property or leadership decisions. Insurance offers different kinds of protection for those risks. Start by asking what your church actually needs covered.

Use this reference to prepare for a conversation with a licensed insurance agent or broker. Ask them to connect each recommendation to your ministry activities and the terms of the proposed policy.

---

## Describe the ministry before requesting a quote

Give the agent a written picture of your operations. Include meeting locations, equipment, paid workers and volunteer activities. Describe children's programs, transportation and any space you rent. Ask which activities need separate coverage or an endorsement.

If you already have insurance, provide the current policy for review. Ask the agent to identify gaps and overlapping coverage. If a sending church or network arranges insurance, ask whose organization and activities the policy covers, including your plant's.

---

## Match coverage to the risk

Use these categories as a discussion list. Ask which protections appear in the proposal and which require additions.

| Coverage | What to discuss |
|---|---|
| General liability | Claims that your operations injured someone or damaged someone else's property, plus defense of covered claims. |
| Property | Buildings and belongings, including furniture and equipment, against covered damage or loss. |
| Management liability, including directors and officers | Claims arising from leadership decisions, including protection for the organization and its leaders. |
| Employment practices liability | Employee allegations of discrimination, harassment or wrongful dismissal. |
| Crime | Theft, fraud and employee dishonesty. |
| Cyber liability | Financial losses and liabilities involving data breaches or cyberattacks. |
| Umbrella liability | Additional liability protection above the limits of underlying policies. |

General liability can address injury and property-damage claims from your premises or operations. Ask about legal defense as well as damages. For an umbrella proposal, ask which underlying policies it extends and which risks remain excluded.

---

## Read the venue agreement with your agent

Do not assume the landlord's insurance protects the church's belongings. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners warns tenants to check their own property coverage and read their leases carefully.

Give your agent the venue's insurance requirements. Ask a local attorney to review the agreement's liability obligations. Confirm who must provide a certificate of insurance, whether the venue must be an additional insured, and what policy terms would provide that status.

<Callout type="warning">
A certificate of insurance summarizes coverage. It does not expand the policy. Ask the agent to verify the actual coverage supporting any additional-insured request.
</Callout>

Check that the agreement describes the rooms, access times and intended activities accurately. Include setup and teardown when describing how you will use the space. Ask about the church's liability for damage to property in its care.

---

## Follow equipment and vehicles beyond the venue

Property questions should follow your equipment wherever you use or store it. Describe instruments, sound equipment and computers, including items kept away from your meeting location. Ask about inland marine coverage for movable equipment in transit or temporarily off-site.

Document the assets and keep purchase records and photographs. Ask the agent how to value the equipment for the proposed coverage, including whether payment would reflect replacement cost or depreciation.

<Callout type="tip">
Walk the agent through an equipment move. Where is it stored, how does it travel, and where is it used? Ask them to identify coverage for each part of that trip.
</Callout>

Discuss vehicles separately. Hired and non-owned auto liability addresses organizational risks when workers or volunteers drive personal vehicles for ministry or the church rents a vehicle. Ask separately about damage to a rented vehicle itself and about any church-owned vehicles.

---

## Ask explicitly about abuse coverage

Sexual misconduct and molestation liability is a specialized coverage category. Ask about allegations involving the church, employees and volunteers. Have the agent explain who is insured, the covered allegations, exclusions and the available legal defense.

Ask them to identify the relevant policy wording rather than relying on a general description of church liability insurance. Coverage details vary. Ask whether the insurer requires or offers abuse-prevention measures, and discuss them alongside the coverage review.

Keep the discussion about insurance specific. Ask what the proposed policy requires of your church and how to report an allegation to the insurer.

---

## Check workers' compensation with your state

Ask your state's workers' compensation agency how its requirements apply to your church and each worker's duties. Do not decide that every worker is exempt because the employer is religious.

For example, New York's Workers' Compensation Board lists a nonprofit exception for clergy and religious-order members whose work consists solely of religious duties. Ask the Board about the actual duties before relying on that exception. Treat this as a New York example, not a rule for another state.

<Callout type="important">
State requirements and policy offerings can change. Confirm current requirements with your state's workers' compensation agency and confirm available coverage with your agent. The New York example and insurer descriptions here were checked on October 15, 2026.
</Callout>

---

## Compare the policy terms

Ask the agent to explain the proposal's limits, exclusions and endorsements. Have them show what each recommendation covers in your actual operations.

Bring these questions to the review:

- Who and what does the policy insure, and at which locations?
- When does coverage begin and end?
- What is the deductible, and can the church pay it after a loss?
- What limits apply, and what losses would remain the church's responsibility?
- Which activities or property are excluded?
- How should you notify the insurer about a claim?

Ask for clarification before choosing. Keep the policy documents and the agent's explanations with your insurance records.

---

## Review coverage as the church changes

Review coverage annually and when your operations, property or activities change. Use the review to revisit your inventory and the ministry description you gave the agent.

- [ ] Describe changed activities and meeting locations.
- [ ] Update the equipment list and supporting records.
- [ ] Revisit staffing and transportation arrangements.
- [ ] Compare the policy with current venue requirements.
- [ ] Ask the agent to explain remaining gaps or exclusions.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Commit your works to Yahweh And your plans will be established."* — Proverbs 16:3 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Coverage categories and questions to take to an insurance agent about your church, rented venue, equipment, workers and volunteers.
articles.title: Church Insurance Basics

articles.content:
Before you add a form to your church website, decide what information you need and who will receive it. Use the FTC's advice to collect less and protect what you keep as a starting point for your church's procedures.

Give visitors a clear explanation of what you do with their information. Build newsletter sign-ups around an intentional choice, and check that the site's settings match what you tell people.

---

## Map what your website collects

The FTC recommends tracing information from collection through storage and access. Work through your site with whoever manages it, including your outside providers. Use this inventory as a worksheet, adding only the tools you actually use.

| Website feature | Questions to record |
|---|---|
| Contact form | What fields do you request, and which inbox receives them? |
| Newsletter form | Where is permission recorded, and who can export the list? |
| Event registration | What information is necessary for this event? |
| Analytics and embedded tools | What do they collect, and which providers receive it? |

Include downloaded spreadsheets and forwarded form submissions in your review. Remove fields you cannot justify keeping.

---

## Write a notice you can honor

The FTC urges organizations it regulates to honor their privacy promises. Apply that discipline to your church's notice. Write about your actual practices, then have your website provider and a qualified attorney review it.

Explain what you collect, why you use it, and which providers receive it. Describe your retention approach and give visitors a way to ask privacy questions. Put a clearly labeled privacy link near your forms and in the footer as a practical way to make the notice easy to find.

<Callout type="warning">
Check broad promises such as "We never share your information" against your provider arrangements. Describe the sharing that actually occurs. Review the notice whenever you change how the site collects or uses information.
</Callout>

---

## Review cookies and tracking tools

A cookie stores information in a browser and can help a site recognize a returning device. Cookies can support preferences, usage measurement, or targeted advertising. Ask your provider to identify each tool's purpose and duration.

Review tracking pixels too. According to FTC staff, third-party cookie blocking may not entirely stop a pixel's data collection and sharing. Ask what your analytics, advertising tools, and embedded content send to other companies before enabling them.

<Callout type="important">
The CAN-SPAM, COPPA and CCPA statements are general guidance, not legal advice, checked October 15, 2026. Before launch, confirm current requirements with the FTC, your state attorney general, and counsel. Ask which privacy, cookie-consent, and opt-out rules apply to your church and its visitors. California's attorney general says the CCPA generally does not apply to nonprofits. Treat that as guidance about that law, not a decision about every privacy obligation.
</Callout>

---

## Make email sign-ups a separate choice

Use a distinct newsletter sign-up or a separate optional choice on another form. As a recommended practice, do not treat a request for directions as permission for ongoing newsletters.

Mailchimp, for example, defines permission as express, verifiable consent and distinguishes it from agreement to something else. Check your own email provider's terms before importing contacts. Keep a record of the permission you receive.

Explain the messages people are choosing. For example, offer church news and event invitations only if that describes the list you intend to send.

Mailchimp offers double opt-in, which asks people to confirm their signup. If you use it, test the confirmation email as well as the form. Its opt-in settings do not control form integrations or API sign-ups, so check those separately.

---

## Check commercial email before sending

CAN-SPAM focuses on commercial messages. The FTC says the message's primary purpose determines coverage. Ask counsel about mixed messages or promotions; do not classify an email solely by the church's nonprofit identity.

For covered commercial email, check the FTC's compliance guide and these requirements:

- Use accurate sender information and a truthful subject line.
- Identify advertising clearly. The Act has an exception to its advertising-identification requirement for prior affirmative consent.
- Include a valid physical postal address and a clear way to opt out.
- Keep the opt-out mechanism working for at least 30 days after sending.
- Honor opt-out requests within 10 business days, without a fee or a demand for personal information beyond an email address.

Include an option to stop all marketing messages. Hiring a sending service does not remove your legal responsibility for covered email.

<Callout type="tip">
Use a test address to check the unsubscribe process before sending. Confirm that the sender, postal address, and opt-out instructions appear in the delivered message. Check the result in your sending system, too.
</Callout>

---

## Check children's forms separately

COPPA addresses online collection from children under 13 by covered operators. The FTC says nonprofits generally are not subject to COPPA, while encouraging them to provide its protections to children.

For children's registrations, consider directing the form to a parent or guardian. The FTC distinguishes information collected from adults about children from information collected online from children. Have counsel and your provider review the actual collection process. A general newsletter checkbox should not stand in for a review of children's information practices.

---

## Limit access and retention

Give staff and volunteers access according to their responsibilities. The FTC recommends separate accounts and access limited to a person's need to know. Review provider access as well as church accounts.

Write down what you retain, why you need it, and how you will dispose of it securely. Check legal retention needs before setting deletion rules. Protect information throughout its journey, including form notifications and downloaded files.

Use fictitious information for training or development. FTC security guidance recommends avoiding real personal information when it is unnecessary for those activities.

---

## Test before you invite sign-ups

Use this final check to compare your promises with the working site:

- [ ] Submit test information and follow it to its destination.
- [ ] Confirm that newsletter permission matches the visitor's choice.
- [ ] Read the privacy notice against the inventory and provider settings.
- [ ] Test any cookie choices the site offers with your provider.
- [ ] Confirm that unsubscribe requests take effect.
- [ ] Assign someone to review access, retention, and changed tools.

Repeat the relevant checks when your forms or providers change. Keep the notice and the working process in agreement.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Lying lips are an abomination to Yahweh, But doers of faithfulness are His delight."* — Proverbs 12:22 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Review your church website's privacy notice, tracking tools, email permissions, and handling of visitors' information.
articles.title: Website Privacy, Cookies and Email Sign-Ups

articles.content:
You need a place where your church can meet and a clear reason for choosing it. Compare the same requirements at every venue, using the owner's terms and what you observe on site.

Use this guide to build a comparison sheet, check costs and discuss the tradeoffs. A score helps organize that discussion. It does not grant permission to use a building or replace checking the rental agreement.

---

## Define what the venue must do

Write your requirements before rating buildings. Separate conditions you must meet from preferences you can trade off. Keep a venue out of the final ranking while an essential condition remains unresolved.
