Ask each owner whether your proposed worship use is permitted, which rooms you may use and which dates and access times they can offer. Describe your expected attendance and the time you need before and after the gathering.

School requests can involve priorities beyond your own calendar. Conway School District in Washington gives school and youth activities priority and reviews whether suitable space is available. Treat its process as a local example, then ask your prospective owner how approval works there.

<Callout type="warning">
Keep approval separate from scoring. Mark a missing permission or unanswered requirement as unresolved. Do not turn it into an average rating that disappears inside a total.
</Callout>

---

## Compare the surrounding areas fairly

Attach the area research from your demographic brief to each venue. Record the geography, table, period and margin of error with every American Community Survey estimate you use.

Use the same survey product and period across the areas you compare. Census guidance says to compare one-year estimates with one-year estimates and five-year estimates with five-year estimates. Check that the definitions and geographic boundaries match your question.

For small areas such as census tracts, the Census Bureau identifies five-year estimates as a source. These combine data collected across the period. Keep that period visible rather than labeling the figures as a current snapshot.

Use the findings to describe the surrounding area. Keep your observations about the building in a separate part of the sheet.

---

## Walk the site with access in mind

Use the Washington Governor's Office of the Education Ombuds event checklist as a starting point for a visit. It asks about accessible parking, entrances, meeting rooms, restrooms, seating and emergency exits. Involve people with disabilities in planning, as the checklist recommends.

- [ ] Follow the route from accessible parking or drop-off to the entrance.
- [ ] Check the routes to gathering rooms and restrooms.
- [ ] Identify barriers, unclear signs and inaccessible entrances.
- [ ] Check access to the speaking area and seating arrangements.
- [ ] Ask about emergency evacuation arrangements and assistance.

Record what needs follow-up with the owner. Keep these observations alongside the checklist rather than treating a general description of the property as proof that every room works for your gathering.

---

## Ask for the terms for your actual use

Request the agreement, fee schedule and insurance requirements for the rooms and activities you propose. At Conway, an approved applicant must provide proof of insurance, and the district arranges specific services with the applicant.

Theatres also need a specific inquiry. Regal's request form includes a Theatre Church option for weekly worship services. It asks about the planned start date and expected launch attendance. Use that route to ask about your proposed gathering instead of assuming a movie screening offer covers it.

Ask how competing uses affect the dates offered. Ask which staff and services come with access, and what happens when either party needs to change a reservation. Keep the owner's answers with the proposed agreement.

<Callout type="important">
Rental processes and examples were checked October 15, 2026. Confirm current availability, charges, deposits and insurance requirements directly with the named school district or theatre operator before committing funds.
</Callout>

---

## Compare the full cost of using the space

Build a cost sheet from each owner's written quote. Clover Park School District in Washington distinguishes space rental from special equipment and lighting. Its guidance also describes staffing charges, possible security and possible cleaning or damage deposits.

Use those categories as questions for every quote, not as charges you assume every venue imposes.

| Cost question | What to request |
|---|---|
| Space | Rooms included and chargeable hours |
| Staffing | Required staff and how their time is billed |
| Equipment | Included items and separately charged services |
| Cleaning and damage | Deposit terms and cleaning responsibilities |
| Insurance | Required evidence and coverage terms |

Ask whether billed time includes access before and after the gathering. Confirm staffing minimums and special-day charges in the owner's current schedule. Leave an unquoted item marked unresolved until you receive an answer.

---

## Build a simple scoring sheet

ASQ's decision-matrix procedure starts with criteria and relative weights. Give more weight to what matters most in this decision, then rate every eligible venue against the same criteria.

Use its simple scale of 1 for low, 2 for medium and 3 for high. Define what those ratings mean for each row before scoring. Higher must always mean more desirable, so label a cost row "affordability" rather than "cost."

| Criterion | Evidence beside the rating |
|---|---|
| Fit with intended area | Area brief and location notes |
| Usable gathering space | Rooms offered and site observations |
| Ease of access | Visit checklist and unresolved barriers |
| Affordability | Complete quote and required services |
| Practical access times | Owner's offered schedule |

Choose your own weights. Multiply each rating by its weight, then add the results for each venue. Retain the evidence beside the scores.

<Callout type="tip">
Write the rating definitions before comparing totals. A high affordability rating should mean a more affordable option, not a higher bill.
</Callout>

---

## Challenge the result

Discuss disagreements about ratings before settling on a total. ASQ advises reaching agreement rather than averaging conflicting ratings or taking a popularity vote.

Recalculate with different reasonable assumptions where your team disagrees. HM Treasury's decision-analysis guidance uses sensitivity analysis to examine how changes in scores or weights affect rankings. Apply that question here without presenting this simple worksheet as its formal appraisal method.

If a different assumption changes your preferred venue, record the tradeoff and investigate the disputed evidence. Do not change weights merely to make a favorite building win.

---

## Keep the reasons with the recommendation

Save the comparison, quotes, visit notes and unresolved questions together. Record which option you recommend and the evidence and assumptions behind that recommendation.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"He who responds with a word before he hears, It is folly and shame to him."* — Proverbs 18:13 (LSB)
</Callout>

Before committing, return to unresolved permissions and rental terms. The highest score is a prompt for discussion, not an instruction to sign.
articles.excerpt: Compare venue permissions, access, rental costs and area data. Build a scoring sheet that keeps evidence and unresolved questions beside the ratings.
articles.title: Comparing and Scoring Venues

articles.content:
Give your church a way to receive mail, answer calls and share working documents. USPS offers mailboxes, and office services can provide phone and collaboration tools across the devices your team uses.

If you work from home, use the same workstation and information-security checks you would use for an office elsewhere. The OSHA and FTC guidance below provides practical starting points for arranging your work and protecting the information you handle.

---

## Choose a mailing address

A USPS PO Box holds mail at a Post Office until you collect it. It can help keep your home address private. Compare locations, box sizes and access hours against your mail volume and pickup schedule.

A private mailbox is a different arrangement. USPS calls businesses that receive mail for customers commercial mail receiving agencies, or CMRAs. They hold mail for pickup or remail it with new postage. If you are considering a virtual mailbox, ask the provider how it handles physical mail and digital delivery.

USPS rules cover mail received through an agency, including PS Form 1583, Application for Delivery of Mail Through Agent. Ask the provider to explain its application and identity-verification process before you subscribe.

<Callout type="warning">
USPS Street Addressing can support private-carrier deliveries at participating PO Box locations, subject to restrictions. Its agreement prohibits using that address as your physical residence or place of business in legal documents. Keep that limitation in view when completing forms.
</Callout>

---

## Arrange mailbox access and pickup

To reserve a USPS PO Box online, select the location, size and payment period, then complete the application and payment. Bring the printed application and two acceptable forms of identification to that Post Office within 30 days of submitting the online application.

PS Form 1093 explains the identification requirements, including current photo identification and proof of your physical address. Check the acceptable documents before making the trip.

USPS encourages you to empty the box regularly and keep application information current. Check the location's lobby and counter hours, including how to collect packages that do not fit in the box. Confirm which people may collect your church's mail.

<Callout type="important">
Postal procedures and product features were checked on October 16, 2026. Before paying, confirm current fees, renewal terms, identification requirements and available services with USPS or your chosen provider. Confirm phone and productivity-plan features with the vendors too.
</Callout>

---

## Arrange your home workstation

Use OSHA's workstation evaluation checklist to review the place where you will do church administration. Treat it as practical setup guidance rather than a determination of your church's legal obligations.

Check that your back has support and your feet rest on the floor or a stable footrest. Position the mouse beside the keyboard so you can use it without reaching. Adjust the screen so you can read it without bending your neck or leaning forward.

If you use the phone while typing, consider a headset that lets you keep your head upright and shoulders relaxed. Review the arrangement while doing your actual computer and phone work.

---

## Evaluate equipment before acquiring it

Use OSHA's purchasing checklist when considering a desk, chair, monitor or laptop accessories. Check screen visibility and adjustability, space for your keyboard and mouse, and room for your legs under the desk.

OSHA recommends an external keyboard and pointing device for laptops and tablets. Its guide also suggests trying a chair for comfort and fit before purchasing it. Apply those fit checks to equipment you are offered as well as equipment you might buy.

<Callout type="tip">
Check the workstation before deciding which item to acquire. OSHA provides both an evaluation checklist for the setup and a purchasing checklist for equipment. Use the evaluation to identify what needs attention.
</Callout>

---

## Set up a church phone number

Compare a phone service's calling devices and administrative controls. For example, Google Voice supports mobile devices, laptops and supported desk phones. Its managed service offers number assignment and porting, with call-routing features depending on the plan.

Ask whether the plan includes the routing your church needs, such as a ring group or automated attendant. Check the selected edition rather than assuming every feature on a vendor's product page comes with every subscription.

Before sharing the number, make a test call and check the configured routing and voicemail. Use the provider's administrative tools to assign the number to the intended user.

Read the emergency-calling instructions separately. Google says Voice emergency calling is unavailable during a power outage, lost internet connection or Voice service outage, and directs users to an alternative phone service. Include that limitation when explaining the phone setup to your team.

---

## Choose everyday productivity tools

Compare the tools for email, documents, spreadsheets, file sharing and calendars. Google's Workspace nonprofit offering, for example, lists Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive and Calendar, with email at your own domain. Confirm eligibility and the features of the edition you are considering.

For shared administration, Google allows administrator roles with different privileges. Assign a role according to the tasks a person will manage, such as users or service settings. Keep broad administrative access limited to people responsible for that work, following the FTC's access-control advice.

Use individual user accounts to control access to information. The FTC recommends considering separate accounts rather than giving everyone unrestricted access to stored personal data.

---

## Protect paper and shared files

Use the FTC's information-security guidance to review what you collect and who can access it. Limit access to the information people need for their responsibilities. Store sensitive paper records and removable media in a locked room or cabinet, and control access to the keys.

For team documents, check ownership as well as sharing. Google distinguishes shared drives, whose files belong to the organization, from an individual's My Drive. Files in a shared drive remain when a member leaves and an administrator deletes that person's account.

Check the sharing settings before putting sensitive documents into a team drive. Google notes that shared-drive members generally see the same content, with limited-access folders available to restrict access. Choose the applicable permissions rather than assuming every office helper should see every file.

---

## Check the setup with your team

Use this final checklist to revisit the services and controls you selected:

- [ ] Confirm mailbox pickup arrangements and current application information.
- [ ] Review the workstation with OSHA's evaluation checklist.
- [ ] Test the phone number's routing and voicemail.
- [ ] Explain the phone provider's emergency-calling limitations.
- [ ] Assign administrative roles according to responsibilities.
- [ ] Check shared-file ownership, permissions and sensitive-paper storage.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Whatever you do, do your work heartily, as for the Lord rather than for men,"* — Colossians 3:23 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Set up your church’s mailing address, home workstation, phone service and shared office tools, with checks for access and sensitive information.
articles.title: Setting Up the Church Office

articles.content:
Use your church calendar to publish events, and use registration tools to collect sign-ups. Keep the handoff to children's check-in visible when you compare software. A form submission and a recorded arrival are different steps in the documented tools below.

Start with the features you can demonstrate. This guide uses Google Calendar, Planning Center, and Breeze documentation as examples, without ranking them or recommending a vendor.

---

## Separate public events from private records

Google Calendar can share a public calendar through a link, and people can subscribe to it. Google warns that a calendar displayed on a searchable website can appear in search results. Treat public event information as public wherever you display it.

Keep children's registration responses out of public calendar descriptions. Use a separate, restricted place for family records, applying the FTC's advice to limit personal information access to people who need it for their work.

<Callout type="warning">
A shareable calendar link is not a private registration system. Review the public calendar and the family records separately, using the visibility and access controls each tool actually provides.
</Callout>

---

## Decide who can edit and publish

In Google Calendar, viewing event details, changing events, and managing sharing are different permissions. Choose the access that matches each person's responsibilities. For work or school calendars, the administrator controls whether sharing is available.

If your church uses an approval process, ask the provider to demonstrate it. Planning Center Calendar offers event-level approvals. Pending events under that setting stay off Church Center, shared calendar feeds, and kiosks until approved.

Check each publication destination. Planning Center documents separate controls for Church Center visibility and calendar feeds. An event unpublished in Church Center can still appear in an iCal feed. Use that distinction as a question when evaluating another platform, rather than assuming its controls work the same way.

---

## Compare the jobs you need done

Use this worksheet for a demonstration with your Technology Leader and Children's Ministry Leader. The examples identify documented capabilities, not promises that every product includes them.

| Job | What to ask the provider to show |
|---|---|
| Public calendar | How guests see events and how editors control sharing |
| Sign-up | How a form response reaches the family or attendee record |
| Arrival | How the team records a child as checked in |
| Pickup | How workers use parent labels and record checkout |

Google Calendar documents calendar sharing. Breeze documents forms that link responses to profiles, plus check-in and checkout settings. Planning Center documents event sign-ups and Check-Ins as connected products. Ask to see your intended combination working together.

---

## Trace registration through arrival and pickup

In Breeze, an event can limit its check-in list to respondents to selected forms. Its settings also offer a parent copy of a child's name tag and a checkout record. Being on the eligible list is distinct from recording check-in.

Planning Center supports sign-ups through Registrations and arrival through Check-Ins stations. Its Church Center app can generate a pre-check QR code. With Allow Complete Check-In turned off, the person must scan that code at a station to complete check-in.

<Callout type="tip">
Ask the provider to demonstrate the exact arrival setting you intend to use. Planning Center also offers a complete-check-in option without scanning when labels are removed. Do not assume that every app confirmation means someone has arrived at your station.
</Callout>

---

## Understand the federal privacy distinction

COPPA addresses covered operators of child-directed websites or online services for children under 13, and other operators with actual knowledge that they collect personal information online from children under 13.

The FTC says nonprofits generally are not subject to COPPA, while encouraging them to provide its protections to children. It also distinguishes information collected online from children from information adults provide about children.

Consider addressing your registration form to a parent or guardian. Have counsel and your provider review who actually supplies information and how the tool collects it, rather than treating the form's label as the whole review.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance and vendor features checked October 16, 2026. Confirm current COPPA guidance with the FTC and counsel, and current settings with your provider before launch. The nonprofit and adult-submission distinctions do not establish that every privacy obligation has been resolved.
</Callout>

---

## Collect less and restrict access

Use the FTC's business security guidance as a practical starting point for your church. It recommends collecting only necessary personal information and limiting access according to the work people do.

Review each proposed registration field with the Children's Ministry Leader. Ask what job it supports before adding it. A provider's ability to collect a field is not a reason to collect it.

Check the station screen as well as staff accounts. Breeze distinguishes a staff-facing list from its public kiosk mode, which it recommends when people should not see names outside their family. Ask your provider to demonstrate what a family can see at the station you plan to use.

---

## Rehearse with fictitious information

The FTC recommends fictitious information for training or development when real personal information is unnecessary. Use a test family to walk through the documented controls with your team.

- [ ] Open the public event and inspect its visibility.
- [ ] Submit a test registration and find the resulting profile or eligible attendee.
- [ ] Complete the configured arrival step and print the intended labels.
- [ ] Check the parent-label matching process and checkout record.
- [ ] Review what the public station displays about other families.

Compare the result with the provider's documentation. Bring questions about children's pickup procedures to the Children's Ministry Leader rather than trying to settle them through software settings alone.

---

## Plan access changes and retention

The FTC recommends procedures to remove access when workers leave or change responsibilities. Apply that advice when a staff member or volunteer hands off calendar or registration duties.

Write down what information you retain, why, how you secure it, and how you dispose of it. Check legal retention needs before choosing deletion rules. The FTC's records guidance ties retention to business or legal needs, rather than a universal period for every record.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Compare calendar sharing and children's pre-registration tools, check privacy boundaries, and rehearse the handoff to arrival and pickup.
articles.title: Church Calendar and Kids' Pre-Registration Tools

articles.content:
Your church's books need to show what came in, what went out, and where each transaction belongs. A bookkeeper records and checks that work; accounting software holds the records and produces reports.

Choose them together under your Financial Leader's oversight. Start with the church's financial policies, then ask candidates to show how they would record transactions, explain differences, and prepare reports for the people authorized to see them.

---

## Start with the federal recordkeeping rule

The IRS requires tax-exempt organizations, including churches, to maintain accounting books and other records supporting their exemption and any required federal returns. Records of activities, income, and expenses are still necessary when no return is filed.

The IRS does not prescribe a specific recordkeeping format. Its examples include ledgers, receipts and disbursements journals, payroll and banking records, and invoices. Choose a system that can keep those records available for examination rather than assuming a product's church label establishes compliance.

---

## Define the work before seeking help

Write down which tasks you want the bookkeeper to perform. The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes transaction entry, account coding, accuracy checks, reconciliation, and financial reporting as typical bookkeeping work. Payroll may be an additional responsibility; ask whether it is included.

Use the church's existing separation of duties when assigning that work. Keep responsibility for counting, recording, disbursing, and approving in the roles established by your financial policies. The Financial Leader oversees accounting under the elders' direction.

If you outsource payroll, retain church oversight of tax deposits. The IRS says the employer remains responsible for federal tax liabilities when a payroll service fails to pay them. Ask how your church will verify deposits independently.

---

## Ask candidates to show their work

Use the duties you listed as interview prompts. Ask a candidate to explain how they assign a receipt or bill to an account, check the entry, and investigate a difference between records. Ask them to walk you through a financial report they would prepare for your Financial Leader.

Look for evidence of computer and bookkeeping-software skills, attention to detail, and integrity, including keeping financial records confidential. BLS lists these among the important qualities for bookkeepers. Ask how the candidate would protect individual giving records while making authorized financial reporting available.

For church-specific work, ask about experience with your fund structure and any payroll responsibilities you propose to assign. Keep clergy payroll questions with the separately reviewed payroll process.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"In this case, moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful."* — 1 Corinthians 4:2 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Compare fund tracking and reports

Bring your approved fund list and budget to a demonstration. Your designated-giving policy calls for separate tracking of each fund's income, expenses, and balance. Ask to see those results in the proposed system.

| Ask to see | What to examine |
|---|---|
| Fund activity | Beginning balance, income, expenses, transfers, and ending balance |
| Budget comparison | Actual results beside the budget for the same period |
| Leadership reports | Financial information without individual donor details |
| Downloaded reports | Files your authorized reviewer can open and read |

Ask the demonstrator to explain any difference between funds and project tags or categories. In the documentation reviewed for this guide, tags track income and expenses but do not appear on the balance sheet like funds. Check the proposed product's behavior directly.

---

## Check access against church policy

Have the Financial Leader review permissions before inviting users. Follow the existing accountability policy, including its limits on the Senior Pastor's financial access and its confidentiality rules for individual giving.

Ask the vendor to demonstrate the roles available in the exact subscription under consideration. Check who can enter accounting records, approve bills, read reports, and manage users. Test the proposed reviewer's access rather than giving everyone administrator permissions.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not replace the church's payment approvals with permission to use accounting software. Follow the existing disbursement policy when deciding who initiates and who approves a payment.
</Callout>

For a product with electronic bill approval, ask to see the approval status and the steps between receiving a bill and paying it.

---

## Try a sample workflow

Use this exercise to evaluate the candidate and software together:

- [ ] Enter a sample gift into an approved fund and locate its accounting entry.
- [ ] Enter a sample bill against the appropriate expense account and fund.
- [ ] Show how the bill follows your church's approval process.
- [ ] Import a sample bank transaction and check the target register and coding.
- [ ] Compare the deposit with the giving record and investigate any difference.
- [ ] Produce the fund and budget reports your reviewer needs.
- [ ] Export a report and open the downloaded file.

Ask what happens when your bank does not support a direct connection or older transactions are needed. The bank-integration documentation reviewed here offers file import as an alternative in those cases; confirm the options for your own bank and proposed software.

<Callout type="tip">
Ask the candidate to explain an unexplained difference rather than simply changing an entry to make totals match. Checking accuracy and reporting differences are part of the bookkeeping work described by BLS.
</Callout>

---

## Compare the complete scope and cost

Ask for a proposal matching the tasks and features you demonstrated. Identify what the bookkeeper will handle and which work remains with the church or another provider.

Check the subscription's included users, permission controls, budgeting, and bill-approval options. Product documentation may place these in different plans or add-ons. Ask separately about setup work, including the chart of accounts, funds, starting balances, and training.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance and product documentation checked October 16, 2026. Confirm current recordkeeping guidance with the IRS. Confirm features, subscription terms, and any additional charges with each vendor before purchasing.
</Callout>

---

## Plan the handoff

Document the bookkeeping procedures so another authorized person can follow them. Include the records used, account and fund assignments, review steps, and reports to prepare. Keep supporting records with the accounting work.

Before a bookkeeper leaves, have the Financial Leader check the records and unresolved differences with them. Confirm that the church's authorized people can retrieve reports and manage account access. Ask the vendor to show how to disable or remove a departing user's access.

Keep a church-controlled copy of exported reports and the underlying supporting records. The IRS's recordkeeping obligation remains with the organization, and a report download alone does not replace its receipts, invoices, banking records, or other necessary documentation.
articles.excerpt: Choose bookkeeping help and accounting software by checking responsibilities, fund reports, access, costs, and a sample workflow.
articles.title: Choosing a Bookkeeper and Accounting Software

articles.content:
Your church's federal income-tax exemption does not make a minister's pay tax-free. A minister can be an employee for income-tax purposes while paying self-employment tax on ministerial earnings.

Use this reference to separate the church's tax questions from your own before reviewing compensation and reimbursements with a CPA familiar with clergy tax rules. It summarizes U.S. federal rules; it does not resolve individual tax situations.

---

## Start with the church's exemption

A church that meets section 501(c)(3) requirements is automatically exempt from federal income tax and does not have to apply for IRS recognition. The exemption depends on meeting those requirements, whether or not the church obtains a determination letter.

The church must be organized and operated exclusively for qualifying exempt purposes. It cannot distribute net earnings for private benefit or intervene in political campaigns. No substantial part of its activity may be attempting to influence legislation. Its purposes and activities also cannot be illegal or violate fundamental public policy.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance checked October 15, 2026. This reference uses IRS Publication 1828, revised August 2015, and Publication 517 for 2025 returns. Confirm current forms, thresholds, payment dates and any later changes with the IRS before acting.
</Callout>

---

## Know which filings can still apply

Churches are generally not required to file Form 990, Form 990-EZ or Form 990-N. That exception does not eliminate employment-tax obligations or a return for unrelated business income.

Unrelated business income generally comes from a trade or business that is regularly carried on and is not substantially related to the church's exempt purpose. Using the money for ministry does not, by itself, make the activity related. Exceptions exist, including certain activities where substantially all the work is performed by volunteers, so review the activity before deciding its tax treatment.

A church with $1,000 or more in gross income from an unrelated trade or business during a taxable year must file Form 990-T. The filing test uses gross income, not the activity's profit.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Render to all what is due them: tax to whom tax is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor."* — Romans 13:7 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Distinguish employment from ministerial tax treatment

The IRS clergy rules refer to duly ordained, commissioned or licensed ministers and services performed in the exercise of ministry. Review those qualifications and the work being paid for before applying ministerial treatment.

If a congregation employs you and pays you a salary, you are generally an employee with wages for income-tax purposes. The church reports an employee minister's compensation on Form W-2. Self-employment tax treatment does not, by itself, make you an independent contractor.

Ministerial earnings are generally subject to Social Security and Medicare under the Self-Employment Contributions Act, or SECA, rather than payroll FICA. An applicable IRS-approved exemption can change that treatment. Do not assume the church's income-tax exemption is a personal exemption from SECA.

---

## Designate a housing allowance before payment

If your compensation includes a qualifying housing allowance, the employing church must officially designate a definite amount before paying it. It cannot determine the amount afterward. If no amount has been officially designated, the full salary is included in income.

An employment contract, church minutes, a budget or another official action taken before payment may show the designation. If a local congregation employs and pays you, that congregation must designate the allowance; a national church agency's resolution does not substitute for its action.

---

## Apply the housing exclusion limits

For a minister who owns a home, the income-tax exclusion is limited to the smallest of the following amounts:

- The amount actually used to provide a home.
- The amount officially designated as a housing allowance.
- The home's fair rental value, including furnishings and utilities.

The allowance must also stay within reasonable pay for your services. If the church provides a parsonage as part of your pay, you can exclude its fair rental value, including utilities, from income tax, up to reasonable pay for your services. Include any excess rental allowance in gross income.

<Callout type="warning">
The housing exclusion is for income tax. For a minister in active ministry subject to SECA, the housing allowance or parsonage value is included when figuring net earnings from self-employment. An official designation alone does not make the payment free of all federal taxes.
</Callout>

---

## Plan how personal taxes will be paid

A duly ordained, commissioned or licensed minister's salary for ministerial services is not subject to mandatory federal income-tax withholding. A minister who is a common-law employee can agree with the church to voluntary withholding to cover income tax and self-employment tax.

Without withholding, or with too little withheld, estimated tax payments may be needed. Review the payment arrangement with your CPA instead of treating the absence of mandatory withholding as an absence of tax.

---

## Keep reimbursements separate from compensation

An accountable reimbursement plan must have a business connection, require adequate expense accounting, and require the employee to return excess reimbursements. Both the accounting and the return of excess amounts must happen within a reasonable period.

Provide enough detail to identify the business nature of each expense and substantiate it. Broad labels such as "miscellaneous business expenses" are not sufficient. Qualifying accountable-plan reimbursements are excluded from income and are not reported on Form W-2.

Payments under a nonaccountable plan are included with wages or other compensation on Form W-2. For employee ministers, that reporting does not itself create mandatory federal income-tax withholding or FICA on ministerial compensation.

---

## Prepare for your tax review

Use these questions to review the records behind the tax treatment:

- [ ] Has the church reviewed which employment and unrelated-business returns apply?
- [ ] Does the minister's employment reporting agree with the work arrangement?
- [ ] Was the definite housing allowance officially designated before payment?
- [ ] Do actual housing costs and fair rental value support the exclusion?
- [ ] Is voluntary withholding or an estimated-payment plan in place where needed?
- [ ] Do reimbursements meet the accountable-plan requirements?

<Callout type="tip">
Have a CPA familiar with Publication 517 review the minister's tax treatment, housing allowance and reimbursements before you rely on them. Publication 517 reminds you that you remain responsible for the accuracy of every item reported on your return, even when a paid preparer signs it.
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Understand church income-tax exemption, ministerial SECA, housing allowance limits, withholding and expense reimbursements under U.S. federal rules.
articles.title: Church and Clergy Tax Basics

articles.content:
Your church's federal income-tax exemption does not settle its state sales-tax or property-tax treatment. Before claiming relief on a purchase or a worship space, check the rules for that tax with the agency that administers it.

Use this guide to prepare those questions and the supporting paperwork. The state examples illustrate differences, rather than provide rules you can carry into another state.

---

## Start with the federal distinction

A church that meets section 501(c)(3) requirements is automatically exempt from federal income tax without applying for IRS recognition. That federal rule concerns income tax. Check state purchase exemptions and property exemptions separately.

| Question | Where to begin |
|---|---|
| Does the church qualify for federal income-tax exemption? | IRS church guidance and section 501(c)(3) requirements. |
| Can the church buy an item without sales or use tax? | Your state's tax agency and its rules for the transaction. |
| Does a particular property qualify for exemption? | The office administering property exemptions where the property is located. |

<Callout type="important">
Tax guidance checked October 16, 2026. Before relying on an exemption, confirm current eligibility, application forms, filing dates and continuing requirements with your state tax agency and the local property-tax office. The examples below name the Texas Comptroller, California Department of Tax and Fee Administration, and California State Board of Equalization.
</Callout>

---

## Find the right offices

The Federation of Tax Administrators maintains a directory called "Tax Agencies" that takes you to state tax-agency websites. The IRS also has a "State Links" directory with information for tax-exempt organizations.

Use your state's agency site to find its religious-organization guidance. For property, check who receives the claim. In California, county assessors administer the Church and Religious Exemptions. The California Department of Tax and Fee Administration handles sales and use tax questions.

Prepare separate questions about purchase eligibility, supplier documentation, property eligibility and filing requirements. Use the relevant agency's instructions to answer each question rather than treating "tax-exempt" as a complete answer.

---

## Check whether purchases qualify

Texas offers an application route for qualifying nonprofit religious organizations. Its religious category requires an established group regularly meeting at a designated location for worship. Federal exemption is not required for that category, but the group must apply for the state exemption.

California has no comparable broad sales-and-use-tax exemption for nonprofit and religious organizations. Specific exemptions and exclusions exist, so check the actual transaction before claiming relief.

Ask your own agency whether your church and proposed purchase qualify. If the agency offers a religious category, read its definition before choosing it. A religious purpose alone does not establish eligibility under every category, as the Texas guidance explains.

---

## Gather the application evidence

Use the application for the exemption category you are claiming. For example, Texas Form AP-209 is its application for religious organizations.

The form's independent-church option requests a statement of faith, the regular order of worship, evidence that services are open to the public and how they are advertised, and a description of the worship facility. Its affiliated-church option instead asks for evidence of the qualifying parent relationship.

Treat those as examples of activity evidence, not a nationwide document checklist. Read the instructions that apply to your church's structure and affiliation. Supply the supporting information the application requests.

<Callout type="tip">
Build your application file from the agency's own checklist. Texas AP-209 warns that applications received without supporting documentation will be returned. Check the attachments before sending yours.
</Callout>

---

## Use an approved exemption correctly

Approval and purchase documentation are separate steps. In Texas, an approved organization documents a qualifying purchase by giving the seller a completed exemption certificate. The exemption-certification side of Form 01-339 is distinct from its resale-certificate side.

Texas requires exempt purchases to relate to the organization's exempt purpose. Personal purchases by employees or volunteers do not qualify, even when the organization reimburses them. Check the purpose of the purchase before using church exemption paperwork.

<Callout type="warning">
A purchase exemption does not settle tax on items your church sells. The Texas Comptroller says exempt organizations must collect tax on most sales of taxable items. Check the sales rules before a fundraiser or merchandise sale.
</Callout>

---

## Check the property's ownership and use

Ask the property-tax office which exemption fits the property and its actual use. Describe who owns or leases it and what happens there.

California's Church Exemption can apply to property owned, leased or rented by a religious organization and used exclusively for religious worship services. Its separate Religious Exemption concerns property owned by a religious organization and used exclusively for religious purposes. Use the correct category rather than assuming the names are interchangeable.

If you rent, ask about the lease as well as the claim. California's Church Exemption guidance says a qualifying reduction on leased property must benefit the church. Ask the assessor how the ownership and use of your proposed space affect eligibility.

---

## Confirm filing dates and continuing eligibility

Ask the administering office for the initial filing date and any later claim or eligibility-confirmation requirements. Check the specific exemption you receive.

In California, the Church Exemption requires an annual claim. The Religious Exemption has a one-time claim, but claimants receive an annual form to confirm continued eligibility. A one-time application does not mean you can ignore that later form.

California's Religious Exemption remains effective until terminated or the property is no longer eligible. Check with the assessor when ownership or activities change rather than relying only on the original approval.

---

## Keep the evidence with your records

IRS church guidance calls for records that support exemption and document receipts and expenses. Keep the evidence behind your claim and the transactions recorded in your books.

Use this filing checklist as an organizing suggestion:

- [ ] Keep the submitted application and its supporting documents together.
- [ ] Add the agency's decision and the instructions for using it.
- [ ] File purchase invoices and receipts with the relevant accounting records.
- [ ] Keep property records with the evidence of qualifying ownership and use.
- [ ] Add later claims and eligibility confirmations to the same file.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s."* — Mark 12:17 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Distinguish federal income-tax exemption from state purchase and property exemptions, then check eligibility, paperwork and continuing requirements with the right agency.
articles.title: State Sales and Property Tax Exemptions

articles.content:
A gift registry gives supporters a way to buy the equipment your church has selected. A nonprofit Giving List can bring items from different stores together behind a shared link.

Start with your equipment plan and keep a separate record of gifts actually received. The registry helps donors shop; your church still needs to acknowledge donated property accurately.

---

## Start with approved needs

Use your existing equipment plan to decide what belongs on the list. Distinguish essentials from optional additions, and keep purchases aligned with the approved budget. Work through equipment choices before inviting donors to shop.

The portable-equipment guide covers venue needs, team capabilities, storage and purchasing priorities. Carry those decisions into the registry.

<Callout type="tip">
Put an approved item on the list only after you can identify the product and quantity you want. Use item notes to explain details that a donor might otherwise have to guess.
</Callout>

---

## Choose and name your list

MyRegistry offers an organization/nonprofit Giving List and supports adding items from different retailers. It is the worked example in this guide. If you choose another provider, check its own instructions for the same steps.

Create the list using your organization's name. MyRegistry also allows a chapter name, which may help distinguish your plant from another part of a sending church or network. Customize the list with your church's logo and a welcome message explaining the equipment request.

<Callout type="important">
Provider features and IRS guidance were checked October 16, 2026. Before sharing your list, confirm current nonprofit account options, privacy settings and purchase tracking with MyRegistry. Check the current acknowledgment rules in IRS Publication 1771 before issuing receipts.
</Callout>

---

## Make each item specific

With MyRegistry's browser button, you can add an item while viewing its retailer page. Review the title, image, price and quantity in the add-item panel. Add instructions in the item's note field.

Use these fields to make your request clear:

- Confirm that the product matches the item in your equipment plan.
- Set the requested quantity to match your current need.
- Put details such as the selected size or version in the item note.
- Group related needs into categories so donors can browse.
- Favorite the items you most want donors to see as priorities.

MyRegistry supports categories and favorites. Give those tools a purpose, such as grouping storage items together or highlighting an essential item. Keep the details in the item note consistent with the retailer listing.

---

## Check delivery and address visibility

For MyRegistry purchases, donors enter the recipient's address at the retailer's checkout. The shipping information on the list helps them find that address. Check it before you distribute the link.

MyRegistry's privacy statement says your address is visible to people with access to your gift list. It also lets you password-protect the list and make the address private. With a private address, a donor enters a delivery address or requests yours by email. Decide which delivery address your church is comfortable sharing before you send the link.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not assume the registry completes shipping details for the donor. Ask donors to check the recipient and delivery address at the retailer's checkout.
</Callout>

---

## Share the list with instructions

MyRegistry lets nonprofits share their Giving List by email, on a website and through social media. It also offers a website embed. Choose the sharing method that fits how you already communicate with supporters.

Use the welcome message to explain the request, then give donors the list link. Include instructions about the delivery address and marking purchases. For example, ask them to check the item details, use the listed recipient address and confirm the gift's purchase status.

Keep this message about the requested items. Use the church's donor-receipt process to answer acknowledgment questions.

---

## Track purchases and arrivals

A purchase marking and a delivered gift are different events. MyRegistry lets you mark a gift manually when a donor forgets, and restore an item that was marked purchased. Check with the donor before changing a disputed entry.

Use the Thank You Note Tracker to help identify gifts and prepare thanks. Match that information with what your church receives before acknowledging the property. If a gift has not arrived, contact the retailer with the donor's purchase details; MyRegistry stores purchase information under the gift's details.

The retailer handles returns and exchanges. Keep those questions with the store that sold the item, and update the registry when an item needs to become available again.

---

## Acknowledge equipment as property

Under the U.S. federal rule in Publication 1771, a donor needs a contemporaneous written acknowledgment to claim a deduction for a single noncash contribution valued at $250 or more. Additional substantiation requirements may apply.

Use the receiving church's name, describe the donated item and record its receipt date. Describe property without assigning its tax value. If the church provided no goods or services in return, say so; if it provided a benefit, follow the applicable wording in the donor-receipts guide.

The donor handles the valuation used on their return. Keep an equipment gift separate from monetary gift totals, consistent with the published donor-receipts guide. Use the church's acknowledgment process even when the registry has already helped you send a thank-you.

---

## Review before sending the link

- [ ] Match listed items to the approved equipment plan.
- [ ] Check product details, quantities and notes.
- [ ] Organize the list and identify priority items.
- [ ] Review the recipient address and its visibility to donors.
- [ ] Explain how donors should mark a purchase.
- [ ] Plan to compare purchase records with actual arrivals.
- [ ] Use the church's property-gift acknowledgment process.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"In this case, moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful."* — 1 Corinthians 4:2 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Build an equipment gift list, guide donors through purchases and delivery, and acknowledge donated items accurately.
articles.title: Using a Gift Registry for Equipment

articles.content:
Search engine optimization, often called SEO, helps search engines understand your website and helps people decide whether to visit it. For your church's site, begin with clear information a guest can use.

Search Console can show how your site appears in Google Search. Website analytics can help you understand activity after someone arrives. Use these reports to ask specific questions about the site.

---

## Choose the question before the tool

Start with the question you need to answer. Google's tools serve different purposes.

| Your question | Where to start |
|---|---|
| Can Google find an important page? | Search Console's URL Inspection tool |
| Which searches bring people to the site? | Search Console's Performance report |
| Where does website traffic come from? | Google Analytics' Traffic acquisition report |
| Is a website action being recorded? | Analytics' Realtime report or DebugView |

Search Console is free. You do not have to register for it to appear in Google Search, and registration does not buy a better position.

<Callout type="important">
Google documentation checked October 16, 2026. Before setup, confirm current instructions and policies with Google Search Central, Search Console Help, and Google Analytics Help. Report names and available settings can change.
</Callout>

---

## Connect Search Console to your site

Open Search Console and check whether an existing owner can grant you access. Otherwise, add a website property and complete ownership verification.

Choose the property type that fits the access you have:

- A Domain property covers its subdomains and protocols. For an ordinary independently hosted domain, verification uses a DNS record.
- A URL-prefix property covers addresses beginning with the exact prefix you enter, including the protocol. Google offers several verification methods for this type.

For example, `https://www.example.org/` does not include `https://example.org/`. Ask the person managing your domain or website to help with verification if needed. Check the selected property before interpreting an empty report.

---

## Check whether important pages are indexed

Indexing means Google has processed a page and added it to its index, making it eligible to appear in results. Use URL Inspection to check your home page and other important public pages individually.

If a page is missing, read the reported reason with your website provider. Some pages legitimately remain unindexed, including duplicates. Avoid treating every unindexed address as an error.

You can consider submitting a sitemap, a file listing the pages you want search engines to know about. Google can discover pages without one, and your website platform may already provide it. Ask your provider before creating a second process.

<Callout type="tip">
Being indexed makes a page eligible for search results. It does not guarantee that your page will appear for a particular search or hold a fixed ranking.
</Callout>

---

## Make each page clear and useful

Write for the person trying to understand your church. Use ordinary language, readable paragraphs, and headings that describe the content. Keep information current and connect relevant pages with descriptive links.

Give each page a distinct, concise title that matches its contents. As an example, a visit page could use "Plan a visit | Grace Church" instead of repeating "Home" across the site. Use your real church name in the example's place.

Write a page-specific meta description, the summary field your website editor may provide. Google often creates its search description from the page itself and may use your meta description when it fits better. The wording you enter is a suggestion, rather than a promise about the result shown.

Avoid repeating city names or church-related phrases merely to fill the page. Google's guidance rejects keyword stuffing and does not prescribe a magic word count for ranking.

---

## Add Analytics if you need website activity reports

Google Analytics 4, commonly called GA4, measures website and app activity using events. If you choose it, follow Google's setup guide with your website provider.

- [ ] Create or select the Analytics account and property.
- [ ] Check the reporting time zone.
- [ ] Add a Web data stream for the church website.
- [ ] Review the enhanced measurement options and the events you intend to collect.
- [ ] Follow your platform's supported Google tag installation instructions.

Some website builders provide a field for the Google tag ID. Others need a different installation method. Ask your provider which route your site uses.

Check the installation using Realtime. If data is missing, confirm the account, property, tag ID, and page installation before drawing conclusions about traffic. Google warns that installing both the direct Google tag and Tag Manager implementations can overcount activity.

---

## Read the labels before comparing numbers

In Search Console, impressions count appearances in search results; clicks count clicks to your site from those results. Click-through rate divides clicks by impressions. Use the Queries and Pages views to see what the totals describe, and record the date range when comparing reports.

In Analytics, Traffic acquisition reports where new and returning users' sessions come from. Its channel groups include Organic Search, Direct, and Email. If that report is missing from your navigation, an Editor or Administrator can add it back.

A session is a period of interaction with your site. A person can start multiple sessions, and Analytics estimates session counts. Keep the label "sessions" when sharing that number.

An event records an interaction or occurrence, such as loading a page or clicking a link. You can mark an important measured action as a key event. Confirm the event and its parameters in Realtime or DebugView before relying on it.

---

## Keep personal information out of measurement

Google prohibits sending information it can recognize as personally identifiable, including email addresses and personal mobile numbers, to Analytics. Its basic page tag collects page addresses and titles, so check those as well as form fields and event settings.

Ask your provider to inspect URL parameters, search terms, and custom event data for personal information.

Google requires disclosure of Analytics use and how it collects and processes data. Review the site's privacy notice against the actual setup before enabling it. Review account data-sharing choices, too.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not send names, email addresses, or personal form responses as Analytics event details. Check the data being sent, rather than assuming a generic event name makes its contents safe.
</Callout>

---

## Review the site without watching it all day

Google suggests checking Search Console around monthly or after site content changes. It also sends email alerts when it finds new issues.

Use this checklist for a focused review:

- [ ] Check for reported search problems affecting important public pages.
- [ ] Review search queries and pages over the selected period.
- [ ] Recheck titles and descriptions when page content changes.
- [ ] If Analytics is installed, check traffic sources and verify the actions you measure.
- [ ] Review what information the measurement tools receive.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"He who responds with a word before he hears, It is folly and shame to him."* — Proverbs 18:13 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Use Search Console and optional website analytics to check search visibility, understand traffic, and protect visitors' information.
articles.title: Website Analytics and Search Basics

articles.content:
Your venue comparison identifies a promising place to meet. Before you commit, check the written terms for the rooms, activities and hours your church needs. Keep unresolved permissions separate from the venue's score.

Use this checklist with the proposed agreement, current fee schedule and insurance instructions in front of you. Bring unclear terms to a local attorney and insurance questions to your agent.

---

## Start with access and legal scope

Under the federal Americans with Disabilities Act, religious entities are exempt from Title III. Public entities are subject to Title II. The Department of Justice describes these as different obligations, so ask an attorney which rules apply to the parties and activities in your arrangement.

Review practical access alongside that legal discussion. Washington's Education Ombuds checklist asks about parking, entrances, routes to meeting rooms, restrooms and emergency exits. Use those questions to check the specific areas offered to you.

<Callout type="warning">
This is general guidance, not legal advice. The district agreements below are local examples. Ask a local attorney to review your proposed agreement before signing.
</Callout>

---

## Name the use, rooms and hours

Ask the venue to identify your permitted activities and each room included. Describe worship and children's activities rather than leaving the use unclear. Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia uses an agreement specifically for religious and cultural programs. Its sample excludes storage, so ask about equipment storage separately.

Check access before and after the gathering. Fairfax's auditorium guidelines include setup and breakdown in requested time, tie fees to total time in the building, and require separate requests for dressing rooms.

- [ ] Which rooms are included, and which need separate approval?
- [ ] Do the requested hours include setup, sound checks and teardown?
- [ ] Are additional rehearsal dates included?
- [ ] What equipment must you request separately?

---

## Price the whole reservation

Use the owner's current quote to fill in the cost questions below. Clover Park School District in Washington separates space rental from special equipment and lighting. Its guidance also describes staffing charges, possible security and possible cleaning or damage deposits.

| Cost item | What to confirm |
|---|---|
| Space | Rooms and hours the quote covers |
| Staff | Required employees and billable time |
| Gear | Included items and extra charges |
| Deposits | Refundable amounts and conditions |
| Payment | Due date and what confirms the booking |

Clover Park describes its booking fee as nonrefundable and says the booking is not confirmed until payment of that fee. Ask your venue how its own process works. Keep the booking payment separate from questions about cleaning and damage deposits.

<Callout type="important">
Examples were checked October 15, 2026. Confirm current terms, fees, deadlines and insurance requirements with Fairfax County Public Schools, Frederick County Public Schools or Clover Park School District before relying on their examples. Confirm current federal accessibility guidance with the Department of Justice and Texas insurance guidance with the Texas Department of Insurance where relevant.
</Callout>

---

## Check insurance against the policy

Give your agent the venue's written insurance instructions. Clover Park asks for a certificate showing the district as both certificate holder and additional insured. Ask what your own venue requires and which policy documents support that status.

The Texas Department of Insurance explains that certificate wording cannot expand policy coverage. Its guidance also says a certificate's cancellation-notice provision cannot go beyond the policy's requirements. These are Texas examples of why the underlying documents matter.

<Callout type="tip">
Ask your agent to show the policy or endorsement supporting an additional-insured request. Texas insurance guidance permits requesting policy copies. Keep the coverage question separate from what appears in the certificate-holder box.
</Callout>

---

## Read what the signature commits you to

Look for personal payment obligations as well as obligations of the church. Fairfax's religious and cultural sample makes the signer financially liable if the organization does not pay in full. Ask your attorney what the signature would mean under your agreement.

Read indemnity and hold-harmless language with the attorney, too. Fairfax's sample places liabilities arising from the organization's use on the organization and includes attorneys' fees. Ask which losses you would accept and which your insurer would cover.

Do not treat a certificate of insurance as an answer to every contractual promise. Compare the agreement with the actual policy documents.

---

## Check cancellation in both directions

Ask what happens when you cancel, when the owner needs the space, and when weather closes the building. Fairfax's sample allows relocation or cancellation because of school activities and programs.

Frederick County Public Schools in Maryland says event cancellations and modifications must be made by email to its coordinator and school site administrators at least 10 calendar days before the event. It says full facility fees and/or custodian fees apply when cancellation or modification occurs less than 10 calendar days before the event.

Use that as a local example of a deadline to record accurately. Ask your venue about the notice method, recipients, charges and any refund terms. Distinguish cancellation of one gathering from ending the whole agreement.

---

## Check the end date and renewal

Read the start and end provisions before planning beyond the term. New York City's commercial-leasing guide recommends negotiating a renewal option and addressing how renewal rent will be determined. Use that as a discussion prompt for your arrangement, without assuming a recurring school permit works like a commercial lease.

Ask whether continued use needs a new application, written renewal or another approval. If there is a renewal option, ask how to exercise it and how the next price is set. Keep the owner's answer with the proposed terms.

---

## Review the final packet

Return to unresolved permissions and costs from your venue comparison. Consider an attorney's review of unclear lease terms, as the Small Business Administration suggests.

- [ ] Match the rooms, activities and access hours to your request.
- [ ] Match the quote to the staff and equipment you need.
- [ ] Review liability wording and insurance documents with the appropriate professionals.
- [ ] Record cancellation and renewal instructions before committing.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Without consultation, plans are frustrated, But with many counselors they succeed."* — Proverbs 15:22 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Questions to review with a venue, attorney and insurance agent before committing to a facility rental agreement.
articles.title: Facility Rental Agreements: Terms to Check

Your church's employee records include identity information, wage records and tax forms. Federal agencies give these records different retention rules, so the date someone leaves does not start the same clock for every document.

Use this reference to distinguish the forms you retain, the records behind payroll and the files that need restricted access. Apply each federal rule only where it covers your church and the employee's work.

---

## Check which rules apply

The Department of Labor distinguishes FLSA enterprise coverage from individual employee coverage. A nonprofit's charitable or religious activities do not themselves establish enterprise coverage, but an employee may still have individual coverage through interstate work. Check coverage before applying the wage-record rules below.

EEOC coverage also varies by the law and type of employer. Its retention rules apply to covered employers. Use the applicable agency's coverage guidance rather than assuming every federal employment rule has the same reach.

<Callout type="important">
Federal guidance checked October 16, 2026. Confirm current forms and retention instructions with USCIS, the Department of Labor, the IRS and the EEOC before using this reference to dispose of records. The periods below address different record categories and do not replace one another.
</Callout>

---

## Keep the hiring forms

Form I-9 documents verification of a new employee's identity and authorization to work in the United States. The employee completes and signs Section 1 no later than the first day of employment. Complete Section 2 within three business days after that first day. If employment will last less than three business days, complete Section 2 no later than the first day.

Make the I-9 instructions and Lists of Acceptable Documents available to the employee. Let the employee choose acceptable documentation. Retain the completed form rather than mailing it to USCIS or ICE.

Ask each new employee for a signed Form W-4 when work starts, and make it effective with the first wage payment. Keep withholding certificates among the employment-tax records. Use the related payroll article for the separate review of clergy tax treatment.

---

## Calculate the I-9 retention date

USCIS requires you to keep the completed I-9 and its attachments throughout employment. Once employment ends, retain them until the later of these dates:

- Three years after the first day of employment.
- One year from the date employment ends.

Compare both dates before deciding that the retention period has ended. Do not discard a current employee's form merely because three years have passed since hiring.

Retain supplement pages containing entered information and any photocopies you made of the employee's documentation. You do not have to retain the pages that contain the instructions or the Lists of Acceptable Documents.

<Callout type="tip">
USCIS says completed I-9s and accompanying documents should be stored in a safe, secure location. Electronic generation, signing and retention are permitted when they comply with DHS regulations. USCIS encourages employers that create or store Forms I-9 electronically to review those standards.
</Callout>

---

## Preserve the wage calculation

For covered nonexempt workers, DOL Fact Sheet 21 calls for accurate identifying information and records of hours worked and wages earned. No particular record form is required.

The basic records include the employee's full name, Social Security number, address, sex and occupation, plus birth date if younger than 19. Record when the workweek begins, daily and weekly hours, pay basis, regular hourly rate, straight-time and overtime earnings, additions and deductions, total pay, payment date and pay period.

| FLSA record category | DOL retention guidance |
|---|---|
| Payroll records, collective bargaining agreements, sales and purchase records | Preserve for at least three years. |
| Records used to calculate wages, including time cards, wage-rate tables, work schedules and additions or deductions | Retain for two years. |

Any timekeeping method is acceptable if complete and accurate. If you use a fixed schedule and the employee works longer or shorter hours, record the actual hours worked. Keep the records available for DOL inspection.

---

## Retain the employment-tax support

The IRS employment-tax recordkeeping page says to keep these records for at least four years after filing the fourth quarter for the year. This is a tax-record rule, separate from the FLSA periods above.

The IRS list includes:

- The church's EIN and employees' names, addresses, Social Security numbers and occupations.
- Employment dates, wage amounts and payment dates.
- Withholding certificates, including Forms W-4.
- Tax-deposit dates, amounts and EFTPS acknowledgment numbers.
- Copies of filed returns and confirmation numbers.
- Fringe-benefit and expense-reimbursement records, including substantiation.
- Employee copies of Forms W-2 and W-2c returned as undeliverable.

The same IRS page identifies longer retention for certain tax-credit records. Check the credit-specific instructions if those records are in your files, rather than applying the ordinary period to every tax document.

---

## Retain personnel and applicant records

The EEOC's Part 1602 summary covers personnel and employment records that covered entities make or use. Examples include applications, accommodation requests, hiring and termination records, pay decisions and training selections.

For covered private employers, retain these records for one year from creation or the personnel action involved, whichever is later. For an involuntary termination, keep the terminated employee's personnel or employment records for one year from termination. The summary gives educational institutions a different period, so a church operating a school should check that category separately.

EEOC guidance also identifies three-year payroll retention under the ADEA, where applicable. Keep employee benefit plans and written seniority or merit systems for their full effective period and at least one year after termination under those requirements.

<Callout type="warning">
An EEOC discrimination charge changes the disposal decision. Preserve relevant personnel or employment records until final disposition of the charge or any lawsuit based on it, including appeals. An ordinary retention date does not override that requirement.
</Callout>

---

## Separate confidential medical information

Under the ADA's confidentiality rules, medical information belongs on separate forms and in separate medical files. The EEOC says not to place medical material in the regular personnel file. That confidentiality obligation continues after the person is no longer an applicant or employee.

For personal information generally, follow the FTC's practical security guidance. Limit access to what each person's job needs. Keep sensitive paper files and backups in a locked room or cabinet. Inventory electronic copies and outside service providers as well as the main filing cabinet.

Use Social Security numbers only for required and lawful purposes. Do not reuse them as routine employee identification numbers.

---

## Check before closing a file

Use these checks when employment ends or records reach a review date:

- [ ] Confirm the employment end date and compare both I-9 retention dates.
- [ ] Check the applicable wage, tax and personnel-record periods separately.
- [ ] Preserve records subject to an EEOC charge or related lawsuit through final disposition.
- [ ] Keep medical information separate and confidential after departure.
- [ ] Review who still needs access to sensitive files.
- [ ] When retention needs end, dispose of sensitive paper and electronic records securely, following the FTC's guidance.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"But all things must be done properly and in an orderly manner."* — 1 Corinthians 14:40 (LSB)
</Callout>
articles.excerpt: Keep church employee forms and records with precise federal retention periods, confidential storage and checks before disposal.
articles.title: HR Records and Required Forms
